The search for new physics beyond the Standard Model of particle physics is an ongoing effort in experimental work involving $B^0_s$ mesons. To discover such phenomena, researchers are utilizing advanced technologies to conduct precise measurements of $B^0_s$ lifetime components, which involve breaking down the meson's decay process into individual stages, and comparing the outcomes to theoretical predictions made using the Standard Model. By carrying out these experiments at the LHC using the LHCb detector, scientists have achieved very accurate measurements of $B^0_s$ lifetimes and low-energy particle physics forces, as well as constraints on hypothetical new particles that could affect the meson's behavior. With the upcoming upgrade of the LHC, where the collision rate is expected to increase by twenty times, researchers are working on implementing data processing improvements that will allow for more sensitive experiments, leading to a potential discovery of new physics forces or particles in the near future. As an example of the precision already achieved, the current understanding of $B^0_s$ morphology is so refined that it can distinguish between the Standard Model's subtle influence on the meson's decay stage, known as "Electric Dipole Moment," which results from a tiny distribution of charge associated with the W and Z bosons, and could be as sensitive as detecting new physics forces as weak as those occurring in high-energy particle collisions. With continued advancements in this field, researchers are confident in their ability to make even more precise measurements that will further explore the underlying physics forces behind the $B^0_s$ meson's behavior. The research presented in this paper has been reviewed by the International Journal of Modern Physics A, and it represents the findings from a comprehensive study conducted for the European Physical Society's Conferences Directors Group. The work involves a comprehensive examination of theoretical and experimental studies related to $B^0_s$ meson lifetime components, as well as discussions on the implications for new physics searches and potential improvements to the ongoing experiments at the LHC. This research focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem involving the optimal control of a stochastic partial differential equation (PDE). The main challenge arises from the presence of rough signals, which prevents the use of traditional finite element methods to solve the PDE. To address this issue, the paper develops a method of discretization that begins with a coarse scale solution and gradually refines the scale to solve the PDE. The scale refinement process is represented by a sequence of approximation problems defined by the solution of stochastic PDEs with increasingly finer scales. The paper proves that with proper choice of scale refinements, the solution of the control problem converges to the optimal solution. The key components of the method are the selection of the time step and the choice of the spatial scale refinement. The paper also provides numerical results illustrating the effectiveness of the method. The main contributions of the paper are the development of the scale refinement method, the proof of the convergence of the solution, and the discussion of the time step and spatial scale refinement. The paper further discusses the relationship between the method and other numerical solutions of the control problem. The research and results are relevant to applications in audio processing, such as the optimal separation of sound sources from raw wave signals. The paper is part of the author's doctoral research completed in 2023 under the supervision of M. Hairer and S. Krenger. This paper introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model to analyze non-linear patterns and significant shifts within time series data, specifically focusing on counting processes. Unlike static Poisson models, TV-PARX allows for dynamic interpretations of variables and incorporates exogenous factors. We enhance the model's performance by utilizing recursive equations based on conditional means, which enables the analysis of complex dynamics and allows for the inclusion of time-varying variables. Furthermore, TV-PARX includes mechanisms to deal with exogenous factors, both through mean shifting and changing rates, thus capturing changes in the underlying processes over time. This is further illustrated through the application of TV-PARX to analyzed datasets of electricity demand and hate crime rates. Empirical results show that the model effectively identifies non-linear dynamics and structural breaks in these datasets. Additionally, TV-PARX is compared to other models, including a time-varying Poisson ARIMA, TV-PARX with fixed covariates, and a static PARX model, through the use of AIC and BIC information criteria. This leads to the conclusion that TV-PARX is a valuable tool for counting process analysis, capable of capturing complex patterns and shifts, and can be readily used for policy evaluation and understanding the underlying processes of time series data. In our investigation, we apply this concept to a broader range of tasks and more intricate scenes, and we discover that Neural descriptor fields can be accurately trained when they are given explicit guidance through the study of optimal solutions. Additionally, we introduce an intuitive and efficient way to provide distance function predictions, which enables the learning of tasks from simply observing them, without the need for demonstrations. By integrating these innovations with the Neural descriptor fields framework, we devise a mechanism for learning tasks from observations, and through extensive simulations and a real-world experiment, we demonstrate its capabilities. Researchers studied the mass spectrum of meson states in QCD's three-dimensional version using a novel application of the light cone quantization method. To simplify the calculations, only the lowest self-energy correction was considered and assumptions were made about the meson's internal structure. This approach enabled the 3d AdS gravity scenario's Witten-like equation to be compared with 4d N=4 Super Yang-Mills theory's spectrum. Our findings show that the AdS boundary value $\left|z_c\right|$ significantly decreases from 4 to 2 dimensions, where it approaches a constant value. Furthermore, using the AdS/CFT correspondence, a dimensionless AdS soliton value was determined and found to be in agreement with $\left|z_c\right|$ when considering the 4d N=4 Super Yang-Mills theory. Additionally, both the 4d N=4 Super Yang-Mills theory and the 3d AdS gravity scenario's mass spectra share identical patterns when the AdS soliton's mass parameter varies. However, a dimensionless mass is required to accurately match the 4d N=4 Super Yang-Mills theory's mass spectrum with its 3d AdS gravity counterpart. Our research demonstrated that the AdS boundary value $\left|z_c\right|$ is a 4d N=4 Super Yang-Mills theory-specific constant, rather than a general 3d AdS gravity scenario constant. Consequently, we propose using the term "AdS soliton value" to describe $\left|z_c\right|$ within the 4d N=4 Super Yang-Mills theory framework. Our study also revealed that the meson mass spectrum in 3d QCD is not accurately described by the AdS/CFT correspondence, where the predicted mass spectrum remains constant and cannot be modified, in contrast to the 4d N=4 Super Yang-Mills theory. Our team is now planning to apply the light cone quantization method to the 4d N=4 Super Yang-Mills theory directly, with the aim of comparing its mass spectrum with both the 3d AdS gravity scenario and its own AdS soliton value. Our current understanding suggests that the AdS/CFT correspondence successfully reproduces the 4d N=4 Super Yang-Mills theory's AdS soliton value and mass spectrum when the AdS soliton mass parameter is varied. We investigate how well the approximate message passing algorithm for Z-2 synchronization performs compared to its theoretical limit, as defined by the TAP free energy. Our analysis occurs at a critical point where the performance of both the algorithm and its theoretical limit significantly change over time. Our results show that near this change point, the algorithm's performance differs from the theoretical limit by a factor of 3.5, which we believe is the minimum difference factor of 2. This investigation involves studying the statistics of phase transitions in random doped holographic error-correcting codes. We previously established that these transitions are abrupt, yet in this paper, we focus on examining the boundaries around these transitions. Our primary finding can be summarized as follows: the TAP free energy and the sparsity of the remaining errors exhibit power law characteristics with scaling factors that proportionally relate to -3.5 and -1.5, respectively, with respect to the distance from the transition boundary. We also examine the relationship between the TAP free energy and the APMP algorithm's performance, determining that this proportionate relationship remains constant, thereby explaining the algorithm's performance fluctuations near the transition boundaries. Our research builds upon the foundations established in our previous studies. We employ the TAP free energy as a measure to characterize the algorithm's performance near the transition boundaries, discovering that this energy's statistics at the edge of a transition demonstrate power law characteristics. This discovery enables us to broaden our previous results, which were specifically limited to the 3.5 scaling factor, to the entire range of scaling factors. This expansion involves developing an analytical formula that accurately captures these power law statistics, whereas our previous approach was restricted to the 1 scaling factor. Our research introduces a new model, referred to as the holographic vector multiple random doped code, which comprises a set of vector errors sourced from a random Gaussian distribution, a parameter called the doping level, and a linear combination of random matrices known as the holographic ensemble. This model serves as an analytical equivalent to the holographic error-correcting codes that we previously introduced. We also establish that the TAP state's dynamics in time can be mapped to a specific Z-2 synchronization problem, whereas the TAP state's statistics at any given time correspond to the outcome of the APMP algorithm on a specific Z-2 synchronization problem. We then examine the boundaries around which the TAP state's dynamics change, identifying these boundaries as the transitions between the frozen and active states in the holographic vector multiple random doped code. We developed a new method for estimating the aerosol content in the atmosphere's lower layer by using wide-field photometry data from a fully calibrated camera. We found that photometry from a camera with wide-field viewing can determine the aerosol depth in the lower atmosphere without needing absolute calibration, thanks to the system's sensitivity to changes in brightness and the uniform aerosol distribution. By applying this approach to data from the Sun planet camera at the Big Bear Solar Observatory and a all-sky camera at the Mauna Loa Solar Observatory, we calculated the aerosol depth in the lower atmosphere as 0.33+0.04-0.03 for a location at an altitude of 2.4 km and 0.25+0.03-0.02 for a location at an altitude of 4 km. Notably, this approach allows for continuous monitoring of the aerosol depth with a precision of 0.03 and provides a valuable tool for correlating aerosol depth with other atmospheric phenomena. Additionally, we discovered that the atmosphere's lower layer can be divided into two distinct aerosol populations with different optical depths based on the results from the Mauna Loa Solar Observatory. We also found that the aerosol depth in the lower atmosphere varies with altitude, pressure, and temperature but not with temperature differences or humidity. Moreover, we calculated the aerosol depth in the lower atmosphere as 0.13+0.03-0.02 for a location at an altitude of 4.4 km based on data from a sun photometer at the Mauna Loa Solar Observatory. We compared our estimates with previously published measurements from the same locations and found them to be in agreement, with the exception of one study that overestimated the aerosol depth by 0.03. We also used our method to validate the calibration of a sun photometer at the Mauna Loa Solar Observatory by calculating the difference in aerosol depth as 0.02+0.04-0.03 based on comparisons of daily measurements. We recommend using wide-field photometry from a fully calibrated camera as a simple and effective approach for continuously monitoring the aerosol depth in the lower atmosphere with a precision of 0.03. We propose using the term "aerosol optical depth at ground level" to describe this measurement and have made the code for our method and the raw data from the BBSO and Mauna Loa Solar Observatories publicly available. However, estimating the projection parameters required to connect a projection to the 3D model can be challenging, especially in complex scenes with many possible poses. To tackle this issue, we're introducing a method called projection grouping, which connects local projections by analyzing their edges, and ensures the resulting pose explanation aligns with the 3D model. By reducing the search space and focusing on projecting onto visible surface parts, our approach accelerates the estimation process while producing more accurate results compared to existing methods, especially in complex scenes. Furthermore, our approach generates a set of the most likely poses, ranking them by probability, which can be utilized for tasks like object manipulation. Our experiments demonstrate the benefits of projection grouping, and the code well as detailed experiment settings is available online. We're also introducing a new evaluation metric, the pose explanation accuracy, which measures the accuracy of estimated poses based on 3D annotations, and showcase the accuracy gained through various configurations. We're presenting preliminary research on projection grouping, and the underlying ideas can be applied to other 3D understanding tasks, such as autonomous driving. Our approach and evaluation metrics are designed with autonomy in mind, and we believe that projection grouping, coupled with the proposed evaluation framework, could facilitate the development of more efficient 3D object representation methods. This work introduces GLTDC, a method that enhances the popular Graphical Lasso for sparse inverse covariance estimation by incorporating latent variables and multiple data sources. We also derive a Generalized Granger causality framework that combines linear and nonlinear models, including those with sparse representations. Theoretical convictions in the effectiveness of GLTDC are validated through simulations, and it is shown to outperform existing methods, including the Graphical Lasso for multiple data and the Extended Graphical Lasso with latent variables. Furthermore, we provide a practical example of integrating multiple brain imaging data to identify brain network Granger causality. This example is pioneering in its kind and demonstrates the benefits of combining multiple, complementary data sources and models to uncover nonlinear causal relationships within complex networks. This research showcases the versatility of GLTDC and the Generalized Granger causality framework, and it is intended to be a starting point for further development of these methods in various applications. This study evaluates the performance of multiple numerical approaches for solving the Boltzmann equation in the context of a simple biomolecular system, the alanine dipeptide. Various methods, including the sub-diffusion algorithm, the multilevel method, the lattice Boltzmann algorithm, the optimal algorithm, the sub-diffusion algorithm with variable time steps, and the combined method, are compared to represent typical numerical solutions. The evaluation criteria consist of the formation of alpha helices, the distribution function, and the computational time. The results reveal that the multilevel method achieves the best balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. Although the sub-diffusion algorithm demonstrates the highest computational efficiency, it leads to numerical noises that interfere with the correct alpha helix structure formation. On the other hand, the lattice Boltzmann algorithm and the optimal algorithm fail to reproduce the correct distribution function. Furthermore, increasing the time step in the sub-diffusion algorithm with variable time steps initially improves computational efficiency but eventually loses effectiveness due to numerical inaccuracy. The assessment presented in this study provides a practical guide for biomolecular chemists and physicists to choose the most suitable numerical solutions for their specific problems, ensuring that the methods used are both computationally efficient and accurate. The findings also highlight the limitations of current numerical methods and the need for further development, such as the optical algorithm and the coupled method, to better model complex biomolecular interactions and dynamics. The evaluation process itself is seen as part of the broader assessment, as it involved selecting the most computationally efficient and accurate numerical solutions from a pool of 12 diverse methods, a strategy that can be applied to other similar evaluations in the future. The study's focus on a simple alanine dipeptide system allows for a thorough examination of the numerical solutions, whereas the proposed evaluation process is scalable enough to be applied to more complex biomolecular systems consisting of thousands of atoms. The most performing method, the multilevel method, is then utilized to simulate the alanine dipeptide system with solvent, a more intricate and comprehensive model of the system already examined. The resulting alpha helix structure formation and surrounding solvent distribution function dynamics are found to be consistent with experimental data and previous molecular dynamics simulations. The multilevel method's effectiveness is attributed to the combination of the sub-diffusion algorithm and the variable time steps, which together prevent numerical noises that interfere with correct alpha helix structure formation while simultaneously achieving the highest computational efficiency among the compared methods. The proposed evaluation process and the most efficient method are seen as valuable contributions

Importance assessment in multilayer networks can be performed using the Kirchhoff or Shimojama method, but these algorithms fail to consider inter-layer constraints, offering complete networks for calculation. To address this limitation, we develop the Kirchhoff-Shimojama method for multilayer networks with inter-layer constraints, breaking down the process into sequential sub-problems to compute node importance. This involves determining equivalent resistance in single-layer networks and combining them for the overall network importance assessment. We then apply and extend this approach for multilayer networks with inter-layer constraints, demonstrating its efficiency with large-scale datasets. Experimental results demonstrate a significant speed-up for the Kirchhoff-Shimojama algorithm relative to the original methods, indicating its improved computational efficiency while maintaining accuracy. Furthermore, we analyze and validate the approach using mathematical theories and realistic datasets, highlighting its practical implications and potential applications. The proposed algorithm has been made available for public use through the NetworkX library in Python. The associated code, data, and further information are available at the networkx repository on GitHub. This study investigates how the pressure within a cavity beneath an aircraft surface affects dynamics, specifically for surface seals near high-speed jets. The generalized Witten effect is investigated in quantum gravity, where the Witten effect refers to the generation of a charge distribution when a condensed state of zero-momentum massive scalar field is broken due to the presence of a curved spacetime. This investigation considers a state of the scalar field that is both charged and has zero momentum, and it examines how this state's interaction with an arbitrary gravitational field results in a specified distribution of charged states. The generated charged state includes not just the original charge but also additional charges linked to the scalar field's conformal properties. These additional charges behave similarly to the original charge but are differentiated by their reaction to the scalar field's self-interaction. The impact of the self-interaction on the original charge can be determined by integrating the reaction of the additional charges to the self-interaction, which allows for the distinction between self-compliant and self-repelling charges. The effect of the self-interaction on the additional charges is characterized by its depth, which is proportional to the AdS space's compact dimension. The relationship between the additional charges and the scalar field's self-interaction indicates that the self-interaction's strength is linked to the central charge of the dual conformal field theory. Furthermore, the spatial arrangement of electrons supports our observation of long-range ferromagnetic ordering. Moreover, we found that cubanite's electronic structure is resistant to alteration by either fast cooling from high temperatures or slow cooling from low temperatures. This resilience is exceptional among transition metal oxides and hydroxides. In a study involving a quantum dot within a silicon microid cavity, controlled Rabi beating through near-resonant illumination was achieved, and several factors that affect this phenomenon have been identified, including its dependence on laser frequency, cavity detuning, and the quantum dot's energy levels. Unlike typical applications, the driving laser's frequency can be adjusted during operation, and as a result, a novel mechanism affecting Rabi oscillations becomes apparent. By adjusting the laser frequency, the authors demonstrate the ability to switch between two different Rabi oscillation patterns, centered around the microid cavity's frequency, and observe mechanical modes connected to the quantum dot's levels through a phenomenon known as dressed mode architecture. Furthermore, the silicon microid cavity's high quality factor allows the authors to extend Rabi beating periods up to 100 times that of its natural frequency. The findings present a versatile quantum system capable of maintaining prolonged Rabi oscillations through adjustment of the driving laser frequency, and the associated mechanical cavity's high quality factor may facilitate efficient energy transfer between remote levels in quantum dots. The approach also offers a mechanism for resolving spectral disorders arising from the random alignment of quantum dots relative to mechanical cavities in silicon quantum dot arrays. As a result of the research, a theoretical model of the driven quantum dot-coupled acoustic cavity system has been developed, which incorporates the effects of photon-assisted tunneling and higher-order sidebands on the Rabi oscillations. Additionally, the study's limitations and potential improvements, such as reducing dissipation losses, are discussed. The approach demonstrates a unique combination of quantum mechanics and mechanics, with an anticipated application in developing robust solid-state quantum processors. The analysis involves single-pass generation of quadrature-symmetric even-cat states, whose minimal uncertainty occurs at 2.414, a value that falls short of the ideal 2 for coherent states. The success probability for producing these even-cat states varies significantly depending on the generation method, with a 10-fold difference observed between beam splitters and parametric amplifiers for the same number of pump pulses. This interpretation offers a novel understanding of the Weyl tensor's properties and the 3rd law's entropic formulation. Furthermore, it provides a framework for analyzing and solving Einstein's equations in the presence of axially symmetric, self-gravitating systems. This approach has been successfully applied to the non-linear regime of both Einstein-Hilbert action and conformally coupled scalar field theories. It is observed that the Weyl tensor's coefficients' singularities at the event horizon can be described by a Dirac delta function and an individual invariant coefficient's order-$n$ singularity may be attributed to a $\delta$-function times an $n-1$ order polynomial. This finding is related to the physics of the 3rd law of black hole physics, specifically how the 3rd law governs the coefficients of the Weyl tensor's singularities at the event horizon. We introduce a novel variational approach to approximating distributional objects, such as Gaussian distributional polymers, using a generative adversarial network. In contrast to existing methods that represent a polymer as being composed of specific monomers, our framework instead seeks the most likely composition of the polymer, assuming it has gone through a process known as equilibrium sampling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our variational approach by approximating the conditional distribution of a polymer's sequence given its properties, using a relatively simple property--sequence length--as an example. Furthermore, our approach is capable of accurately predicting sequences of arbitrary length that conform to a specific distribution, even in cases where the distribution is non-stationary along the sequence. We have publicly available code to replicate our results at the address indicated in the citation below. We believe this new variational approach provides a useful tool for inferring the composition of complex objects on the basis of limited information. We hope it also paves the way for further study on the relationship between generative adversarial networks and distributional objects. We would like to thank our researchers for their valuable input and assistance with this work. We view this effort as a starting point for a broader project aimed at developing variational methods that can approximate high-level structural aspects of objects that have multiple complex structures, encompassing both spatial and temporal domains. We plan to extend this framework for future work, exploring its potential in modeling objects with multiple structures that evolve over time. We aim to make the framework more efficient, investigating options such as using a fewer number of variational objects or integrating the variation process with the generative adversarial network itself. We will test and evaluate our approach on synthetic data sets created using the Wright-Fisher process and the birth-death process, as well as real-world data sets consisting of electronic music genres and mathematical objects known as Feynman graphs. We anticipate this new variational approach will find applications in fields such as biology, physics, and social science, in addition to its potential in modeling electronic music genres and mathematical objects. Recent attention unet variations, such as DDUnet, have achieved significant performance improvements in medical image segmentation tasks. However, the primary challenge of consistently segmenting large-scale structures, like the wall of the esophagus, remains unsolved when using these models. This study introduces a novel attention unet framework called Dilated Dense Attention Unet, which is a variant of the original network, and successfully applies it to the task of automatically identifying tumors from endoscopic images of the esophagus. The proposed network enhances segmentations of large structures by leveraging a two-tier attention mechanism and significantly reduces computational costs. Experimentally, our model demonstrates a substantial decrease in both memory consumption and training time while achieving the best results compared to other competing methods, based on metrics such as Dice coefficients and Ascension metrics. This research provides a preliminary step towards addressing the difficult task of modeling long-range relationships in images and offers a solution that can be refined for other challenging medical image segmentation tasks. In highly multilingual communities like Singapore, understanding how people switch between languages and use them in different contexts is vital. This knowledge can be valuable for developing language technologies that reflect real-world language use, as seen in social media platforms. To that end, this study aims to collect high-quality, multilingual text data for Singaporean users by gathering Twitter posts in four languages: English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil. We then employed a machine learning model to analyze these tweets and identified patterns of language use among users, including how they switch between languages and use them in different contexts. Furthermore, we used a statistical model to predict the probability of users switching languages in certain contexts. This research has several significant contributions. Firstly, it presents one of the largest datasets of Twitter posts ever reported in Singapore, consisting of over 290,000 texts in four languages. Secondly, it offers novel insights into language use patterns in Singapore, including how users switch between languages and use them in different contexts. Thirdly, it has made the code and data set available for future research into language use dynamics in multilingual communities. Lastly, it demonstrates the effectiveness of a specific machine learning model in predicting language use among Singaporeans, which can be refined for other similar populations. In addition, we observed an unusually high frequency of language switching in Singapore, which we found to be associated with specific contexts, particularly when users are referring to food or describing their daily activities. In such cases, users often switch between languages within the same tweet, which we found to be more common among younger users and those who speak multiple languages as part of their regular communication. Notably, we discovered that language switching is not simply a random event, but rather it is governed by its own set of dynamics and probabilities, which we were able to predict using a statistical model. This research and the associated data set have significant implications for NLP researchers and the industry, which often struggle with developing models that account for real-world language use dynamics, particularly in multilingual communities. The surge in visually impaired users and social media sharing has created a significant need for accurately generating image descriptions. Compared to text classification and other sequence generation tasks, image description generation possesses a unique challenge due to the intricate nature of visual elements that require consideration. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring the capabilities of generative adversarial networks (GANs). However, current GAN-based models fail to generate precise descriptions in relation to the visual content, likely due to the difficulty in designing a critic that can effectively distinguish real from fictitious data. To overcome this difficulty, we propose a novel GAN-based approach called Deep Aspect Image Description Generator (DAIDDG), which enables a critic to focus on specific aspects of an image by implementing a segment-by-segment strategy. Furthermore, DAIDDG incorporates a description generator that leverages attention mechanisms to generate detailed and precise descriptions. Experimental evaluations conducted on the Flickr30k dataset demonstrate that DAIDDG achieves superior performance compared to existing GAN-based models and conventional baselines. A qualitative analysis of DAIDDG's generated descriptions reveals that it is capable of accurately describing complex scenes and distinguishing between primary and auxiliary aspects of an image. To facilitate further research, the proposed DAIDDG model is applicable to various description generation tasks, including both short and lengthy descriptions. Researchers have created a method to compute the energy loss functions for bulk tantalum oxides by accurately modeling local field effects and spin-orbit coupling. The resulting model shows a marked improvement over previous approaches, especially in the higher energy range, and reveals the emergence of a forbidden region in the energy loss function of the bulk oxide. This finding resonates with experimental observations of a missing photoelectron peak in the energy distribution of tantalum oxides and suggests that the oxide's energy surface can alter in response to environmental changes. Furthermore, the new model highlights the energy loss function's sensitivity to the simulation of local field effects, providing a practical tool for exploring the impact of environmental changes on the energy loss functions of tantalum and oxide layers at the atomic interface. The success of this model has been validated against previous methods and experimental data from electron energy loss spectroscopy. The method has further applications in the computation of other optical properties of tantalum oxides. The approach can also be extended to model energy loss functions for oxide interfaces in general, and is particularly useful for studying the spatial distribution of valence band holes in oxides. This study has two objectives: it develops a method to automatically analyze teaching speech from videos, and it explores the factors that influence the semantic meaning conveyed in speech during teaching. To achieve this, a text-based representation of speech was created using a vector semantic space, and variations in demonstration types, audio instructions, subtasks, and errors were investigated through experimental designs. The results show that the proposed vector semantic space effectively captures the underlying structure and concepts of speech during teaching, and it can be used to compare the semantic meaning of speech in different conditions. This research contributes to the development of speech-based teaching models and provides insights into the underlying semantics of teaching speech. It also demonstrates the utility of the proposed method in comparing the semantic meaning of speech in different scenarios, and it presents a data set of vector semantic spaces for speech during teaching tasks. This research paves the way for addressing the generative aspects of teaching speech, and it presents an explicit representation of the underlying concepts of teaching speech that can be fine-tuned to reflect the specific characteristics of particular tasks and domains. This is achieved by incorporating the proposed vector semantic space into a sequence-generation model, and by exploring the addition of domain-specific and task-specific components. The resulting model is a hybrid generation model that incorporates the underlying concepts of teaching speech, and it is evaluated through the completion of instruction-based subtasks and teaching demonstrations. The outcome shows that the proposed hybrid model effectively captures the underlying structure of teaching speech and successfully generalizes to novel tasks and domains by incorporating the underlying concepts of teaching speech. The experimental design also compares different generation models and architectures, and it investigates the impact of different speech streams and instruction types on the proposed vector semantic space. optimal transport principles, to solve a significant problem in quantum field theory.
The proposed framework, based on a deep learning formulation of Euler-Arnold equations,
efficiently solves a critical optimization problem and leverages the intrinsic
geometry of the target domain to enhance solution accuracy.
By incorporating a gradient-based update method for the optimal transport distance,
the approach achieves a unified solution to the Euler-Arnold and optimal transport equations.
The effectiveness and advantages of this method are demonstrated through comprehensive
numerical experiments, showing its substantial gains in solution accuracy, as well as
comparable computational costs, as existing solutions. The proposed approach has far-
reaching implications for the solution of Euler-Arnold equations in various applications.

Conversational systems, found in user interfaces such as virtual assistants, pose a significant challenge to validation through automated testing frameworks. The dynamic nature of user input and the inability to predict exact conversation paths makes validation of these systems' behavior a complex task. As a result, developers often prioritize testing the individual components of the system rather than testing its interactive aspects. This approach may lead to software delivering subpar user experiences and inaccurate responses to user queries. To address this challenge, we propose an approach that generates random conversations to test the system's behavior and flexibility in response to unexpected user input. Through the use of a automated testing framework called VexBot, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by subjecting the Amazon Alexa virtual assistant to a large set of randomly generated conversations. Our results show that VexBot effectively identifies critical issues associated with the flexibility of Alexa in responding to unexpected user input. Furthermore, our research highlights the potential risks of relying on deterministic design patterns in conversational systems and highlights the potential benefits of using unconventional conversation flows to improve user engagement. Additionally, we provide system developers with potential solutions to address these challenges. Our research and testing methodology are fully reproducible, and our findings are expected to contribute to the advancement of testing methodologies for conversational systems. Our VexBot framework is available for public use, and we encourage other researchers and system developers to utilize it in the future. Our proposed GAPE module integrates a dynamic aspect preference enhancement framework for user preference learning, incorporating both historical interaction aspects and explicit user preferences. This approach leverages a novel two-way gated network that efficiently fuses multiple sources of information, thereby enhancing the representation of user preference. The GAPE module is part of a recommendation system architecture that utilizes user-specific embedded vectors and advances the concept of enhancing user preference by aligning it with historical interaction aspects. Unlike existing methods that focus on enhancing aspect representation based on user preference, our proposed framework develops a more sophisticated strategy that dynamically combines the two, thereby improving user preference learning. Our approach is particularly effective in addressing new user interactions and learns to prioritize both historical and current preferences dynamically. Experimentation on real-world datasets highlights the superiority of our approach over competing methods. Our proposed GAPE module provides a unique contribution to user preference learning and recommends a suitable structure for future recommendation systems. Medical imaging analyses often rely on neural networks, and to ensure their reliability, it's crucial to assess their robustness. We investigate the robustness of MRI analysis models to data combinations they haven't been trained on. Our research discovered significant variability in models' performance when evaluating them on new data from different sources, highlighting the need for robustness testing. To simplify robustness testing, we created a synthetic, multi-site MRI dataset by combining publicly accessible datasets. This dataset comprises 500 scans without apparent anomalies and has been labeled for brain volume measurements. Our findings showed that models perform poorly on unfamiliar data combinations, even within the same population group. To improve models, we recommend training them on data combinations different from their original training data. To facilitate robustness testing and improve models, we present a framework that combines data combinations with model performance, along with the code and synthetic dataset used in our research. This initiative is the first step towards evaluating and enhancing the robustness of neural networks in medical imaging, and it paves the way for investigating other robustness aspects, such as anisotropic data. Our work and resources are designed to be beneficial to the medical imaging community, particularly in relation to brain analysis using MRI scans. To build on this research, visit https://robustai.github.io/medical_robustness/. We are committed to continuing this research and encouraging further exploration of robustness in medical imaging. This paper introduces a novel framework for solving network-based cooperative optimization problems involving multiple agents, where each agent has a separate subproblem to solve, and these subproblems are interconnected through a network structure. The framework's requirements ensure that solving the combined problem is equivalent to solving the individual subproblems for a minimum total cost, with constraints linking the subproblems according to their connection in the network. The study focuses on optimizing the performance of a robust and distributed algorithm previously developed for a similar problem, by enhancing the algorithm to address additional considerations such as delayed information, degree constraints, and node prioritization. The improvements are demonstrated to result in better convergence and performance of the algorithm. Simulations based on real-world data illustrate the benefits of the new framework and algorithm. The study's methods and results are applicable to a wide range of applications involving cooperative optimization among multiple agents, including those related to electric power grids. The underlying idea and algorithmic framework are highly versatile and can be adapted to various problems and systems beyond the examples presented. The Motivation Dynamics theory, initially developed for single-agent scenarios, has been successfully expanded to accommodate multiple agents. This advancement provides a comprehensive decision-making model, incorporating both individual motivations and social interactions. In the context of multiple agents, the framework's capabilities include facilitating rendezvous and optimizing system performance through efficient assignment of tasks and resources. To demonstrate the practical applications of this extended model, we present a case study where we use the Motivation Dynamics framework to guide a robot in finding and collaborating with other robots already present in a given environment, with the common goal of completing specific tasks efficiently. By incorporating this model into a controller, we show that the resulting system is capable of achieving optimal task completion through active search and successful task execution, outperforming a random search approach and showcasing robust performance in the presence of varying robot populations. Through this integrated design of controllers and robots, we highlight the potential benefits of motivated robotic systems in complex, dynamic environments. Experimental data from a 20-robot test scenario is presented, along with a simulation study examining the overall performance of this motivated system when the number of robots varies significantly. This includes a discussion on the observed effects of changed robot populations on task completion rates, average task completion time, and total reward earned. The Motivation Dynamics framework has been publicly available since 2021 at https://motivations.github.io/. The related code for the controller, robot architecture, and simulation tools can be found on the following GitHub repositories: https://github.com/motivations/mds, https://github.com/motivations/md-robot, and https://github.com/motivations/md-sim. The experimental data from the 20-robot test scenario is available on the following dataset repository: https://data.nature.com/papers/10.1038/s42005-024-00115-3.dat. This paper is concerned with an elliptic system of partial differential equations, consisting of the Laplace equations $ \Delta u_i = f_i (x, v_1, \ldots, v_n)$ for $i = 1, \ldots, n$, where $v$ represents the vector $(u_1, \ldots, u_n)$. When the right-hand side function $f_i$ satisfies the condition $ |f_i (x, v)| \leq \psi_i (x) \big( 1 + |v|^\gamma \big)$ for $(x, v) \in \Omega$, with certain restrictions on the functions $\psi_i$ and the domain $\Omega$, it is demonstrated that there exists a solution $u \in T^2_\delta (\Omega)$ to the system. This result represents an enhancement of the previous solution existence theorem, which required the right-hand side functions $f_i$ to satisfy the bound $ |f_i (x, v)| \leq \psi_i (x)$ for $(x, v) \in \Omega$. In addition, this enhanced result is illustrated with an example featuring the system of Laplace equations, where the right-hand side functions $f_i$ are defined as $f_i (x, v) = |v_{i-1}|^{1/2} \delta (x)$ for $i = 1, \ldots, n$, and it is shown that it obeys the desired condition following suitable choice of the weight functions $\psi_i$. Furthermore, it is proven that there exists a solution $u \in T^2_\delta (\Omega)$ to the resulting system of partial differential equations. This solution satisfies the property $\big( |u_1| + \cdots + |u_n| \big) (x) \leq C (1 + |x|)^{1-n}$ for $x \in \Omega$, and it is also demonstrated that it minimizes the energy functional $\mathcal E (u, \Omega)$ among all possible solutions $u \in T^2_\delta (\Omega)$. This represents an enhancement of the previous solution existence theorem, which only considered the case $n = 2$. A numerical example illustrates the potential benefits of considering incompatibility, showing that the optimal policy can be more effective at achieving temporal consistency than simply pairing donors and recipients with the current state in mind. Finally, we outline the potential applications and challenges of incorporating incompatibility into pairings for other collaborative scenarios. We also discuss the potential extensions to our model, including incorporating multiple agents and asymmetric reward structures. This research paves the way for various extensions and incorporates pairing decisions with future-state preferences, leading to a natural extension of the problem to recursive utility. This, in turn, enables us to analyze the relationship between our model and recursive utility, especially in the context of temporally consistent incompatibility. Ultimately, our work provides a foundational framework for examining pairings with future-state preferences and incompatibility, offering a meaningful contribution to the field of decision-making under incompatibility. We also present an algorithm to compute the value function and decision policy under incompatibility, which we refer to as the Successive Approximation Policy Iteration (SAPI). This SAPI algorithm is proven to converge to the optimal policy and value function. Notably, we demonstrate that the value function resulting from the SAPI algorithm exhibits a Markovian property, providing a key insight into designing our model. We take advantage of this property to extend our model to consider the arrival of new state-incompatibility pairs, which, in turn, enables us to analyze the relationship between the value function and the recursive utility. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our SAPI algorithm through multiple numerical examples. This work proposes a novel complex-valued deep neural network, termed the Characteristic Element Neural Network (CENN), which efficiently models unstable hydrodynamic phenomena such as Rayleigh--Bénard instability. Consisting of multiple characteristic elements, CENN accurately replicates unstable fluid dynamics behaviors by capturing their spatial structures. We introduce a unique weight update method for the network's elements to enhance stability during training and operation. Our CENN model achieves this breakthrough without relying on traditional numerical solvers, making it a significant advancement in the field. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of CENN by comparing it to a complex-valued LSTM network using a precise solution as a training target. This comparison shows that CENN exhibits better performance than LSTM in predicting the evolution of these unstable phenomena. This research paves the way for a deeper understanding of how deep neural networks can be modified to effectively model complex, time-dependent physical processes governed by partial differential equations. This study is an initial step towards developing a general framework for modeling Rayleigh--Bénard instability via nonlinear partial differential equations. This approach has the potential to be expanded upon, enabling the application of deep learning to a wide range of complex physical processes marked by nonlinear interactions and wave breakdown phenomena. We introduce a novel mechanism for multiagent learning that incorporates the concept of iteratively dominated actions, drawing on the principle of cognitive architectures where thoughts influence each other, to create a framework for dynamic decision-making. Within this framework, we show that a specific algorithm, Policy Mixture Learning, causes individuals to relinquish pointless action choices in response to observing peers' behaviors. By doing so, they reduce pointless effort and accelerate the convergence towards optimal strategies by eliminating dominated actions. When paired with algorithms like FALSE and SOLORLS for peer learning, Policy Mixture Learning yields improved performance, action choice efficiency, and fair outcomes in various scenarios, including both single-component and component-switching scenarios. Experimental evidence, supplemented by theoretical support, confirms that this algorithm facilitates efficient learning and adaptable component selection through efficient action choice. In addition, we share a cognitive learning model that provides theoretical insights into the dynamics of policy mixture learning. This model reveals crucial information about the conditions under which learning from the distribution of peer actions, combined with self-experience, leads to efficient action choice. This efficient action choice, in turn, contributes to efficient learning and component adaptation in dynamic environments. We also explore the parameter settings that influence action choice probability in Policy Mixture Learning, revealing that all default parameters, with the exception of action choice temperature, result in action choice probabilities that are nearly uniform across all possible actions, except in scenarios where learning from peer actions and self-experience leads to a shift in these probabilities. We further investigate the emergence of action choice patterns that are consistent with cognitive biases, such as the representation of multiple possible actions as a mixture of precise policies. By incorporating the concept of iteratively dominated actions into policy mixture learning, we observe associated action choice patterns that reflect the underlying structure of an environment, demonstrating that the mechanism of policy mixture learning is robust across various cognitive architectures and learning algorithms, while leading to cognitive biases that reflect the underlying dynamics of an environment. We conclude by discussing the implications of policy mixture learning for our understanding of multiagent learning, cognitive architectures, and the emergence of cognitive biases, as well as its potential applications in designing learning systems that are capable of adapting to changing environments. We also explore potential avenues for future research, including the investigation of policy mixture learning in scenarios with multiple populations, the integration of external influences on learning, and the development of cognitive architectures that incorporate action choice temperatures. We further propose that policy mixture learning provides a framework for explaining cognitive biases through the lens of action choice temperatures, offering a quantitative approach to cognitive bias analysis. With the ability to track the exact unconditional probability of a specific network configuration developing over time, we've been able to explore various unconditional network evolution properties in depth. Our previous research revealed that the probability of a specific network configuration arising can be precisely calculated using special functions like the Gamma function. This paper makes available to the public the code used to calculate consistency metrics for fit assessment, written primarily in Python with some components in C, and is designed to be used with the HH PDF fit dataset. The code, which complements the content of [1], calculates consistency metrics, including consistency coefficients, predicted polynomial fits, the standard deviation of divergence, the predicted standard deviation of divergence, the 99th percentile of absolute density, the 99th percentile of density density, and the implied alpha_s bar. It further enables calculation of consistency metrics at various energy scales, including those pertinent to Drell-Yan and top-quark production, using Monte Carlo methods. The code is compatible with popular PDF fitting packages, namely NNPDF, ABSPDF, and HHPDF, following the standard PDF fitting protocol. Moreover, it leverages the PyPDF fit management package to streamline the process. The code can be acquired via GitHub, accompanied by clear installation instructions, and allows for both local and cloud-based execution of fits following standard PDF fitting protocols. The consistency metrics themselves, detailed in [1], necessitate an understanding of DGLAP evolution, PDF evolution, and factorization theorems. The code framework itself, besides enabling fit assessment, demonstrates how to integrate large-scale projects utilizing object-oriented programming, while the utility of the code serves as an illustration of how "scientific code engineering" facilitates reproducibility in physics research. The code and accompanying guidelines can serve as a blueprint for integrating large-scale projects utilizing object-oriented programming, thereby facilitating reproducibility in physics research. The content of this paper is focused on [1] and comprises Chapter 3 of the associated PhD thesis. We introduce the variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework, a general method that refines policy gradient estimates through experience data reutilization. We then customize the VRER framework to address policy gradient estimation challenges in reinforcement learning. Within this structured approach, we derive a specific variance-reduced estimator and combine it with existing advantages of experience replay, yielding a gradient estimation algorithm called sampled cumulative variance reduced policy gradient (SCVRPG). We further establish the convergence rate of SCVRPG utilizing the corrected function approximation error term, achieving a superior convergence rate of $O(1/n^2 \log Q(n))$ for the mean squared error of the estimated policy. This improvement is demonstrated to be an enhanced result compared to the current state-of-the-art methods through rigorous comparison. Finally, we test the efficacy of our proposed SCVRPG algorithm through numerical experiments, showcasing its performance in multiple scenarios. This includes evaluating the effectiveness of incremental learning in SCVRPG and comparing it with alternative state-of-the-art methods such as SARSMAx and CJSRGx through rigorous statistical analysis. This analysis reveals the statistical significance of the improvement achieved by our SCVRPG algorithm over these competing methods based on the 5% level of significance. This represents the superior performance of SCVRPG when considering both its theoretical and practical convergence rates as well as its incremental learning capabilities. This makes SCVRPG an appealing choice for complex high-dimensional problems. This research is an extension of the variance-reduced experience replay algorithm proposed in the initial stage of this research, resulting in additional findings that were initially obtained. This additional work led to further significant enhancements, prompting the extension of the initial research stage through the conduct of additional experiments and the development of new theories. This resulted in the creation of a new algorithm, the sampled cumulative variance reduced policy gradient (SCVRPG), which not only improved upon the initial variance-reduced experience replay algorithm but also achieved superior performance when compared to the current state-of-the-art methods, leading to the publication of the extended research findings in this manuscript. A key aspect of conversational AI involves generating relevant dialogue based on initial statements. To achieve this, the underlying assumption is that the system possesses a basic understanding of the other party's mental state, specifically the ability to recognize unexpressed thoughts and intentions. To investigate this, a simple generative model was developed which generates dialogue that considers the listener's unexpressed thoughts. To evaluate the system's ability to mimic this kind of dialogue, a dataset was created consisting of dialogue generated using the model, as well as the same dialogue with the system's perspective reversed. Human assessors were then tasked with distinguishing between the two versions of dialogue. The goal of this research is to lay the groundwork for further investigation into how conversational dialogue processes with a focus on the theory of mind. Moreover, the newly developed dataset can be utilized to test various conversational dialogue systems with respect to theory of mind. Furthermore, the current approach provides a straightforward framework for generating dialogue that considers the listener's unexpressed thoughts, which can be applied to various dialog-based tasks and games that require a similar level of understanding. To demonstrate the flexibility of this approach, the development team successfully modified the model to generate dialogue that considers multiple mental states at once, as well as a variant of the dialog-based game TextCall in which the system anticipates the user's unexpressed thoughts and introduces them into the conversation. The resulting system showed an observable improvement over a random control group in the game. The underlying model also exhibited a notable ability to engage in superfluous conversation, which can be enabled or disabled at will. When disabled, the system shows a decrease in overall dialogue generation. When enabled, the system shows an increase in dialogue generation, but the content becomes less relevant. When enabled with a specific dialing pattern, the system's performance converges with the random control group. The research and the associated dataset both contribute to a better comprehension of theory of mind in conversational AI. To accelerate the evaluation of Newtonian gravity for molecular systems with multiple bodies, a new algorithm called MG-GLAM is proposed, achieving a significant boost in performance for large systems through the use of a well-conditioned basis of molecular vectors. Compared to the original code, MG-GLAM exhibits approximately ten times improved computational efficiency, with further gains possible for large molecular simulations. This efficient algorithm takes advantage of molecular characteristics to manipulate a minimal set of basis molecules, thereby reducing the number of N-body interactions needed for accurate results. The name "MG-GLAM" originates from the methods for Gaussian-like atomic masses, with further developments in the form of MG-GLAM-REU and MG-GLAM-LMP. These codes have been utilized to model various chemical reactions, including nitrogen oxide dimer decomposition, cyanogen dimer dissociation, and trimer formation from cyanogen and nitrogen oxide. Furthermore, MG-GLAM has been applied to study atomic arrangements in metal-ammonia compounds and the conductivities of oxides in molecular hydrogen and oxygen reactions. The code has also been used to simulate molecular dynamics and electronics in magnesium with embedded hydrogen and oxygen atoms. The efficiency gains in MG-GLAM are attributed to multiple strategies, including the utilization of a minimal set of basis molecules, the incorporation of molecular connectivity information, and the use of efficient numerical integration techniques. This algorithm has the potential to extend the reach of N-body simulations in chemistry by making them several orders of magnitude more computationally feasible. The code for MG-GLAM is available online. The developments in MG-GLAM-REU and MG-GLAM-LMP are discussed, along with the code's limitations and potential future enhancements. The impact of force field parameter variation on the results is also demonstrated. The approach presented in MG-GLAM has implications for the integration of classical and quantum mechanics in molecular simulations. A comparison is drawn with related approaches, along with a discussion of the relationships between the basis sets employed. The code's efficiency is examined in relation to other force fields, with a focus on the effects of basis set change and parameter adjustment. The performance of MG-GLAM is evaluated on workloads consisting of chemical reactions and molecular dynamics, along with a detailed analysis of its scalability and performance characteristics. The potential applications of MG-GLAM in the simulation of classical-quantum hybrid systems is explored, along with the benefits of using a minimal basis set in quantum systems. The behavior of the algorithm with multiple levels of basis set change is examined

We introduce WorkingWiki, a fully-automated system designed to simplify the collaboration on scientific manuscripts and software by leveraging a wiki platform. WorkingWiki enhances the standard wiki features to accurately track textual material flows, incorporate automated version control, and provide easy access to collaborative history through Git. This approach facilitates seamless documentation and software development by minimizing distractions from mundane tasks. As a result, authors can focus exclusively on developing content and software. To illustrate WorkingWiki's capabilities, we present a concrete application where we transformed the Mizar proof system's development environment by incorporating WorkingWiki. This effort resulted in a substantial improvement in the efficiency of developing and verifying sequences of logical theorems, as demonstrated by a sample test. Furthermore, WorkingWiki's documentation, source code, and an example of using it to develop the Mizar system are all available at https://workingwiki.gitorious.org/. More information about WorkingWiki can be found at http://workingwiki.logicol.com/. By showing the benefits of integrating Git, WorkingWiki encourages other researchers to adopt a similar collaboration framework. Moreover, it is intended to be a versatile system that can be applied across various domains. We propose WorkingWiki as a scalable, open-source infrastructure for concurrent development in any field of mathematics. In addition to its scientific applications, WorkingWiki also offers valuable insights for web-based wiki development. In particular, it suggests the value of combining a wiki with a full-featured version control system and provides a potential solution for managing open-source software development in academia. This is achieved by generating executable code from the underlying source files, thereby linking the formalized content to relevant educational and research resources. As a result, WorkingWiki enables the discovery of relevant educational materials and research related to its underlying content, thus making a convenient classroom tool that can be integrated with existing educational curricula. Ultimately, WorkingWiki's modular structure allows its components to be used separately, offering various customization options for users, institutions, and developers. We investigate the implications of ultralight dark matter (ULDM) that couples to neutrinos for its behavior during the early universe, particularly examining the effects on neutrino physics and the formation of density fluctuations. Using a general effective theory approach, we develop a novel numerical method to maintain consistency with the neutrino sector's behavior. This allows us to explore the ULDM impact on neutrino oscillations, neutrino abundance, and cosmological density fluctuations. Our study reveals that neutrino-driven phonon fluctuations can dominate the ULDM density field, leading to a loss of coherence and the formation of ULDM lumps. As a result, the typical ULDM mass is shifted from $\mu$ to $M_{\rm J} \approx \left( M_{\rm Pl}^2 / (60 \pi^2 \bar{N}^2) \right)^{1/3}$, with implications for its behavior in the early universe and its ability to influence neutrino oscillations and drive density fluctuations in the early universe. Notably, this mass scale maps the phonon fluctuation mean free path to a characteristic length scale, leading to a universal density fluctuation spectrum with a kinetic energy distribution indexed by the number of neutrinos, and results in a neutrino-free 'window' in the mass range $10^{-12} \text{eV} \lesssim \mu \lesssim 10^{-8} \text{eV}$. Furthermore, this mass range corresponds to a phase of oscillatory expansion for the early universe, with a duration of approximately $10^3$ years, influencing the cosmological abundance of neutrinos and affecting the formation of structure in the universe. Additionally, this study predicts novel effects on bootstrap parallax measurements of the cosmic microwave background radiation due to the interaction between ULDM and neutrinos. Overall, our study highlights the interconnected nature of ULDM, neutrinos, and the early universe, emphasizing the necessity of considering multiple cosmological parameters simultaneously when examining their individual behaviors. Furthermore, it highlights the potential for future direct detection through the quantum fluctuation-driven sources of dark matter and the availability of a 'window' for future laser interferometry beyond the existing limits by approximately two orders of magnitude. This research paves the way for a deeper understanding of the early universe through the study of its darkest and coolest components. Additionally, we determined the critical angles of rotation for stars with masses below 0.1 solar masses, mapping out the regions on the mass-angle plane where hydrogen burning is possible. Our analysis revealed that in stars with masses above the hydrogen minimum mass, the threshold angle of rotation is approximately 85 degrees, and the angle remains largely unchanged with changing mass. We also explored models with cores above the hydrogen breakdown point and found that in some cases, hydrogen burning can continue in spins closer to 100% than previously thought. However, in most instances, such cores end up being broken down into two segments with different rotation rates. Our research revealed that above a certain mass threshold, the segments rotate differently and rotate each other down, resulting in deaths of the stars known as gravitationally driven spin mergers. Our study also showed that in stars with masses between the hydrogen breakdown point and the Chandrasekhar limit, hydrogen burning can occur in spins closer to 98% than previously thought, and the minimum mass threshold for such stars is approximately 0.45 solar masses, changing only slightly with changing mass. This paper proposes a new random access (RA) protocol called NOVR-XL for next-generation XL-MIMO systems. Our protocol is designed to address the significant RA performance issues caused by massive MIMO systems, particularly in initial connection establishment. To tackle this problem, we introduce a new scheduling mechanism that prioritizes user selection, leveraging a novel algorithm called NOVR to efficiently identify the most suitable users for RA. We develop a non-cooperative and semi-cooperative NOVR-XL protocol, as well as an algorithm to determine user roles. Simulation results show that our proposed protocol achieves significant improvements in RA performance, throughput, and connection establishment delay. Specifically, it reduces the RA time and connection establishment delay by approximately one order of magnitude in both non-cooperative and semi-cooperative scenarios. Additionally, our protocol delivers elevated throughput in both scenarios. We also validate the feasibility and scalability of our protocol by conducting extensive simulations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our NOVR-XL protocol is highly effective in minimizing the number of RA attempts and connection establishment delays, surpassing existing protocols by a wide margin. This leads to significant reductions in energy consumption, RA costs, and connection establishment delays in both scenarios. This protocol can be applied to various XL-MIMO systems, including those with coordinated transmission and massive MIMO architectures. This research proposal builds upon our previous work presented at the 2023 ICC conference. A fundamental challenge in protoplanetary disk research arises from the discrepancy between the small scales required for planetesimals to form and the larger scales observed for gas and solids. Various processes, such as gravitational perturbations, wind loss, and thermal instability, have been proposed to bridge this gap, but the role of substructures, like density pulses and gaps, in forming planetesimals remains unclear. Density pulses, generated by density fluctuations that give rise to particle growth, were previously proposed to create planetesimals. In a study of a simplified single-zone model with particle interactions and a temperature function that varies with particle density, it has been found that submicron particles can grow into meters-sized particles within a few tens of years in the disk's upper atmosphere, but larger particles may not reach the necessary sizes to stick together and form planetesimals. On the other hand, in the hot inner regions of the disk, particles of all sizes can combine to form larger particles, but a transition occurs in which only medium-sized particles remain. In both situations, a distinct population of particles forms that can efficiently grow into meter-sized particles, and it has been proposed that these particles could aggregate into planetesimals through a process known as dead zone migration, in which the population of particles is drawn into the inner regions of the disk. In addition, another process, called snow line cycling, has been discovered that also leads to planetesimals forming in the inner regions of the disk. Both processes are continuous and can result in the formation of a distinct ring-shaped distribution of particles that could give rise to planetesimals in particular regions of the disk. It has been proposed that these regions could be associated with the formation of certain planetary characteristics, such as the presence of super-Earths in the region around 2-3 astronomical units or the presence of gas giants in the region around 5-10 astronomical units. It has also been suggested that these processes could lead to the formation of certain types of asteroids, such as those found in the region of the solar system known as the solar disk asteroid belt. If applied to the solar system, it could explain the characteristics of certain asteroids that show evidence of having formed through a process known as dead zone migration. If this is the case, it has implications for our understanding of the formation of planets and asteroids in the solar system. It has been proposed that rather than considering the formation of planets and asteroids as two separate events, they could be considered as two stages of the same process, with planets forming as a result

A nonlinear energy density functional called BigApple is proposed to describe the energy of atomic nuclei. This functional accurately predicts the properties of nuclear matter at saturation, including the equation of state, neutron-proton symmetry, and the kaonic nucleus $^{48}Ca K^-$. The strength and width of the M3$^0$ giant dipole resonance also agree with experimental findings. Compared to the standard Skyrme-Hartree-Fock approach, the predicted binding energies and particle separations in even neutron and proton magic number nuclei show greater precision, with an average deviation of 0.92 MeV in relation to experimental values. This functional's success is attributed to a novel combination of the density-dependent term, the Walecka term, and the Brueckner-Hartman-Heenen (BHH) bulk contribution, as well as accurate parametrization of the density functional within the BigApple framework. It is noteworthy that the BHH contribution is derived theoretically from the BHH equation of state, which is obtained using the BHH approach based on the random phase approximation, while the Brueckner-Bartello equation of state is not employed. This achievement supports previous findings that the BHH equation of state is more suitable for nuclear matter at saturation. The BigApple functional offers significant improvements over existing energy density functionals and provides a valuable resource for theoretical studies of atomic and heavy atomic nuclei, as well as nuclear matter in extreme densities. It is particularly useful for investigating the equation of state in neutron star matter and the kaon condensate phenomenon. The predicted properties of the M3$^0$ giant dipole resonance in even magic number nuclei also make the BigApple functional a valuable tool for testing experimental findings in the future. Our analysis indicates that the most robust performance is achieved with equally spaced frequencies, and by optimizing the duration and amplitude of these gates, we can significantly enhance the establishment of entanglement across the chain. Furthermore, our investigation reveals that a specific pattern of frequency errors can result in the creation of odd-numbered entangled states in ions, and by modifying the gate design, we can introduce a frequency gap to avoid this issue. Additionally, we explore the consequences of this pattern on the formation of universal entanglement and find that it can be overcome by adjusting the optimization process. Our proposed approach is applicable to various scenarios, including a wide range of frequency errors, and requires only a minor increase in laser intensity. Neural language models have made significant advancements in modeling complex language patterns and probabilities, yet they can benefit from combination with more rule-based $N$-gram models to achieve superior performance in various tasks and metrics. Building upon this idea, our research develops a unified neural network that can be used for tasks like machine translation, summarization, and language modeling by seamlessly integrating $N$-gram models. We achieve this integration by employing a specific branching technique that appends the neural network to a sub-network of the base model, effectively allowing for mixing with $N$-gram models via weighted averaging. We support weighted averaging through the introduction of a decay factor, which enables the network to dynamically adjust the importance of integrated models during training. Our proposed model is termed the Neural Hybrid Network. Through thorough experimentation, the Neural Hybrid Network has demonstrated superior performance in tasks like translating Japanese to English, summarizing text in English, and language modeling in French, by accomplishing state-of-the-art results on widely used datasets. The code for the Neural Hybrid Network is available at https://github.com/zhong-jian/NNH.

Unlike previous methods, SDARNet predicts the coefficients of a fixed set of points rather than conducting convex hull reconstruction. The proposed model has applications in the reconstruction of 3D faces from images with unknown indoor or outdoor lighting settings. We provide new formulas for the following average values in standard and marked ordered trees: the average number of deepest nodes, the average length of the longest path, and the average number of nodes at a given depth. Our calculations involve analyzing the properties of ordered trees using counting principles and combinatorial methods. Our findings also imply that the standard ordered tree distribution can be expressed in terms of derivatives of exponential generating functions. We compare our results to existing research on marked ordered trees, including those with designated roots, to illustrate the generality of our approaches. Our formula for the average number of deepest nodes in standard ordered trees was previously unknown and differs from the corresponding marked ordered tree value by a factor of 1+structure, which we interpret as a form of the structure factor seen in queueing theory. Our results for the average number of deepest nodes, the longest path, and the number of nodes at a given depth also provide a tree analogue of well-documented random variable distributions, which we refer to as the deepest level distribution, the longest queue length distribution, and the given level distribution, respectively. This expression shares similarities with the well-known Borel-Cantelli distribution (lim_{n\to\infty} (log N)/log n = \gamma), which it reduces to for large n.
