This research addresses a prevalent issue affecting optical character recognition systems - the presence of spelling errors in input text.  A novel approach is presented that leverages neural language models to correct these spelling errors.  In comparison to conventional techniques, this method exhibits superior performance, as evidenced by our experiments using a publicly available dataset, MCDV.  To enhance the pipeline for optical character recognition, this research also offers a more efficient spell correction algorithm, incorporating a categorical approach that caters to words without common prefixes.  In evaluation experiments utilizing the MCDV dataset, significant improvements are observed in the effectiveness of the optical character recognition system, particularly in correcting words with typos that cause partial matches.  The proposed spell correction algorithm demonstrates its versatility and shows comparable performance when evaluated on another dataset, CMC.  This research's contributions are reflected in two novel implementations: a command-line tool for post-processing OCR output and a web-based interface for interactive spell correction, both of which are publicly accessible through dedicated repositories.  Furthermore, the code for the neural language model used in the research is publicly available on GitHub, along with evaluation code and data preprocessing tools. This research addresses two broad issues common in real-world applications: infinite data dimensions and time-dependent input variables. A linear model can be identified as the optimal solution when data dimensions are infinite, particularly when data follows a specific pattern known as the "signal-to-noise ratio" threshold. We developed two algorithms to handle these cases, providing dimensionality-related and time-related guarantees for model efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of these algorithms, showing performance improvements in various scenarios. As risk-management becomes increasingly vital in electricity storage operations, incorporating uncertainty is crucial for optimal management and policy development in low-carbon grids. This study develops a stochastic mixed-integer linear programming model that accounts for storage risk-aversion, depending on risk preferences and probability weights, and demonstrates the model's efficacy with a day-ahead simulation for a hypothetical grid with 16 nodes in the Nordic region, considering weather forecasts, stream flow, and price variability. The results show that risk-averse storage operations prioritize self-sufficiency, charge at low prices, and discharge at high prices, and that the model's risk aspect can be viewed as an additional marginal cost structure, with implications for grid resilience and storage policy design. Furthermore, the research highlights the robustness of the model to changes in storage risk-preferences, storage capacity, and demand flexibility. Ultimately, the study provides a feasible and illustrative framework for evaluating policy decisions and grid resilience in the face of increasing risk-storage operations. The code for this study is available on GitHub at https://github.com/yashen87/SART-SD. The study receives funding from the Nordic Working Group on Risk in Energy Markets (NWG-REM). The paper's structure is based on feedback from two anonymous reviewers and inputs from the NWG-REM community, and it benefits from discussions with Hans Auer, Axel Anderson, and Jussi Saarinen. The code for the SART-SD model is currently being tested on real-time data from the Nordic market operators for the Nordic Working Group on Risk in Energy Markets (NWG-REM). The research's limitations include its focus on a single region and day-ahead time frame, and the absence of electricity price volatility and storage degradation costs. This study investigates the behavior of an idealized baroclinic storm on Mars within a computer-simulated Earth-like atmosphere. Our model incorporates an elliptical shape to represent the storm's influence and allows for the inclusion of an atmospheric circulation pattern known as the "polar jet." By simulating the storm's development within this model, we observed similarities between its behavior and that of the Earth's North Atlantic Oscillation. Furthermore, the storm exhibited a pattern of circulation that reversed seasonally, mirroring the behavior of the Martian polar jet. By analyzing these results, we gained insight into the factors that influence the storm's development, including the temperature contrast between the planet's poles and its midlatitudes, the strength of the polar jet, and the presence of persistent high and low pressure areas. Finally, we drew parallels between the persistent high-pressure areas that form on the Martian poles during the southern spring and the Arctic highs that develop on the Earth, suggesting they may both be linked to the same polar temperature increase that prevents the formation of baroclinic storms. Additionally, we found that the model could simulate the formation of multiple storms along the Martian equator by increasing the temperature contrast between the planet's poles and its midlatitudes. By simulating this change on a global scale, we observed an increase in the number of storms that formed on Mars during the southern summer, and were able to describe this phenomenon as a polar cap-driven baroclinic instability that results in the formation of persistent high and low pressure areas on the Martian poles. We also explored the model's parameters that affect the position and shape of the storm systems and found that the application of a small amount of atmospheric turbulence had a significant effect on the formation of the Martian storms. Ultimately, this study provides a foundation for the understanding of baroclinic storms on Mars within a broader, more complex atmospheric context. We also present a baroclinic instability theory that can be applied to the study of Earth's atmospheric circulation patterns. Finally, we reflect on the limitations of this study's model and propose ideas for its improvement, such as incorporating a solid surface and atmospheric moisture. We recognize these limitations as opportunities for future research that can build upon the framework established here. We propose that the approach used in this study could be applied to the simulation of baroclinic storms on other planets and moons within the solar system. Most existing active learning methods are straightforward, selecting the most uncertain samples for labeling based on confidence scores. Although these methods effectively reduce the labeling workload for small datasets like MNIST and SVNH, their performance significantly lags behind random sampling when dealing with large datasets like ImageNet. We believe this performance gap exists because these methods poorly capture the concept of uncertainty and suffer from a "over-selecting" issue, particularly when considering models that are nearly certain but have high confidence levels. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel active learning method called Uncertainty Pessimism Estimation (UPE), which creates a more precise uncertainty measure by integrating the influence of pessimistic estimates and confidence scores. Additionally, UPE mitigates the "over-selecting" issue by introducing a threshold-based sample selection process. Our method successfully adapts to various query strategies, including uniform sampling for comparison. We support UPE with comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets, demonstrating its superior performance and scalability. Our code and models are available open-source on GitHub. When applied to large datasets like ImageNet, UPE significantly improves active learning performance. Our study offers a comprehensive understanding of active learning uncertainty estimation and provides a valuable foundation for further research in the field. Our findings and research approach are further validated by an independent study conducted by fellow researchers. Through rigorous evaluation and comparison, we confirm the superiority of UPE, along with some interesting findings, and propose potential future research directions, particularly exploring the integration of data augmentation with active learning. The effectiveness of two-qubit logic gates relies heavily on specific local arrangements being met, and achieving this efficiency requires precise control over the energy levels of qubits. In the case of silicon-based quantum computing, qubits are made from silicon with donor atoms, and modifying the position and energy of these donor atoms can facilitate the desired outcome. By conducting comprehensive simulations, we evaluated various configurations of donor atoms to determine the most suitable ones for executing two-qubit logic gates efficiently. Our study indicates that adjusting the position of donor atoms can facilitate the entanglement necessary for two-qubit operations, and allowing some donor atoms to occupy higher energy levels successfully completes the required conditions necessary for two-qubit logic operations. Furthermore, our simulations revealed that certain donor atom positions can significantly reduce the duration needed to execute two-qubit logic gates by minimizing the distance between the energy levels of qubits. Consequently, our recommendations for optimizing the placement and energy of donor atoms can serve as a blueprint for implementing two-qubit logic gates and varying the energy levels of qubits in silicon-based quantum computing. Moreover, our approach can be extended to other quantum systems that involve the use of donor atoms. Additionally, our study suggests that modifying the energy of qubit pairs based on the required duration of computation can lead to a significant decrease of order $10^4$ in operations when employing the Rxx gate. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that employing the Rxx gate leads to a better performance compared to the usage of the Ryy and Ryx gates, and thus it is recommended for use in silicon-based quantum computing. Finally, our simulations are compatible with both bulk and nanoscale silicon-based quantum computers. Nonetheless, the analysis of the latter requires further consideration of boundary conditions and the placement of donor atoms within the device. Nonetheless, our study provides a foundation for investigating the behavior of small-scale donor atoms in the nanoscale. Moreover, it is essential to note that the duration needed to execute two-qubit logic gates is highly sensitive to the location of donor atoms, and thus it is crucial to select the most efficient configurations to achieve the required conditions necessary for two-qubit logic operations with silicon-based quantum computers. Nonetheless, our research indicates that there are many efficient configurations available. Nonetheless, it is also noteworthy that the most efficient configurations are not necessarily the most robust ones with respect to decoherence caused by the interaction between the qubit system and the surroundings, and thus it is also necessary to consider the stability of donor atoms in silicon-based quantum computers. A dynamic TDD system is proposed where, based on channel conditions, certain bands shift between uplink and downlink to maximize throughput. Determining optimal power allocation and scheduling in such a system becomes a complex problem. To address this issue, a new algorithm is developed for power allocation and scheduling in dynamic TDD systems, leveraging the proposal's flexibility to change the direction of data transmission. To improve efficiency, a new criterion is introduced, allowing for faster convergence when determining the optimal power allocation and scheduling. To validate the algorithm's effectiveness, simulations were conducted, revealing significant improvements in throughput in dynamic TDD systems.

In this work, we test a Hamiltonian Neural Network (HNN) as a meta-learner in a variety of tasks. Our findings show that HNN outperforms an LSTM-based meta-learner in tasks that incorporate the well-known MNIST dataset, including serving as a prototype for the dataset (known as the protocol known as few-shot learning) and predicting temperatures in a nonlinear regression based on input identifiers. Moreover, we discover that HNN excels in a linear regression against randomly generated targets when compared to an equal number of LSTM learning trials. We believe its success is due to the consistent, deterministic dynamics of HNN, which allows for the efficient learning of meta-representations by leveraging physical laws. We also present a novel method to update the Hamiltonian of HNN, which we term the discrete reversible iREINFORCE algorithm. This new update mechanism significantly reduces the physical learning noise encountered in prior approaches. We make our code publicly available as part of the Hamiltonian Neural Network toolkit. This toolkit also includes examples of HNN applications, such as a linear regression against randomly generated targets and a nonlinear temperature prediction based on an MNIST encoder, as well as a comparative study of different Hamiltonian update algorithms. We provide the iREINFORCE algorithm as a supplemental toolkit to facilitate researchers' comparison with other Hamiltonian update algorithms. We hope this toolkit facilitates others' access to HNN, enables the evaluation of our proposed update algorithm, and sparks the development of novel applications for HNN. We propose a novel collaborative framework for machine learning, consisting of multiple agents that work together to improve the accuracy of their individual models and boost the trust in them by addressing the challenges faced in modern machine learning. Our research introduces an innovative two-stage algorithm to update model precision and another to update the trust score in a fair and equitable manner, ensuring that no agent is disadvantaged as a result of cooperation. We test this proposed framework with multiple scenarios using real-life data and find that it achieves significant improvements in model accuracy and trust score compared to existing techniques, such as local update and uniform distribution of data. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that this proposed framework showcases self-organizing properties, as seen in recent machine learning initiatives, including federated learning and distributed learning. Our proposed framework provides a foundation for further development of collaborative machine learning, particularly in the context of artificial societies. We highlight potential applications and outline the possibilities of combining this framework with other learning approaches, such as evolutionary algorithms, with potential benefits for scalability and security. Deep learning models have shown a strong response to data enhancement, enabling them to excel in a variety of natural language processing tasks. A major challenge remains in determining the ideal combination of data augmentation techniques for a given problem, given the vast array of existing methods. We propose a purposeful data augmentation framework called "Efficient Exploration of Data Augmentation" (EDA), which is designed to efficiently identify the most effective data augmentation techniques for a particular task. EDA achieves this goal by constructing a compact subset of data augmentation methods that are both effective and distinct, allowing it to operate in deep learning with multiple transformations. We test this framework on three distinct text generation tasks and two summary generation models, and the results show that it is possible to develop a small set of effective data augmentation techniques that are task-specific and pure, which enables deep learning models to operate with multiple transformations and results in superior performance compared to conventional data augmentation methods. We also uncover several findings on the efficacy of different data augmentation techniques and the potential of a small set of methods to give big gains. We offer our framework and the findings of our research for other researchers to use and build upon, in the hope that it will contribute to the ongoing quest to understand the magic of data augmentation in deep learning. We also present an interactive tool, known as the Data Augmentation Explorer, which enables other researchers to explore our outcomes and try out new techniques with real-time feedback. This paper aims to explore and present some intriguing aspects and applications of this underrepresented concept. We will examine the relationship between the Hankel path and the complex plane's horizontal strip, discuss the solutions to the Euler--Beta distribution, consider the image of the Hankel path under complex reflection, and also investigate a recently discovered formula related to the Gamma function. Additionally, this study will provide a detailed analysis of a previously published theorem by some Russian mathematicians. We will utilize conventional techniques to derive the Hankel path's relationship with the horizontal strip, and also employ the Hankel path to solve the Euler--Beta distribution equation. Finally, we will also offer some graphical representations of the Hankel path and its reflection. This study is an extension of the ideas presented in the book "Extensive Table of the Complex Gamma Function along the Hankel Path" by Yudhijit Patil, and also draws upon the "Research Report on the Complex Gamma Function along the Hankel Path" published by the same author. This study provides an examination of the top quark pair production cross section in 7 and 8 TeV $p\bar{p}$ collisions based on an analysis of up to 5.9 inverse femtobarns of run II data from the CDF detector. The research involves several advanced top quark identification techniques and multiple variables in cross section measurements. Detailed comparisons with theoretical predictions from perturbative quantum chromodynamics are conducted, yielding closed expressions that allow for a precise estimation of theoretical uncertainties. The study finds the cross section for 7 and 8 TeV collisions to be $9.62 \pm 0.29$ nanobarns and $24.60 \pm 0.47$ nanobarns, with the 7 TeV result exhibiting an inaccuracy of $-0.13 \pm 0.29$ when compared to theoretical predictions, and the 8 Te V result exhibiting an inaccuracy of $-0.37 \pm 0.47$. The research also presents cross sections for sub-processes involving virtual W and Z bosons, as well as the estimation of theoretical uncertainties arising from the use of perturbative quantum chromodynamics. The most accurate of these estimates is obtained via NLO order calculations and amounts to $2.78\%$. A further analysis of high-momentum-transfer top quark production is also conducted, with the 7 Te V data showing an upper limit of $84$ picobarns at $95\%$ confidence, in contrast to the predicted value of $60$ picobarns based on parton distribution functions derived from other measurements. The investigation expands upon prior research by increasing the number of analyzed events by a factor of five, and significantly refines the measurement by reducing uncertainties related to jet identification and clustering. The research remains the most comprehensive top quark pair production cross section measurement conducted to date. The related paper has been accepted for publication in Physical Review D. The research was funded by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, and involved the collaboration of up to $590$ researchers from $60$ institutions across eighteen countries. The CDF detector is a product of international cooperation between Fermilab, Universities, and research institutions in France, Germany, Italy, and Switzerland. The research was conducted using the Fermilab Tevatron particle accelerator, a Congressionally mandated project funded by the Office of High Energy and Nuclear Physics of the Department of Energy in the United States. This is achieved by creating a differential private learning environment that ensures the protection of individual data entries and small changes to the graph structure. We then develop a sensitive reduction procedure to protect our private learning against certain attacks, all while ensuring the privacy of our learning environment. The Euclid mission, set to begin observations in early 2023, is an optical two-focus astronomical research project that will conduct in-depth studies in two areas: determining the structure and the evolution of the cosmos, and examining the properties of stars and galaxies in the observable universe. To achieve this, Euclid will collect high-resolution images and spectral data for three million celestial objects. As a result of its comprehensive data, Euclid will particularly make notable contributions to astronomical research in three key areas. Firstly, it will provide precise information about the properties of dark energy, allowing for an accurate calculation of the Hubble constant and giving insight into the evolution of the cosmos over time. Secondly, Euclid will gather detailed information about the characteristics of five million galaxies observed across the observable universe, spanning all ages and distances, and will also collect data on twenty million stellar objects in the Milky Way, including information about the composition and Scalo. Finally, the spacecraft will conduct deep field studies in areas such as the study of active supermassive black holes and the detection of stellar remnants such as neutron stars and white dwarfs. The comprehensive nature of its data means Euclid will also provide additional discoveries in areas such as the identification of potential targets for future astronomical research projects and the selection of promising planetary hosts for future missions aimed at searching for life outside the Solar System. The significant impact of Euclid is set to be seen in the field of astronomical research for decades to come. The spacecraft is designed to operate for approximately six years, during which it will collect data on approximately 35 billion objects ahead of its retirement in the mid 2030s. Once operational, Euclid will work in conjunction with other spacecraft such as the James Webb Space Telescope, the Square Kilometre Array, and the James Webb Space Telescope to transform our understanding of the cosmos. The Euclid mission will boast a 1.24 meter primary mirror, a three-layer sun shield, a 36 meter long and 1.5 meter wide bus, a 0.35 meter diameter optical test instrument, and an imaging and spectroscopy instrument capable of collecting data across the visible and near-infrared spectrum. The resulting data will be stored on a 500 TB solid-state drive. The mission will require two ground stations: one in Europe and one in South Africa. The successful launch and operation of Euclid is the result of close collaboration between European researchers, engineers, and industry partners working together with teams in Russia and in the Americas. Recent studies of 64Ni, with an energy range of 4-16 MeV, have used the Dalitz-Bruckner analysis to understand the nucleus' response to excitation energy. Based on constraints from the RPB, the monopole interaction was found to influence the neutron and proton pairs' behavior. The observation shows that the (2+) state at 1313 keV is linked to the 54Ni reference frame, and this connection allows for the evaluation of the monopole interaction's strength. This research reveals the complexity of the N=40 subshell gap's breakdown, as seen in 64Ni, and its relation to the monopole interaction. Additionally, the findings demonstrate that the RPB rules must be applied with caution in nuclei beyond the valley of stability. The study's approach, using the Dalitz-Bruckner analysis, provides a new method for examining the monopole interaction's impact on the neutron and proton pairs' behavior in 64Ni. The data for this research come from experiments performed using the 48Ca beam at RIBF, in Japan, and the results were obtained through theoretical analysis carried out in China. The outcomes were published in Physical Review Letters with the reference 10.1103/PhysRevLett.131.132501. This 64Ni nucleus study offers insights into the particle pair interaction's evolution in a environment of excitation energy, and the findings encourage further research into the subshell gap's breakdown mechanics. The methodology used here can be applied to other exotic nuclei, like 60Ni and 62Ni. We've developed a new validation approach, J-K-fold cross-validation, to enhance the stability of performance predictions and model robustness. By breaking the model into J non-overlapping segments and using K-fold cross-validation on each segment separately, this method outperforms standard K-fold cross-validation in terms of both performance estimate accuracy and model accuracy, according to our experiments. We've also created a Python package to facilitate the implementation of J-K-fold cross-validation for other researchers and practitioners. Moreover, our findings suggest that models exhibiting unstable performance tend to benefit more significantly than their stable counterparts from using our proposed validation method. We've tested this validation approach on multiple existing datasets and scenarios and have the results available for other researchers to build upon. Nonetheless, more extensive research is necessary to explore the potential limitations and potential applications of J-K-fold cross-validation across various modeling scenarios and data types. We've made the associated code and guidelines openly available on GitHub for other machine learning practitioners to use and build upon. Bucket Elimination (BE) is a fundamental inference and optimization technique on graphical models, specifically designed to tackle problems that involve calculating marginal distributions and optimizing objectives by combining local information. BE leverages a breakdown of the problem into manageable sub-problems, solving each for a subset of variables, and combines the results to achieve the desired outcome. While BE is a crucial method, the original algorithmic framework is too general, making it important to identify specific instances of BE algorithms that are not only efficient but also easy to implement. In this paper, an in-depth examination is conducted to explore how BE behaves on two representative problems: the network flow challenge and the maximum weight matching problem in bipartite graphs. By deconstructing the BE framework into a sequence of variable elimination steps, the paper delves into a detailed analysis of how the resulting algorithmic structure relates to existing variable elimination methods, particularly with regard to the efficiency and simplicity of the resulting code. The study demonstrates how the underlying graph structure impacts the efficiency of BE algorithms, and it is observed that the resulting algorithms yield interesting and distinct patterns of variable elimination strategies. Furthermore, the paper showcases how the established variable elimination methods on flow networks and bipartite graphs can be viewed as specialized BE algorithms, and it is shown that these algorithms are less efficient when compared to the generic BE on random challenge instances. The study also provides a theoretical analysis of how the underlying graph structure affects the performance of BE algorithms. The paper presents an original contribution to the field of artificial intelligence by illustrating how the BE framework can be utilized to examine variable elimination algorithms on specific graph challenges, offering a novel and captivating application of graphical models in artificial intelligence. The study demonstrates an engaging blend of algorithmic analysis, theoretical examination of graph challenges, and the application of BE algorithms, making it a compelling addition to the field of artificial intelligence. The paper presents an empirical investigation into the performance of BE algorithms on two well-studied challenges, providing a comprehensive analysis of the algorithmic behavior in relation to the underlying graph structure, and it is observed that the algorithms exhibit distinct variable elimination strategies, displaying an intriguing level of complexity that is closely related to the underlying structure of the challenges. We analyzed the impact of a specific quantum phenomenon, photon recoil, on the shape of a light beam absorbed by a high-density medium, using a high saturation level. Our investigation involved studying the absorption of a monochromatic light beam by a medium with a non-zero density, specifically a Bose-Einstein condensate. We studied the influence of photon recoil on the shape of the light beam by observing the motion of its central portion. Our primary finding revealed an asymmetric shape of the light beam, influenced by the interplay of its initial shape, the direction of its propagation, and the energy of the individual photons. We proposed an alternative way to measure the velocity of a cold atomic gas through the interpretation of the shape of a light beam. Additionally, we compared the motion of the central portion of the light beam in both free space and in a stationary wave pattern, revealing an enhanced motion in the latter case. Lastly, we examined the impact of increasing the density of the medium on the shape of the light beam, finding that photon recoil becomes more prominent in a more dense medium. Our study revealed that the shape of the light beam is determined by the interplay of the direction of its propagation, the energy of the individual photons, and the motion of the medium, all of which result in asymmetric shapes due to photon recoil. We believe our research will contribute to a deeper understanding of the effects of photon recoil on light absorption in a high-density medium. Furthermore, our study suggests that the motion of a cold atomic gas can be inferred from the shape of a light beam, and that the shape of the light beam itself retains its own characteristics and physical meaning, even after being absorbed. Our results indicate that frictionless isotropic jamming exhibits unique characteristics, in contrast to the shared properties it shares with frictional jamming transitions, including the exponents associated with which bonds break under pressure. Furthermore, we find that the exponent $\tau$ defining the scalar correlation function varies between frictionless isotropic jamming $2.72 \pm 0.01$ and frictional jamming $3.40 \pm 0.01$, with the latter matching the results from genetic algorithms. Our study suggests that the dynamics of frictionless jamming solids are governed by the same universality class as the disordered contact process, whereas frictional jamming dynamics belong to the same universal domain as the ordered contact process. Our research also recovers the relationship between viscoelastic contrast and jamming transition order, and provides a theoretical explanation for the observed exponent ratios. Ultimately, our work paves the way for interpreting our previous research on jamming transitions facilitated by training, and suggests that the idea of a universal frictionless state requires further clarification. The underlying field is $\mathbb{C}$. Public sector professionals extensively rely on Web search engines for information.
However, they should be aware that Web search results algorithms perpetuate
algorithms' own biases, which can lead to inaccurate conclusions when using
search results as a basis for decisions. This study examines the extent to which
search engine results reflect the UK's population structure, revealing significant
divergences in search results for common public sector-related terms when
conducting searches with different IP addresses associated with specific UK
geographic locations. The investigation discovered distinct patterns in search
engine results across the UK, reflecting both national and regional nuances in
search engine algorithms, which are influenced by Web usage patterns in each area.
Consequentially, searches in some UK locations may yield results shaped by
local populations that differ from the overall UK population, emphasizing the
need for public sector professionals to be cautious of algorithmic biases in
search engine results. This knowledge can aid them in managing potential
prejudices in search engine-based decision-making and policy development. The
research's findings are not isolated to the UK, as similar algorithmic biases
exist in search engine results globally, making this study relevant to a broad
range of contexts. In addition, the transparent search engine used in this
study makes its source code and data readily available for the public to use,
build upon, and modify as needed. The study's approach can serve as a model
for similar investigations in other regions and among different populations. 
Finally, the degree of search engine result fragmentation within the UK may
be viewed as a microcosm of the larger issue of algorithmic bias present in
global Web applications. 
The study's raw data, as well as the code used for the analysis, are available at:
https://github.com/JocelynHao/SearchEngineFragmentation.

A proposed rCASPR sampling method reduces the number of measurements required for linear sampling, which is advantageous in applications like medical imaging where data is frequently expensive to collect. A theoretical analysis of rCASPR's point-spread function and image contrast reveals that it outperforms traditional linear sampling. For a specific contrast threshold, rCASPR uses approximately one-fifth the number of measurements needed by linear sampling. This advantage comes with a computational cost, as shown in a numerical example involving a 3D bone scan. There, rCASPR with 20 measurements produced a point-spread function similar to linear sampling with 100 measurements, and resulted in a usable image 20 times faster. A algorithm for constructing basis vectors is a key component of rCASPR, which can be interpreted as a greedy selection of linearly independent measurements, and which serves as a precursor to a recently introduced sparse regression algorithm. Moreover, it is demonstrated that the basis vectors themselves contain useful information, as they represent possible structures in the data being analyzed. Eventually, the rCASPR basis vectors converge to the same set of structures represented by the sparse regression algorithm, which is the most coherent set of structures according to a coherence measure. Despite being an independent contribution, the coherence measure itself was found to have a connection to a previous research on structure recognition in medical imaging. Ultimately, the rCASPR sampling method and the associated analysis provide a framework for evaluating and creating various sampling strategies, which will facilitate the development of future medical imaging techniques. The US shipping industry is known to be heavily influenced by cartels formed by shipping companies. These cartels divided shipping routes into specific blocks and set prices for them. In 1975, the US government passed a law banning such practices. Initially, the effect was minimal as companies could still engage in price-fixing through other means. However, the lack of shipping cartels eventually started affecting freight rates and shipping quantities. Our research shows that freight rates increased and shipping quantities decreased in the years following the ban. Moreover, our findings indicate that shipping companies adjusted their practices to focus on shorter route blocks, making it harder for them to collaborate and further increasing freight rates. Our data covers the period between 1975 and 2011 and includes monthly freight rates and shipping quantities for twenty different shipping routes along with annual industry reports detailing shipping cartels' practices and structures. We believe that our large dataset and long time frame make our results more accurate and reliable than previous research on this topic. Our conclusions can be applied to other industries with similar experiences of anti-trust laws, demonstrating how the absence of cartels may lead to increased variability in prices and lower overall shipping quantities. Our research also suggests that shipping companies have different strategies to operate in the absence of cartels, involving a balance between collaborating with peers, serving different shipping routes, and charging varying prices for different goods. Our results can be utilized by regulatory bodies, shipping companies, and other stakeholders seeking to navigate this complex and intricate industry. Technical analysis for predicting stock prices relies heavily on indicators such as moving averages and Fibonacci levels, with historical prices being a base for these indications. Existing research often focuses on deep learning methods like CNN and LSTM, leaving traditional techniques like their underlying components unexplored. This study takes a step back to analyze the individual features of historical prices and technical indicators for stock price predictions. Interestingly, combining all indicators and historical prices leads to a significant improvement over their individual contributions. A persistent issue with time series predictions is model forecast accuracy degrading over time. To address this, the study considers two models with changing parameter settings and time-based data sampling, both of which enhance the models' ability to adapt to changing stock markets. Interestingly, using parameter settings optimized for future time frames leads to model accuracy decreasing over time, whereas models using the same parameter settings for both past and future time frames exhibit better performance, indicating a need for more flexible models. To achieve this, the paper proposes a simple yet effective method where the model learns the distribution of current and future parameter settings instead of fixed optimized settings. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of this technique across multiple stock market indices. From the analysis, valuable insights are gained into the individual features necessary for stock price predictions and the optimal model settings, while the proposed method also offers a promising technique for dynamic model parameter learning. From the exploratory analysis, valuable insights are gained into the individual features necessary for stock price predictions and possible applications in other time series prediction domains. Notably, the paper's approach provides a foundation for evaluating model flexibility in other complex stock market scenarios. Moreover, the proposed method can be applied to other time series prediction scenarios with evolving patterns, where the objective is to predict the performance of models with different parameter settings. The code and experiments for this study are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/hienbad/StockPricePredictionExperiments. The drive force, resistance, and object velocity were measured as the cylindrical intruder moved at different speeds within the granular material. The results show that the drag experienced by the object increases substantially with its speed. The reason for this significant acceleration-dependent drag is explained by studying the movement of the object's shadow, which moves through the granular bed at a much faster rate. The shadow's movement creates a trail of compacted granular material that offers considerable resistance to the object as it moves through the bed. The relationship between the object's speed, the size of the shadow, and the drag it experiences was determined through experiments and simulations of the shadow's movement. The results provide a clear understanding of the acceleration-dependent drag experienced by the object as it moves through the granular bed. The effect of the object's shape and the size of the granular material on the drag it experiences is also discussed. The acceleration-dependent drag experienced by the object was found to be influenced by the drive frequency and the grain size, but it was not affected by the depth of the granular bed. This research investigates rare decay events of B mesons, particularly the sensitive observations needed to constrain beyond-Standard Model theories and the development of efficient and versatile methods to calculate rare B-decay processes. The study focuses on rare B_s^0 and B^0 meson decays to leptons, such as mu+ mu-, and provides accurate calculations using the weak interaction component of the Standard Model and the impact of its strong and electroweak components. The analysis utilizes the Gyro 2.0 code, which incorporates theoretical predictions from two-loop perturbative QCD and its weak and electroweak effects, and matches the relevant physical processes to needed observables through evolution equations. The study accounts for substantial QCD corrections to one-loop levels, including the glue and light quark contributions, and includes corrections to weak and electroweak processes, including the impact of radiative corrections on lepton couplings. The research updates previous results on bottom quark semi-leptonic decay, which showed significant QCD corrections to one-loop levels, and provides updated estimates of rare B-decay rates, considering theoretical uncertainties, at the one-loop level. The analysis also compares the predicted rates with experimental limits from BaBar and LHCb, which already surpass the predicted levels, and the potential sensitivity of the Belle II and LHCb experiments to these decay processes in certain momentum cuts. The study paves the way for incorporating these rare B-decay processes into combined fits of B-decay data. The research can be extended to incorporate additional hadronic form factor effects, better treat entangled modes, and consider the impact of charm quark loop contributions. The developed code, which calculates various B meson decay processes and their QCD corrections, offers alternatives to existing codes, such as SuperForm and Convective, and provides versatile methods to calculate general scattering processes. The study motivates the development of better methods to address the vertex function contribution to form factors and the light-cone distribution amplitudes of heavy mesons. The analysis also highlights the importance of accurately calculating hadron masses, particularly for the gyromagnetic ratio of the muon, which remains one of the most precisely measured physical processes in particle physics. The research can be expanded to incorporate the effects of external fields on heavy quarks in finite temperature and density systems. The Standard FGMRES (SFGMRES) method has shown efficiency in solving complex equations arising from the discretization of various partial differential equations. However, the SFGMRES algorithm may produce inaccurate approximations when the residual operator varies significantly, leading to a need for an enhanced method. A new variation of FGMRES, called the Adaptive SFGMRES (ASGMRES), is proposed, where the starting space for the FGMRES iteration is dynamically changed to improve convergence by identifying the most significant residual components. The ASGMRES algorithm is then compared with the SFGMRES and TGMRES methods using numerical examples, demonstrating its superior performance in solving various complex equations. The experiments show that ASGMRES converges faster than SFGMRES and TGMRES for most examples, particularly when solving the Heliholtz equation with the Dirichlet boundary condition, where it achieves an approximately 5 times faster convergence rate than SFGMRES. The research suggests that ASGMRES represents a significant improvement over existing methods for solving complex equations and provides the potential to be an highly efficient solver for various numerical applications. The proposed algorithm is then applied to the 3D Heliholtz equation with the Neumann boundary condition, resulting in a 10 times faster convergence rate than TGMRES. The performance of ASGMRES is also evaluated on the 2D heart model, which involves solving a complex system of equations with 786,432 degrees of freedom, showing that it can achieve a 3 times faster convergence rate than TGMRES for a coarse grid resolution of 5. The numerical examples demonstrate the robustness and efficiency of the ASGMRES algorithm, highlighting its potential as a highly efficient solver for a wide range of numerical applications. The research provides useful insights into the performance of ASGMRES, emphasizing the importance of operator preconditioning in achieving the best possible performance. The proposed algorithm is straightforward to implement and offers significant performance enhancements in various scenarios, although it may not always achieve the optimal convergence rate possible. A critical issue in laparoscopic surgery is the movement of organs, which can cause disturbance in pre-surgical model registration. To address this challenge, researchers are using pose estimation techniques from image data to guide the registration process. However, the quality of intraoperative data is typically poor due to high camera noise, facilitating the development of robust registration methods by addressing the problem as a image segmentation challenge in noisy conditions. To achieve this, a convolutional neural network was integrated with a differentiable binary mask to segment organs from laparoscopic images, resulting in a distinctive training data set called Organs-in-Fault (OIF). To further challenge the model, Organs-in-Fault was modified to Organs-in-Severe-Fault (OISF) with significantly noisier images. The evaluation of models was conducted using the Organs-in-Fault and Organs-in-Severe-Fault data sets based on their ability to accurately segment organs from highly noisy laparoscopic images, and the results showed that a simple CNN performed better than U-net in conditions of extreme noise. Furthermore, the introduction of Organs-in-Severe-Fault data set revealed a notable increase in segmentation difficulty due to the addition of severe noise. To facilitate widespread use of the data set, guidelines were established for models to maintain acceptable performance when applying them to new, unseen data. The code and data sets are now publicly accessible on GitHub, awaiting further development by the surgical community. The challenge described in this study can be expanded to other minimally invasive surgical procedures involving the segmentation of the target organ from a poorly quality, dynamically changing image. The established evaluation framework and data set are unique in the field of surgical computer science, renowned for its rigorous standards, by featuring a robust, artificially constructed disturbance in natural image conditions, rather than relying on the commonly observed disturbances in real-world images. The exceptional characteristics of Organs-in-Fault and the rigorous evaluation process it entails make it an appealing choice for testing and comparing various image segmentation techniques and models, particularly those designed to process noisy images. The implicit requirement of pose estimation in this challenge also provides an opportunity to explore robust models that can handle the variation in pose needed for organ registration during surgery, offering numerous research possibilities. The code and data sets are available at the following GitHub link: https://github.com/duongthiennghia/Organs-in-Fault. However, determining the correct flow field remains challenging, particularly in areas with occlusions. Current techniques rely on the consistency of local neighborhood patterns, which is insufficient to ensure the consistency of distant features, particularly those separated by occlusions. We propose a method to evaluate the consistency of feature consistency across depths using a convolutional neural network, which we call the consistency encoder, based on the assumption that the representation learned by a flow-based transformation should be identical when the input image is reprojected using the estimated optical flow. We assess the feature consistency of deep features in our proposed framework and compare it with other self-supervised optical flow estimation methods that use consistency losses. Although our model processes 3D volumes, the proposed framework can be applied to 2D images by using a linear transformation. We evaluate our model on the MPI-SAI and SCAPE datasets and find that it achieves the lowest SSE and NN scores among self-supervised methods and comparable results with supervised methods on these datasets. However, our model fails to achieve state-of-the-art results on the MPI-SAI dataset when using a smaller search range. In this research, we theoretically examine the impact of a strong magnetic field on spin polarized strange quark matter at finite temperatures, and derive the generalized Baym-Pines equation of state. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of a magnetic field on spin polarized strange quark matter, specifically in relation to its stability in comparison to neutron stars. The study reveals that a strong magnetic field can cause a transition from neutral to charged quark matter, and may result in the formation of quark star seeds around neutron stars. Additionally, we find that the quark star's mass-radius relation is significantly affected by a strong magnetic field, with values that could be tested through future high precision measurements. The research also predicts specific patterns of magnetic field polarization that can influence quark star's energy spectra, and the possibility of quark star's barometric oscillations in relation to a strong magnetic field. Ultimately, the study paves the way for incorporating a weak anomaly term into spin polarized quark models, and suggests possible quark star signatures for future telescopic measurements. The predicted relations between the magnetic field strength and particle densities, as well as the influence of the magnetic field on the formation of quark matter phases, provide a theoretical foundation for ongoing and future magnetic field experiments and quark star observations. The research is relevant to theory and experiments within the fields of quark physics, compact stars, and magnetic field research. We prove that a cubic graph is E2F if and only if it has a strong matching of size 3. Additionally, it is shown that every cubic graph contains a subgraph that is equivalent to a 2-factorable graph if it contains a strong matching of size 3, or if it contains a certain type of 2-edge-connected subgraph known as a pair, respectively. These results expand upon previous findings, especially those related to a concept called 2-edge-connected (2EC) graphs. A 2EC graph is defined as a graph where the removal of all edges from its multiple of 2 factors leaves it with a connected subgraph consisting of single edges. It is important to note that the term 2EC is used interchangeably with E2F in certain sources. However, unlike E2F, the term 2EC does not require the graph to be cubic. We also provide a new and simplified proof for the fact that every cubic graph is 2EC, building upon the initial proof provided by Stocker in 1986. User-level system call filtering is crucial for enhancing the security of computer systems. Unfortunately, implementing system call filtering for applications written in interpreted languages like PHP and Python is challenging, especially for those with extensive memory requirements. In order to address this difficulty, we have developed a method called Timeloops, which carries out system call filtering at the user level for such applications. Unlike conventional methods, Timeloops does not modify existing operating system code; rather, it alters the system call table at the user level. Following a systematic analysis of possible attacks, we have designed Timeloops with an initial memory footprint of approximately 64MB, which can be minimized to 16MB, in order to empower vulnerable platforms with secure system call filtering capabilities. Moreover, Timeloops has the capability to monitor over one million system calls per second on a typical desktop computer. We have additionally implemented system call filtering for important services including Nginx and Apache, as well as OpenVPN and OpenSSH. By doing so, we have successfully prevented various attacks including buffer overflow, format string, and memory leak on target systems. Furthermore, Timeloops has the ability to fix common vulnerabilities and defects in services and applications automatically, following a predefined set of rules. By doing so, we have attained a notable achievement, namely the automatic fixation of a serious format string vulnerability in Apache with a difficult-to-obtain source code, without any prior knowledge of its contents. Finally, we have also developed Timeloops in a way that it can be easily integrated into existing sandboxing solutions, including OpenVZ and LXC, as well as into virtualization platforms, including KVM and Xen. By doing so, we have achieved a breakthrough in the system call filtering domain at a minimal expense, in comparison to conventional approaches. In order to validate the feasibility of our method, we have carried out extensive testing on real-world scenarios and mock attacks with remarkable results. This observability analysis involves developing an inequality based on a integral of the square of the population's density, as influenced by an initial density distributed within a certain observable region. This inequality enables us to classify the population's long-term behavior and determine conditions under which the population becomes extinct. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of this observability approach to a variant of the population model that incorporates a force of tension between individuals. The resulting system, which includes a Laplace operator with a negative coefficient, presents a challenge due to its lack of uniform stability, thus requiring the development of a novel strategy for establishing an observability inequality. This strategy, in turn, leverages recent research on the smoothness of solutions to a system of partial differential equations. We also explore a version of the population model that includes the force of tension as a strong interaction, which leads to the formation of a singular observable control for which we establish the uniqueness of weak solutions and demonstrate the effectiveness of the method of convexity. A key issue in the Elastic Full Waveform Inversion (EFWI) challenge is the ejection of the pressure field from the time domain, as it must be done for the usual Generation-Negation Iteration (GNI) method. This pressure field ejection can result in the loss of valuable information, particularly from the shear wave components, which are more difficult to generate and more sensitive to the iterative process, and thus more likely to be lost. This means that the inversion algorithm is missing important data, especially from the S-wave components, which are more challenging to propagate and more susceptible to being lost during the iteration process, and therefore the information they carry may not be accurately represented in the model. This paper explores an alternative approach, using time-domain wavefields in the EFWI framework. This involves using the recorded data directly on the frequency domain, without the need to convert it, which allows for the creation of a more comprehensive data misfit objective function. This new objective function includes information from both P and S-wave components, which can lead to a better model representation and a more robust inversion process. This research will demonstrate the proposed method's effectiveness by applying it to both synthetic and real-world data sets. It will also highlight the advantages and potential challenges of using time-domain wavefields in the EFWI framework. This new approach has the potential to provide a more precise and robust inversion process, especially in areas with complex geology, which often involve multiple wavefield interactions and S-wave component generation. This means that the inversion algorithm will have access to a broader spectrum of frequency data, which can lead to a more accurate and robust inversion process, even in areas with intricate geology. This research will be further developed in the context of Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) based EFWI frameworks, which also use the time-domain wavefields. This will enable the training of better-conditioned synthetic data generators, which in turn will enable the removal of the generation-negation iteration constraint, which can result in the loss of S-wave component information. This research has the potential to mark a significant advancement in the EFWI challenge, particularly in areas with complex geology, by providing a more precise and robust inversion process that accurately represents both P and S-wave components. This will be demonstrated in the results section, which shows the application of this new approach to both real and synthetic data sets, and the potential extensions to GAN based EFWI frameworks. This research's limitations are also discussed in the context of the results

The asymmetric noisy voter model is a random process that involves two distinct species interacting within a population, as it moves and interacts with others. This model can be seen as an extension of the asymmetric noisy majority vote, where the process's competition between species results in one species predominating, while the other becomes extinct in many cases. Contrary to the original model, the asymmetric noisy voter model allows for the coexistence of species, resulting in one species' rapid growth, followed by a slow decline to a state of equilibrium, where the species' densities remain stable. By utilizing a modified renewal process, we are able to determine the time it takes for one species to become dominant as well as the conditions under which the dominant species will eventually disappear. Additionally, we examine the spatial version of this process and discover a triangular relationship between the model's parameters and the region that will be occupied by one species in particular. The connection between the discrete version of this process and a related continuous process, the asymmetric noisy majority vote, is also explored, as well as the version of this process that includes multiple species interacting with each other. The asymmetric noisy voter model has been found to behave in a way that is essentially nontrivial in all the variations examined so far. The research discussed in this paper also includes the interaction between two distinct populations that are capable of crossing over through a process known as recombination, as it sheds light on the role that recombination plays in the process's competition. The results obtained from this research have been validated through the use of numerical data and already demonstrate some of the asymmetric noisy voter model's fundamental properties. The software used to conduct this research is included with the paper's supplementary material. The research discussed in this paper was initially presented at the 2020 annual meeting of the Mathematical Physics section within the South African Institute of Mathematical Sciences conference. An analytical study of electrostatic phase plates' performance is presented, where the design parameters influencing the distribution of the electron probe include aspects like fill-factor and pixel pattern. We derived expressions for the standard deviation of the probe size and current density as functions of bias voltage, beam voltage, and specific design features. These expressions were then utilized to investigate optimized designs for various applications. For a fill-factor of 50%, we found that the probe current density is more sensitive to small changes in fill-factor than to the probe size itself. For a fill-factor near 50%, the probe size can be described by a simple square-root relationship with respect to the voltage ratio, enabling quick estimation of probe performance for initial design evaluations. Although the ideal fill-factor appears to be 50% for minimizing the 50% fill-factor factor, other design aspects like pixel pattern also significantly impact performance, offering opportunities for improvement through optimized design strategies. Additionally, the probe current density can be maximized by adjusting the bias voltage to optimize the interaction between the probe and phase plate, with the optimal voltage proportional to the beam voltage and depending on specific design features. Through this analytical approach, design guidelines for optimized phase plates can be identified, filling a complementary role to existing numerical methods that focus on precise probe distributions. By utilizing an analytical framework, this study provides a fundamental understanding of the relationship between design parameters and probe performance, offering a useful tool for integrating phase plates into electron optics systems. Furthermore, the derived expressions can be easily implemented in simulation environments like Mathematica, making it feasible to create interactive tools for designing and evaluating phase plates for various applications. Ultimately, this study and the resulting tools can be utilized to explore new phase plate designs, facilitating the development of advanced electron microscopes with tailored capabilities. To analyze how language evolves over time, researchers and practitioners often examine semantic changes in words' meanings. Previously, techniques like WordSense Induction (WSI) focused solely on individual words, neglecting the influence of contextual variance. We introduce a new challenge,, framing variance as a critical factor in understanding semantic change, and present a data generation method to facilitate evaluation of models accounting for contextual variance in semantic change. Our experiments reveal that current state-of-the-art models fail to consider variance when analyzing the semantics of words in a fixed context, yet they succeed when the context is allowed to change. Furthermore, they successfully model contextual variance, capturing its effects on words' semantics, but also risk overfitting the data. To mitigate this risk, we propose a straightforward, clinically-tested model designed to handle varying contextual contexts. Experimentation on existing datasets reveals conflicting results, yet our generated data sets show consistent indications that the model improves both the fidelity and generalizability of semantic analysis. Lastly, we discuss the limitations of our approach and propose potential improvements, including integrating temporal relationships into the context's variance and exploring different contextual variations that affect specific word semantics. By emphasizing the significance of contextual variance in understanding linguistic evolution and releasing the necessary tools for evaluation, this research paves the way for developing more sophisticated models that capture the complex dynamics of language change. Our data and code are available for public use at https://github.com/NicoMN/LASC challenge. In this context, we explore a variety of coherent state functions for a one-dimensional lattice system with periodic boundary conditions. We generate and analyze coherent states for both spinless and spin-based systems. In particular, we investigate the behavior of these coherent states within a multi-site system that has been subject to both local and periodic external driving forces. Our findings indicate that the characteristics of these coherent states play a significant role in maintaining the system's quantum properties when it is driven by an periodic external force. Consequently, these coherent states may serve as stable platforms for implementing quantum simulations in both spinless and spin-based systems. Our research also reveals how the size of these coherent states changes in response to varying the intensity of the local driving force. Furthermore, we propose an approach to generate these coherent states using a local driving force, which may be feasible using current experimental technology. Our study provides theoretical insights that can be applied to various real-world scenarios, including those involving microring resonators, which have been used to create coherent states in both spinless and spin-based systems. Ultimately, our research lays the groundwork for exploring these coherent states within continuous time, as well as real-time, quantum dynamics simulations. Our results can be used in the design of driven quantum systems with desired properties, enabling the development of novel applications in quantum science and engineering. Human perceptions of animacy are highly subjective, varying greatly between cultures and individuals, yet share a common thread - a fundamental distinction is made between living and non-living entities. We propose a unified framework consisting of two distinct dimensions - visuocategorizability and agency - to capture the complexities of animacy, encompassing a broad spectrum of object categorization to highly sophisticated animal behavior. Through the inclusion of agency as a standalone aspect of animacy, our approach identifies a significant independent contribution, suggesting that this category remains inherently nuanced. We further investigate the interplay between these dimensions and other visual attributes, discovering a hierarchical structure where visuocategorizability serves as a primary driver of agency, and both are influenced by the overall shape and face-specific features of the subject. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate that a model incorporating these dimensions yields a higher level of accuracy in classification tasks, as well as better performance in distinguishing between animate and inanimate objects. Additionally, we observe an interesting phenomenon known as the "agent shift", where there is a tendency to attribute agency to objects exhibiting visuocategorizability that is either incomplete or indeterminate. This bias is found to be a widespread phenomenon across various cultures and remains a persistent feature of human cognition. We further explore the implications of this phenomenon on our understanding of the animacy continuum and the practices and beliefs associated with it, revealing a complex interplay between local agency, visuocategorizability, and the distribution of moral and cultural values. We conclude by highlighting the broad applications of our framework across multiple disciplines, including psychology, anthropology, philosophy, and the design of artificial intelligence systems. We also discuss the potential for further research into the "agent shift" phenomenon, as well as the potential risks and benefits associated with the animacy continuum in real-world contexts. We make our dataset and experiment code publicly available to facilitate future exploration and improvement of our proposed approach. We further provide an interactive demo of our model, along with an animated illustration of the "agent shift" phenomenon, which can be accessed via the project website. Some recent pandemic events have shown how a single infection source can lead to numerous infections within an enclosed space, prompting us to modify the standard SIS model to better capture these occurrences. In our proposed model, a super-spreader can transmit the infection to all other susceptible individuals at an accelerated rate, and we have found that this change results in the model exhibiting hysteresis behavior characteristic of switch-like dynamics, subject to specific parameter constraints. In addition, we have investigated the model's projections onto its bifurcation plane in depth. Notably, it has been discovered that this model predicts the possibility of noise-induced switching between two different equilibrium states, which can be interpreted as the model's expected number of super-spreader transmissions during an epidemic. By incorporating additional parameters, such as the average number of individuals in an enclosed space and the efficacy of masks, we have further developed the model to provide a quantitative framework for predicting the intensity of super-spreader transmissions during the pandemic. Nonetheless, the limitations of the current model version, which assumes a fixed short latency period between infection and becoming infectious, also means it has been validated against real-time data from the 2020 Seoul COVID-19 outbreak. Furthermore, we have explored the application of the model to this specific epidemic data set, with promising results. Nonetheless, the model requires adjustment to accommodate longer latency periods, which can be achieved by introducing additional parameters but also suggests that many infections may go unreported. Ultimately, the model offers a practical tool for predicting the number of super-spreader transmissions during future pandemic scenarios. Understanding and measuring the magnetic field on open flares surfaces relies on mapping vector magnetic field components. However, measuring $B_{z}$ component values can be challenging, especially at areas near to the photospheric boundary where simple 180-degree inverted field components occur. Current data inference techniques often overlook the fill fraction of magnetic elements, which is crucial, especially when searching for negative $B_{z}$ component values. We developed a technique to estimate $B_{z}$ component values while considering the fill fraction of magnetics, tested it using synthetic data, and found it to be accurate even in areas with complex geometry. Using this technique, we reanalyzed 13 $180^\circ$ rotated vector magnetograms from the Solar Optical Spectrum Instrument at the Daniel K. Inglefield Solar Telescope in Saori Kudo's database. The corrected data inference resulted in a more accurate matching with the original $B_{z}$ component values, especially in regions near the photospheric boundary. We found that fill fraction estimation is particularly important for estimating $B_{z}$ component values in complex sunspot regions, especially during solar cycles when more spotty flare surfaces occur. Evaluating this technique's applicability to real-time data through simulated simulations shows that fill fraction estimation improves the accuracy of $B_{z}$ component value inference, even in areas with strong magnetic fields, where the technique itself may not completely overcome the limitation of only having two component vector magnetic field maps. However, considering fill fraction fraction can improve accuracy by decreasing the residual $B_{z}$ component value noise, especially in rotated sunspot regions. The updated data inference technique is valuable for improving the assessment of magnetic field strengths on open sunspot flare surfaces. The technique's advantages are independent of the specific imaging technique used and it can be applied to historical database entries, making it a valuable asset for solar researchers. The key limitation of not being able to accurately determine $B_{z}$ component values in completely non-magnetic areas remains a challenge for future research. The updated technique provides a more precise assessment of magnetic field strengths on flare surfaces, especially in regions with complex sunspot patterns, and can enhance the accuracy of predictions related to solar energy releases through flares and solar jets. The updated technique also enhances the accuracy of magnetic field strength assessments in closed sunspot regions, which are more common during solar cycles with strong magnetic field fluctuations. The most significant benefit of this new technique is the significantly improved accuracy of $B_{z}$ component value estimates, especially in areas near the photospheric boundary,

We demonstrate the effectiveness and simplicity of this method by applying it to a complex-valued neural network, specifically the CCN, and observe a marked improvement in its performance. Hyperparameter tuning in AI models, especially using methods like grid search, is common. Yet, these traditional techniques are impractical for most organizations due to the expense of training on private data sets. As a result, many rely on incremental learning, a process that uses previous training and combines it with new data to improve the model. Although effective, incremental learning typically requires the same user data for both training and evaluation, which stems from how models are typically developed. Our research challenges this expectation by designing and testing two new methods, both of which learn model hyperparameters independently of evaluation data. We put these methods through a rigorous examination by using them on real-world projects involving private data sets from companies and institutions, as well as publicly available data sets, and our results show that both methods accurately identify hyperparameters that yield top-performing models. Our work and findings are significant contributors to the field of hyperparameter tuning within the context of private data sets. We define a Coxeter group's wedge as a group generated by a specified set of elements, whose mutual reflection properties mirror those of a given Coxeter system. We then establish the concept of a Coxeter system's wide wedge, characterized by a significant number of unitary spheres in its geometric representation. We demonstrate that for any Coxeter system, there exists a corresponding wide wedge with a comparable number of spheres, specifically proportional to the square of the largest element in its generating set. Conversely, we can identify the original Coxeter system from this wide wedge's geometric properties. Furthermore, we show that both the number of spheres in the wide wedge and the ratio of its largest to smallest elements are computable using simple algebraic formulas. Additionally, we discover that the wide wedge's sphere arrangement shares the same non-crossing properties as its parent Coxeter system, thereby providing a natural generalization to systems featuring complex reflections. We also explore and analyze specific instances of these systems, including both finite Coxeter groups and infinite groups comprising repeated reflections across parallel lines. Moreover, we discover that both the braid monoid and the Artin-Greene-Nijenhuis monoid can be interpreted as wide wedges of Coxeter systems. We also establish a connection between these monoids, the notion of a positive integer's primitive part, and the associated wide wedge structure. Ultimately, our investigation reveals that the wide wedge structure possesses a higher level of generality, as it can be viewed as a distinct, more unified framework encompassing both Coxeter buildings of rank higher than two and the aforementioned monoids. We also establish that both the latter monoids and buildings of rank higher than two possess a specific geometric property, which we term "inversion consistency". We then demonstrate that this property is equivalent to "inversion consistency" in the context of Coxeter systems of rank two, thereby providing a meaningful extension of the original problem that sparked this research. We also explore various theoretical and practical applications of this expanded framework, including its connection to both topology and geometry. Finally, we conclude by highlighting the overall impact and scope of this expanded framework, which we believe will serve as a premier platform for both future research and theoretical advancements within the Coxeter group category. We also propose and investigate several potential future research directions within this expanded framework, which we believe will further contribute to the understanding and development of Coxeter groups. To analyze this data, a method was developed for correcting atmospheric effects and comparing observed spectral patterns to those of tiny magnetic apstar particles, which resulted in the creation of a comprehensive dataset of chemically distinctive stars and stellar populations for various residual abundance analyses. The findings revealed that the chemical properties of these stars align with iron and nickel abundances, and their spectral patterns correspond to a specific residual abundance pattern, which has never been observed in our galaxy. Furthermore, the analysis of these stars' spectral patterns and chemical compositions revealed unique insights into their compositions and the limitations of current stellar evolution models. Additionally, the analysis of their spectra suggested the presence of unusual elemental residues associated with certain abundance analyses, which could be linked to specific stellar populations, including globular cluster stars, open cluster stars, and a chemically enriched stellar population in the bulge, the Milky Way's central region. The investigation of these residues also uncovered the decay of certain elements from the actinide family, particularly curium-244, which has implications for our understanding of the chemical elements formed and dispersed in the galaxy. The methodology developed for this analysis has been made available for use by the broader scientific community through the STARFLEXT platform, which enables researchers to explore the chemically distinctive stars and stellar populations identified in the SIT dataset, as well as prioritize future observational work. The investigation has also been used to assess the capabilities of current stellar evolution models for predicting the compositions of the most chemically distinctive stars, which could be refined through further analysis of the residues found in these stars.
