We investigate the spread of rumors within a population by applying queueing theory to network communities. Our analysis focuses on a simplified model where a single individual spreads a rumor to others, and we examine the results in terms of peak coefficient and attenuation coefficient. We then expand the model to consider the impact of precursor features and location information on the rumor's spread. Through numerical analysis of the expanded model, we find that location information can significantly influence the peak and attenuation coefficients of rumors. We also explore the effects of different distribution shapes on the peak and attenuation coefficients. Furthermore, we develop a prediction algorithm to estimate the peak and attenuation coefficients of rumors based on precursor features and location information. Through simulations with a agent-based model, we compare the results with the predicted outcomes. Our research provides a theoretical framework and quantitative insights into the spread of rumors, in addition to presenting a practical prediction method. Ultimately, our work offers a foundation for exploring interventions that can slow the spread of rumors. We demonstrate the applicability and usefulness of our model by applying it to empirical data from social media platforms. Additionally, we analyze the ethical implications of our research and the potential risks of using our prediction algorithm for malicious purposes, such as spreading false information. Our study presents a unique queueing theory-based approach to analyzing the spread of rumors within network communities. We achieve this by transforming the interdependent relationships between people into independent transactions between a sender and a receiver. Our model assumes that each individual can spread the rumor to a specific number of others before it loses significance, and we refer to this as the rumor's reach. We establish closed-form expressions for the peak and attenuation coefficients of the rumor, in addition to its reach, by applying classical queueing theory techniques. Our research expands on the initial model by incorporating precursor features and location information that influence the rumor's spread. We achieve this by modifying the queueing theory model to accommodate varying transaction success rates at different locations. Through numerical analysis of the expanded model, we explore the effects of location information and precursor features on the peak and attenuation coefficients of the rumor. We also develop a algorithm to predict the peak and attenuation coefficients of the rumor based on precursor features and location information by training the model using empirical data from a social media platform. Our research offers a theoretical framework and quantitative insights into the spread of rumors, in addition to presenting a practical prediction method. Ultimately, our work offers a foundation for exploring interventions that can slow the spread of rumors. We demonstrate the applicability and usefulness of our model by applying it to empirical data from social media platforms.

We have determined the distance to the Fornax cluster by using the planetary nebulae luminosity function (PNLFF). This analysis is based on a comprehensive catalogue of 8,517 faint point sources within the cluster's central region, compiled from Hubble Space Telescope images. The PNLFF measurement was developed through a complete count of the detected planetary nebulae, occurring when the number of sources detected exceeds the background and the rate of new discoveries slows. A comprehensive modelling approach was employed, accounting for the observed population of planetary nebulae, as well as the physical processes that form and fade them over time. The resulting PNLFF was fitted using a detailed theoretical model, incorporating the mass function of the cluster's stellar population, the luminosity of planetary nebulae, the filling factor, the ionizing energy spectrum of the central stars, the absorption and scattering of excess radiation, and the spatial distribution of the sources. The analysis yielded a distance of 4.78 +/- 0.03 megaparsecs to the Fornax cluster, with a velocity dispersion of 259 +/- 16 km/s and a mass range for the dominant component of 1.0 +/- 0.2 x 10^12 solar masses. The detected planetary nebulae comprise 1,560 sources, representing about 18% of the expected total population within the observed field of view, and have an age equivalent to about 1.5 billion years. The study of the PNLFF also provided insights into the mass function of the cluster's stellar population, revealing a significant medium-mass gap, as well as the spatial distribution of the sources, which showed the cluster to be roughly spherical in nature. The data further allowed for the estimation of the absolute brightness of the central stars of the planetary nebulae, which was found to be -6.45 +/- 0.45 megaparsec/solar mass, and the lifetime of the sources, calculated as 25,000 to 37,500 years. Our proposed Generation Architecture for Stream Processing (GASP) serves as a framework for automatically generating high-performance numerical routines on stream processors. Stream processors excel at handling massive amounts of data, but require pre-computed numerical operations, which can be time-consuming to create manually. In contrast, GASP yields numerical routines with superior performance, matching that of hand-optimized codes for real-world datasets, without the need for manual optimization. Furthermore, without losing speed, it delivers numerical routines for theoretical datasets of any size. The underlying GASP architecture is customizable, as proven by our tailored versions of the GASP architecture achieving equivalent performance on real-world datasets with widely different characteristics. The notable absence of hand-optimized codes for certain applications presents an opportunity to apply the GASP architecture in these instances. We demonstrate the efficacy of GASP with specific numerical routines and stream processors, prior to showcasing its broader potential. Our study reveals that networks can be trained to excel at tasks other than classification, such as image segmentation and generating artificial data, using different objective functions. For example, using KL Divergence as the objective function can enable a network to efficiently produce artificial data similar to a given dataset. Consequently, our primary contribution involves presenting an straightforward method to calculate the expected performance of a network on unseen data with the same distribution as the training data, without the need for additional trials. A comprehensive theoretical investigation of the effects of electron interaction and anisotropic pairing on the topological properties of the energy spectrum in superconducting materials is presented. Using a general method to analyze the magnetic susceptibility near the Fermi surface in these materials, we found that the filling factor of the magnetic momentum space, which determines the susceptibility, can vary significantly depending on the orientation of the external magnetic field. Notably, the field-filled condition, a crucial requirement for the $d$+$s'$-wave pairing scenario, results in an irregular Fermi surface and significantly affects the magnetic susceptibility and the energy gap at the extremities of the energy spectrum. Moreover, the dependence of the filling factor on the orientation of the $s'$-wave pairing component leads to an irregular distribution of the energy gap along the Fermi surface, particularly at the points where the pairing function changes sign, leading to zero-energy states at those points. The presence of zero-energy states and the irregular Fermi surface surface barries the realization of the field-filled condition in momentum space, and may explain the limited success of using the BCS model to explain magnetic field-dependent specific heat in superconducting materials. A deep-neural-network (DNN) approach was developed to enhance the quality of low-dose PET images using frame-by-frame training and the support of MRI images.  This research utilized a U-Net architecture to develop a bias-variance tradeoff theory for low-density PET image reconstruction, thereby providing a basis for a variance-reducing technique called multi-forward pass noise augmentation.  To further improve variability, the approach was modified to incorporate MRI images in a way that allows for a variance-increasing block and a fusion layer, resulting in a variational density-based U-Net.  This new model was applied to reconstruct PET images from 2 to 10 times lower dose levels, producing results that are statistically equivalent to conventional RECONSTRUCION methods.  Furthermore, the framework allows for the incorporation of physiological information from other sources, such as bioluminescence images, without significant computational overhead.  A key advantage of this method is its capability to train networks on an extremely small number of patient data sets, specifically 5 sets were utilized in this study.  The results show that this method can accurately reconstruct mid-reconstruction slices from as low as 10 times the standard dose level, or the equivalent of 3 times the standard dose level for all slices.  The framework and variational density-based U-Net model show particular potential for enhancing image quality in whole-body PET scans from extremely low dose levels, or in specific tissues from bioluminescence images of transparent animals. This study examines how contextualized language models affect the performance of coreference resolution tasks, specifically exploring their effect on predictions derived from centering theory. Building on the success of BERT-based coreference resolution, we investigate alternative models including FLERT, SPERT, and C3, and coreference resolution systems trained on the DTB7.0 dataset. Our analysis reveals significant improvements in the accuracy of these models in predicting $\kappa$ and $\gamma$ relations, and we find that these models overestimate the frequency of link relations. Furthermore, our research identifies patterns of coreference errors made by these models and provides an analysis of the features of entities involved in coreference relations. Our findings highlight the potential of these models to capture the complexities of coreference relations, but also highlight areas for future improvement, such as addressing the bias in these models to prefer simpler coreference relations. Our code is available online at https://github.com/liu-lian/c3-flert-spert-coref-ct-analysis. Our research contributes to a deeper understanding of the coreference resolution processes of state-of-the-art language models and provides a quantitative comparison of their performance in predicting coreference relations predicted by centering theory. Our research also offers a coreference prediction dataset annotated with centering theory predictions, which can be used for training new coreference resolution systems or evaluating the performance of pre-trained language models on coreference resolution tasks. Our analysis is specifically applicable to the development of coreference resolution systems for contemporary texts, but our coreference prediction dataset can be used for ancient texts, such as the ones found in the Great Epic of Sundiata, which features a high frequency of link relations similar to modern texts. Our research demonstrates the widespread applicability of our findings to coreference relations found in diverse cultural texts across different time periods. Our research also contributes to the development of a new evaluation metric for coreference resolution systems based on the accuracy of predictions of $\kappa$ and $\gamma$ relations. Our research proposes a simple method to predict $\kappa$ and $\gamma$ relations from the features of coreferential entities, which can be used as a baseline for future research, such as incorporating syntactic features or exploring different language models. As WiFi fingerprint-based positioning systems become more widespread, efficiently estimating the distance between geospatial coordinates and WiFi measurements has become increasingly vital. Nonetheless, traditional regression-based estimation methods tend to yield lackluster performance, as the true distance is often obfuscated by noisy measurements. We propose a novel approach, termed DistanceAware, that leverages neighborhood information to enhance distance estimation by identifying areas of similar distance patterns. Furthermore, to further optimize performance, we introduce a multi-scale approach that facilitates more accurate distance prediction. Through extensive testing on real-world data sets, our method demonstrates significant improvements in distance estimation accuracy across various scenarios. Moreover, the robustness of DistanceAware is validated through the deployment of a real-time application, showcasing the practical viability of our approach. Ultimately, our work highlights the value of considering geospatial context in WiFi-based estimation tasks and provides a framework for improving other location-based services. Our code and data are available at: \url{https://github.com/HaotianWang/DistanceAware}.

A major factor that can influence beam-RF interactions and the threshold current in energy recovery linacs is the choice of filling pattern, which varies depending on the application. To effectively manage beam-RF interactions, it's essential to investigate the impact of filling patterns, particularly in the multi-pass energy recovery linac, where multiple passes of low-energy beams through the accelerator can catch high-energy beams traveling in the opposite direction. Due to the complex nature of linear matrix equations involving both the beam and RF fields, analyzing the effect of filling patterns involves extensive computational work. In this research, we present a simpler approach based on the phase space approach, which enables us to study beam-RF interactions in various linac configurations by examining the relationships between filling pattern properties, current distribution, phase space distribution, and energy loss along the beam path. As a specific example, we explore the dynamics of a 12-pass energy recovery linac using this method and find that even slight changes in filling pattern properties can lead to significant increases in threshold current, up to 100 times in some cases. Furthermore, we identify the filling pattern that results in the minimum threshold current, which we find can increase the threshold current current by as much as 50 times in some cases, achieving this effect without sacrificing beam current. Notably, we discover that the optimal filling pattern involves a unique relationship between beam and RF phase spaces that differs from the relationship typically observed in single-pass energy recovery linacs. In addition, we propose an optimization method that combines the approach based on phase space with conventional numerical methods to further improve the threshold current, achieving a 20 times increase in some cases without reducing the beam current. The research demonstrated here can serve as a foundation for investigating other linac configurations and providing practical guidelines for implementing energy recovery linacs in real-world applications. The proposed method also offers a useful example of a complex problem that can be solved using a simplified model based on a smaller number of parameters, a common challenge faced in many fields of physics and engineering. The code used in this research is available for public use on GitHub, featuring examples of beam-RF interactions in both linear and circular accelerators. The code utilizes the SciPy and NumPy libraries popular in the scientific community, making it accessible to a wide range of users. Given a graph G = (V, E), the geodesic distance tractance problem involves finding the smallest integer k such that for any pair of vertices u, v in V, the number of vertices on the shortest path between u and v is less than or equal to k. This research investigates an expanded version of this problem, where the geodesic distance between any two vertices u and v is limited to a predetermined number k_p, and presents two integer linear programming models to compute the minimum value of k_p. A theoretical analysis of these models reveals that they provide lower and upper bounds for the problem's solution. Additionally, a computational study among real-world datasets reveals that one of these models yields accurate results in comparison to lower bound models. A notable observation from this study is that many graphs have a geodesic distance threshold of 0, and this is shown to be equivalent to computing the metric dimension of the graph, with a further observation that this dimension can vary for truncated versions of the graph. A specific case where the distance threshold is 1 has been previously studied under the name of the "cover time" of the graph. A final example illustrates that the geodesic distance tractance problem and the metric dimension problem have distinct solutions, as the latter does not account for the restriction of staying within the specified distance threshold. The relationship between these two problems is explored, and it is demonstrated that a subset of a graph's vertices that forms the minimum metric dimension can be expanded to include additional vertices, resulting in a new metric dimension of a size equal to a certain threshold k, while maintaining the property of being minimal for any k smaller than the current standard, although this standard itself can also be altered. The investigation of this topic involves introducing a novel ordering of a graph's vertices, which can be utilized to analyze the coverage time of the graph, and it is shown that this order can be used to determine the minimum number of steps required to guarantee that every vertex in the graph has been visited at least once. Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) vary significantly across broad energy spectra, and long observational periods are needed to fully understand their behavior. However, traditional analysis approaches are often hindered by data inconsistencies and different observation lengths, which can affect the accuracy of conclusions drawn from them. In this study, a novel method is introduced that seamlessly connects data sets with distinct lengths, even across different observational periods, enabling a unified, in-depth analysis of AGN variability. By utilizing a linear model to account for changes in count rates between observations, this approach successfully bridges data gaps and provides a comprehensive view of AGNs, including tight correlations between soft and hard X-ray count rates, as well as detailed temporal sequences of count rate fluctuations. By employing this method to monitor data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, crucial variability patterns in the AGN NGC 1068 have been uncovered, also confirmed through soft X-ray spectroscopy with the Advanced X-ray Astrophysics Facility. Despite its success with the current dataset, areas for improvement in the analysis are identified, such as the incorporation of uncertainty quantification and sampling, which are crucial for drawing definitive conclusions from large observational sets. Additionally, this study paves the way for applying this analysis method to other AGNs and other observatories, offering a broad potential for enhancing our understanding of these complex objects through in-depth analysis of existing observational data sets. Although it was developed primarily to analyze X-ray data, this method can be adapted for other energy spectra, such as those in the ultraviolet and gamma-ray bands, or even multiple messengers like neutrino observations. Through this research, a key challenge in AGN research is addressed, namely, how to thoroughly examine these elusive objects' variability over extended observation periods. By combining disparate observations, a unified view of AGNs is achieved, revealing their intricate temporal sequences of energy count rate fluctuations. This study also leverages high-resolution soft X-ray spectroscopy to reveal variable emission line strengths and their connection to continuous energy distributions, thereby eluding the need for assumption-based modeling approaches. As a result, this work fulfills the entire spectrum of low-energy X-ray analysis, from data reconciliation to in-depth examination of variable, complex objects, such as active galactic nuclei. In the context of combinatorial auctions, where multiple bidders compete for multiple items and can submit arbitrary submission strategies, establishing approximate fairness through valuation-based methods is crucial. However, achieving optimal approximate fairness (within a factor of 1+ε) through valuation-based methods in multi-item auctions is currently proven to be computationally challenging for 2-player, 2-item and general n-player, n-item scenarios. This paper addresses these challenges by introducing two novel fair pricing mechanisms. For the 2-player, 2-item scenario, we develop a bipartite matching-based valuation that enables approximating the fair price to an ε-degree precision in O(1/ε) steps. For the general n-player, n-item scenario, we leverage a directed graph-based valuation that allows for approximately fair price determination to an ε-degree precision in O(1/ε) steps. Both valuations rely on a common framework that utilizes a progressive matching process, combining the power of combinatorial anatomy with efficiency guarantees for approximately fair pricing. Moreover, this paper demonstrates a key insight where a certain property of a valuation implies the existence of a related valuation that ensures a specific approximation quality can be achieved in polynomial time. This property serves as an underlying requirement for both the above-mentioned valuations, ensuring that both meet the desired approximation fairness standards while maintaining polynomial-time complexity. This paper also offers an underlying property characterization, valuation properties that ensure polynomial-time approximation fairness for any combinatorial auction, along with a formal algorithm that achieves this approximation for the previously introduced valuations. This characterization demonstrates the inherent significance of this property by showcasing that for any combinatorial auction, validating a valuation's property implies that the associated valuation ensures a specific approximation fairness standard can be achieved in polynomial time. By analyzing three-dimensional density models of small binary asteroids, we tested point spread function analysis techniques used to identify binaries in wide field surveys. Changes in the point spread function due to the motion of asteroids within their orbits were examined using a convolution algorithm. This analysis revealed that the technique effectively captured the dynamics of small binary asteroids but also had limitations, particularly for objects with short orbital periods. The technique's accuracy depended on the shape of the primary body and the distribution of mass within the binary system. We simulated measurements similar to those from wide field surveys and developed a binary detection algorithm. This algorithm rated the likelihood of each asteroid being binary-based on its shape, orientation, and the point spread function. By applying this algorithm to simulated measurements, we found that it successfully identified binary asteroids with orbital periods of up to twenty days, although it was less accurate for objects with closer orbital periods. Furthermore, the algorithm ranked the most probable binaries, enabling the selection of candidates from large populations of asteroids. These findings suggest that point spread function analysis of wide field surveys can be used to discover binary asteroids, specifically those with longer orbital periods, and may be combined with other techniques for detecting binaries, such as periodic light curves, to efficiently identify them among large populations of asteroids. We present an example application of this analysis to the wide field survey Pan-STARRS1, where it enhances the detection of binary asteroids, particularly those with orbital periods of up to 10.5 days, and increases the predicted binary fraction to 0.25 for asteroids larger than 100 meters in diameter. This is significantly higher than previously estimated fractions, demonstrating that many small binary asteroids remain undiscovered and highlighting the value of re-examining existing survey data with advanced analysis techniques. The algorithm used in this study is now a component of the Asteroid Orbitally Linked to a Satellite, a binary detection algorithm that combines point spread function analysis with other techniques to efficiently identify binary asteroids from wide field surveys. This algorithm is potentially valuable for future surveys with high-resolution imaging capability, such as the Lucid Nature Camera on the International Space Station. The approach presented in this research can be extended to detect ternary and quadruple asteroid systems by modeling their densities and orbital periods. However, this would require the development of new algorithms and more sophisticated simulations due to the additional variables involved. The current study provides a foundation for further investigation into the detection of multi-body asteroid systems. We present an original approach to assess network effects resulting from peer influences by utilizing extremity measures. This method enables the estimation of recursive peer effects in various networks, overcoming previous challenges related to collapsing tables due to the inclusion of self-loops. We demonstrate the validity and accuracy of our method by conducting simulations and comparing it to alternative strategies. Furthermore, we apply this approach to empirical data, analyzing peer influences in a network of friends who follow each other's dietary choices and comparing the results with an alternative specification. Our method yields consistent and accurate estimations of the effects of peer group extremity on individual behavior, capturing the influences of friends who adhere to the extreme choice more closely than other specifications. Additionally, we find that the most extreme friends in a individual's network have a greater impact on their behavior than friends who are less extreme. Ultimately, our approach provides a useful tool for researchers seeking to examine peer influences within networks, particularly in cases where relationships are asymmetric. We also contribute to the existing literature on dietary choices by revealing that, despite declines in extreme choices overall, there has been a surge in polarized dietary preferences in recent years. This shift toward greater extremity appears to be driven by peer influences, rather than changes in individual preferences. We urge policymakers and researchers to consider the important role of network effects and preference distribution when designing and evaluating policies aimed at changing behavior. We also propose possible interventions that can counter the tendency towards greater extremity in dietary choices, such as promoting moderate choices as preferred defaults or implementing incentives for individuals to adopt more versatile dietary patterns. We offer our data and analysis code for public use, encouraging other researchers to adopt and build upon our method and analysis. We propose several potential applications of our approach, including the examination of peer influences in other social networks, such as sporting teams, corporations, or online communities, and the analysis of choice extremity in other domains, such as financial, environmental or health-related behaviors. We also outline possible extensions of our method to allow for heterogeneous peer effects, learning externalities, or recursive peer effects across multiple layers of influence. We suggest that our approach can be utilized in policy evaluation by considering the impact of policies on the distribution of preference extremes within a network, and the resulting peer effects on individual behavior. We propose that our method can be applied to guide policymakers in identifying targeted interventions that counter negative tendencies towards greater extremity in choice behaviors. We presented a novel collaborative game framework called MindWiki, where agents work together to reach common goals by modifying the properties of peer agents. We then tested this framework in the "Linking Islands" problem, where agents must connect islands by linking them with bridges of specific lengths. Our results showed that the method successfully incorporating a theory-of-mind approach outperformed both a self-referential and non-self-referential version of the game. Furthermore, it was found that the framework was highly effective in correcting its own mistakes, and its performance could be significant under time constraints. Additionally, we observed an unusual phenomenon where the theory-of-mind version of the game would sometimes achieve the same level of success as the ideal solution but at a lower cost. This was attributed to the abnormal attraction the framework has to changing its own properties, and this abnormal attraction can be adjusted by incorporating a delay mechanism. Finally, we discovered that the framework excels in situations where the available information is inconsistent, and it has the potential to be enhanced as a model of abnormal attraction-based theory-of-mind. Our MindWiki game framework and related experiments are simple but innovative and may serve as a starting point for more complex problems and experiments. Our in-depth analysis of four distinct shallow knotted proteins incorporates molecular dynamics simulations and detailed structural examinations to explore their folding mechanisms. Compared to deeply knotted proteins, which often require multiple steps to fold, our findings reveal that shallow knotted proteins typically follow a single, unified pathway to achieve their knotted configuration. This contrast is attributed to these proteins' relatively simple helical structures, which minimize the likelihood of misfolded, non-knotted intermediates. Our research demonstrates that the side chains' interactions play a crucial role in securing the knotted structure after the core has formed, with a notable example being the protein FKN, which requires significant effort to avoid non-knotted intermediates. Our results also highlight the significance of hydrophobic forces and specific interactions in maintaining the knotted architecture, alongside the core formation that is a common aspect among all proteins. Ultimately, our study highlights the intricate folding processes of shallow knotted proteins, which defy the two-state folding model commonly observed in other proteins. Our data further suggests that these proteins' folding mechanisms are exceptionally robust, with minimal tendency to produce misfolded products, thus offering potential insights for understanding protein folding dynamics and designing suitable experiments. Our findings are compatible with recent investigations into deeply knotted proteins and jointly contribute to the growing body of research dedicated to unraveling the complex, knotted protein structures. Our software packages, including KNTRACER and KNFOLD, which were utilized for this analysis, are specifically designed to examine knotted protein structures and folding processes via molecular dynamics simulations. These tools are available for download at https://sourceforge.net/projects/kntracer/. Our research presents a significant expansion on our previous findings published in the study depicted in Fig. 1. We examine a symplectic form's irrationality concept and demonstrate how it can be adapted to a modified form while the form remains topologically equivalent in a specific category of closed symplectic forms on certain types of manifolds. This investigation arises from a consideration of modified Euler top systems and contributes to an understanding of the relationships between these systems and closed symplectic forms. Furthermore, it provides an initial proof of a conjectured relationship between the modified irrationality of Euler top systems and their conservation laws. These findings also reveal connections between these systems' topological properties and their energy function designs. Finally, it paves the way for studying conservative and dissipative dynamics on the closed symplectic forms' configuration space. This research was motivated by the study of rotating top dynamics, which serves as a key example. This dynamics, with its modified Euler top systems, has an intriguing relationship with the 3-dimensional Euclidean space's closed symplectic forms and reflects the symmetry of the sphere in a non-trivial, altered form. This relationship enables the systematic analysis of these systems' topological properties and their relationship to their energy function designs. It also yields an evaluation of the rotating top dynamics' conservation laws and its energy function's configuration space's topological invariants. This evaluation further leads to an assessment of the stability of these dynamics within the space of all closed symplectic forms. This stability is found to be fragile and can be visually illustrated through various rotating top dynamics' image sequences. The Nambu-Goldstone theorem is inherently linked to the spontaneous breaking of continuous symmetries in the mass spectrum of particles. However, the massive meson, kaon, in the kaon condensation model appears to be an exception to this rule, thus necessitating a reinterpretation of its mass generation mechanisms. We have investigated the quark mass and kaon condensation contributions to the massive meson and have various alternatives to accomplish the mass generation required for the massive Nambu-Goldstone boson, aided by an analogy to the massive Dirac fermion. Moreover, the proposed methods are distinguishable from the massive scenario using the mechanism of partial symmetry breaking. The proposed models can be applied to the massive mesons within the massive vector meson version of the Linear Sigma Model. We have further analyzed the mass spectra of mesons resulting from these models. The results show that the conventional quark-mass and kaon-condensation contributions yield inconsistent mass spectra. Consequently, additional mass generation mechanisms for the massive meson are required, which can be provided by the additional quark or scalar sector interactions. The mass spectra obtained from these additional mass generation mechanisms demonstrate the distinction from the massive meson within the massive vector meson version of the Linear Sigma Model from the mechanism of partial symmetry breaking. The consistency of the mass spectra with the usual quark-mass and kaon-condensation contributions is achieved when the mass scale is adjusted to the appropriate one. The mass spectra also demonstrate the impact of the additional quark or scalar sector interactions on the mass levels of the mesons. The application to the massive mesons within the Linear Sigma Model allows us to interpret the mass generation mechanisms of the massive Nambu-Goldstone boson in the kaon condensation model as being associated with the additional quark or scalar sector interactions rather than the quark mass and kaon condensation itself. The proposed models have the capability to be used in various extensions of the Linear Sigma Model. The name ``glueball mesons" for the $f_0$, $a_0$, and $D_s^*$ states, which were assigned the status of massive Nambu-Goldstone bosons, may now be reevaluated as being misleading. The name "glueball mesons" implies that the mass generation mechanisms of these mesons are linked to the mechanism of partial symmetry breaking caused by the additional quark or scalar sector interactions, which trap the massive Nambu-Goldstone boson mesons in its spectrum

Our research proposes the DISCO approach to counterfactual generation for predictive models. Our counterfactual theory ensures that counterfactuals respect the model's predictive decisions and take into account the underlying data distribution. We achieve this by incorporating a regulatory module in the counterfactual generation process that takes into account both the model and data counterfactual regulations. When generating counterfactuals for a particular dataset, we found that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of both accuracy and similarity to the original data. Furthermore, our counterfactuals demonstrate enhanced generalization and robustness when used for training and testing. Specifically, we found that models trained with our counterfactuals using a semisupervised framework exhibited both improved performance on the original distribution and robustness on distributions that have been altered. These findings are evident across multiple dataset scenarios. Our approach and associated evaluations are part of a wider research effort into counterfactual generation, particularly focusing on machine learning models and counterfactuals for a single dataset. We also outline potential directions for future research and possible applications of counterfactual generation with a broader perspective. Researchers have successfully grown epitaxial materials called palladium germanium alloys on graphene, which serves as a single-atom thick substrate. To better understand these grown materials, detailed investigations of their structure, chemistry, and properties are necessary. By growing these materials at different temperatures, different crystal structures can develop within the same sample, allowing for the study of distinct epitaxial domains. Typically, a certain crystal structure forms at higher temperatures, gradually transforming into another structure at lower growth temperatures. However, contrary to expectations, growing materials at both extremely high and low temperatures can result in the coexistence of both crystal structures across different regions, creating distinct areas with different structures. These studies have revealed how the chemistry of the growing material changes with temperature and how the chemistry of the graphene substrate influences the development of different crystal structures. Ultimately, growing these materials at high and low temperatures can result in the presence of both crystal structures across the entire sample. Given the intricate relationship between temperature, chemistry, and crystal structure, minimizing the influence of the graphene substrate is essential; this can be achieved by growing the material at high temperatures. A computational model has also been developed to predict the chemistry of the growing material and its impact on the crystal structures that form, bringing the field closer to developing scalable and material-independent methods for growing these epitaxial materials.

A significant challenge in developing intelligent models for classification lies in creating large-scale labeled datasets. A novel approach called single-to-multi-label (S2M) sampling is proposed to generate multi-label data with superior quality and minimal costs, by leveraging existing single-labeled training datasets. A probabilistic model is introduced to estimate the label correlation structure, which is then used to generate new samples with enhanced consistency. Experiments using real-world datasets show that our method successfully captures the spirit of multi-label classification and achieves superior performance when using both small and large sets of existing data. In particular, using Wikipedia as an example, we were able to create a massive multi-label dataset covering twenty-nine categories, and demonstrated that our approach could handle complex relationships between labels efficiently. Moreover, our method compared favorably to competing sampling methods and rigorous experiments designed to simulate real-world applications. In addition, a comprehensive analysis was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of our approach in uncovering hidden label patterns, revealing aspects such as its ability to discover both subtle and significant label relationships and its robustness in multiple scenarios. Furthermore, our method was tested on real-world datasets, including MSRC-21, FLICKR30k, and PTC-MR, and the results showed that it yielded performances equivalent to or better than those achieved by current state-of-the-art models, with some cases indicating a significant improvement of up to 12.3%. In contrast to existing sampling methods that focus primarily on generating random label fluctuations, our approach is distinguished by its capability to produce more precise and sustainable samples, ensuring consistent classification performance across various datasets. All the code and datasets used in this research are available for public access at this URL: https://github.com/Chenyue002/s2m_sampling. With its notable advantages and superior performance, our S2M sampling method is anticipated to serve as a valuable reference for the community in the realm of artificial data generation via labeling existing datasets. Furthermore, our proposed approach provides a feasible solution for creating large-scale multi-label datasets from existing resources, as demonstrated by our successful application to Wikipedia. In addition, our method offers a significant improvement over existing sampling methods, alongside an underlying model that enables the analysis of label relationships, as demonstrated by experiments using real-world datasets. Lastly, our work is committed to enhancing the accessibility of our methodology and underlying model, along with the code and datasets used in the research, which can be found at this URL: https://github.com/Chenyue002/s2m_sampling. We then demonstrate the existence of a distinct class of monads that are generated by using the Seely construction on weakly natural transformations, which is a more general case than those classified under the Recursion Monad Hierarchy. Furthermore, we establish that the most general category resulting from applying the Seely construction has a form that can be characterized using a set of equational properties, which we refer to as the $\lambda$-theory of weak applicative structures. By incorporating the concept of positivity, we derive a more specific $\lambda$-theory, which we have previously proposed under a different name. Additionally, this work provides a detailed analysis of the connection between weak applicative structures and linear logic, demonstrating that the former serves as a fundamental framework for understanding the properties of certain classes of monads in a categorical context. Prior work on the Recursion Monad Hierarchy is seen as a limited subset of the diverse range of monads with recursive properties, which share certain common characteristics. We also demonstrate that the set of equations defining weak applicative structures are strong enough to capture basic recursive properties, which can be demonstrated through a step-wise process. By examining the relationship between monads and weak applicative structures through the context of categorical semantics, this work aims to contribute to the understanding of categorical foundations of programming languages by providing a framework that can facilitate the analysis of diverse programming languages based on the common framework of weak applicative structures. Medical research institutions and organizations are increasingly facing data privacy challenges, threatening the scalability of artificial intelligence techniques for healthcare.  To address this issue, a privacy-preserving technique for training machine learning models on a large scale has been developed.  The new method, called FedHealth, is an enhanced version of the Federated Learning algorithm that enables the efficient training of wearable activity recognition models using wearable devices.  When comparing FedHealth to traditional techniques for handling privacy and data security, training models on large scales showed significant improvements.  Specifically, FedHealth demonstrated higher accuracy in recognizing wearable activities than the conventional approach, achieving a 25% better performance when classifying complex activities and a 10% better performance when classifying simple activities.  The research also identified factors influencing the performance of wearable activity recognition, including the quality of data measurement, movement intervals, and sensor usage.  To facilitate widespread adoption, the FedHealth code was released as open-source.  The study's limitations highlight the need for further investigation into the privacy-preserving training of models for other healthcare applications, particularly those involving raw biomedical data.  The current version of the code can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/aliTaheri/FedHealth.  The research described in this paper was funded by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada and was conducted in collaboration with the Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada.  The study's findings have been published in the Journal of Medical Internet Technologies and the Proceedings of the Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society.  The work described within this paper was approved by the Research Ethics Board of McMaster University according to policy 5.16.  The code developed for this research was tested on Windows 10, macOS High Sierra, and Linux Ubuntu 18.04 platforms using pyTorch version 1.7.1 and scikit-learn version 0.22.2.  The research involved human participants whose rights have been respected and protected in accordance with the principles outlined in the Helsinki Declaration.  The data utilized for this research were previously collected with the full informed consent of the participants in accordance with the standards set by the Institutional Review Board of McMaster University.  The issue of data privacy in healthcare research has become a significant obstacle to scaling artificial intelligence techniques.  To address this challenge, a large-scale training model was developed using a privacy-preserving technique called FedHealth.  This model enables the efficient training of wearable activity recognition models using wearable devices by tackling communication costs and data privacy concerns.

Additionally, we provide a program that can be used to generate example problems and solve them using the proposed algorithms, with the option to import problems from a specific format. This program is available under an open-source license, allowing for further modification by others. This research and the associated program can serve as a starting point for ongoing work in this area, which remains susceptible to improvement, as evidenced by the recent publications in the field. A lack of research is evident regarding the molecular gas component in extreme, bursty galaxies, especially when it comes to low-density environments like gas reservoirs around galaxies. The lack of suitable transitions of high-density molecular line emitters, such as CI, is likely the main reason for this gap in knowledge. The recent advancement in radio interferometry allows the study of these lines through sensitive observations with the IRAM Individual Element Array (IEA). Using IEA, we carried out an investigative study of the CI line energies in the core of the galaxy NGC 253 using a 45 kilometer baseline and detected four weak lines: CI J=3-2, CI J=4-3, CI J=5-4, and CI J=6-5. The detection of these lines, particularly the stronger J=3-2 transition, is notable in the central region of NGC 253, which has been previously studied with lower sensitivity. By calculating the relative brightness of these lines and comparing them to laboratory data and model simulations, we found that the usual assumption of photochemical equilibrium fails to explain the observed ratios, particularly for the J=4-3 to J=3-2 transition, which are not consistent with models of dense gas in the galaxy. The discovery of a J=4-3 to J=3-2 ratio similar to that of the Milky Way in the central galaxy M83 also challenges the usual idea of a vast, dense molecular gas phase in galaxy cores. Notably, both NGC 253 and M83 show similar J=4-3 to J=3-2 ratio patterns and both exhibit signs of intense starbursts and central gas outflows. Both cases can be explained by the presence of low-density gas in the galaxies' circumnuclear regions. Therefore, a broader investigation of extreme starburst galaxies is necessary to determine the frequency of such density-independent CI line energies. Nonetheless, this study demonstrates that the IEA and similar arrays can detect the more sensitive CI J=1-0 transition in the core of NGC 253 with an integrated line energy of 0.83 Kelvin, equivalent to a column density of 6.4 x 10 to the power of 10 cm minus 2. Additionally, the investigation of the more distant, more bursty galaxy interacting system ARK 144 with IEA reveals a much lower CI J=1-0 column density of 2.5 x 10 to the power of 10 cm minus 2 in the core of the most actively star

Our analysis focuses on approximate analytic expressions for the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in PTA experiments involving the combination of multiple pulsar sources. We evaluated three existing approximations, which rely on varying constraints, and found that the most limiting one, given current PTA data, is the assumption that the 1017 MHz component of J1745-2900 is negligible. We developed two alternative analytic models for the SNR, one accurate and another simplified, and compared their performance to existing approximations by calculating the differences in SNR. Although the more precise models show similar performance to each other but differ from the existing approximations, which are generally conservative by 1-10%, we observed that the SNR differences among the more precise models are extremely small, on the order of 10^-5. This research examines the ASEP system to explore the statistics of a third class of particles that can move through the system. All interactions involve exchanges of units between the particle of interest and randomly situated first and second class particles. The system's initial condition places the third class particle at the beginning, while first and second class particles are randomly distributed. As time passes, the third class particle gains speed, and we find that its velocity distribution conforms to a gamma function. Additionally, we find that the system reaches a stationary state in which the third class particle's velocity and surrounding unit distribution are determined by a stochastic process identical to that found in a system without the third class of particles, and which we have previously studied. This matching allows us to apply previous findings, yielding new insights into the system's stationary state. Finally, we consider a system without boundaries, where the third class of particles can move freely, and we determine the distribution of its displacement from its original position over time. This distribution is normally distributed, with a mean and standard deviation that evolve in time and are determined by the system's parameters. We also examine the limitations of this normal distribution approximation, finding that it holds for up to a year in a system with 20 sites. This research focuses on developing an optimization algorithm for fitting differential models to extensive amounts of data, an approach commonly used in epidemiological analysis. However, fitting these models is not without issues, as the computation can be extremely costly due to the high number of function evaluations required, which can reach billions for large data sets. In response to this challenge, we created an efficient gradient estimation method based on random point selection, which significantly reduces the computational expense by approximately ten-fold, while also demonstrating numerical stability and accuracy. We then apply this method to an epidemiological model, using real data and comparing the results with existing solutions, and discover that it yields comparable outcomes with substantially less computational time. Furthermore, the algorithm is evaluated for biological feasibility by analyzing the model's parameters, which is crucial in ensuring that the model reflects realistic dynamics and is less prone to numerical artifacts. We also address numerical stability issues by implementing parameter normalization and step-size adaptation, which enable the algorithm to accurately simulate models for a wide range of applications, including those involving noisy data and complex parameter interactions. Our research creates a viable effective non-rigid pendulum model to simulate the behavior of a specific quantum system, comprised of two coupled optical lattices implementing atom-molecule conversions, even under strong coupling. This non-rigid pendulum model is uniquely defined by considering the relative population between atoms and molecules as its oscillatory variable. By employing this model, we explore its dynamics within a continuous time domain and observe the emergence of instabilities. Our findings reveal the presence of two distinct modes of instability in this non-rigid pendulum system. One of these modes is characterized by the disruption of its periodic characteristic and the other by the system's return to a stable state after an initial delay. This threshold for instability is further examined as we adjust the intensity of the coupling between the pendulums. Our study also compares the behavior of this non-rigid pendulum system when the variable of its oscillation includes both atomic and molecular populations simultaneously. We discover that this variant exhibits a higher threshold for the development of instabilities when the variable is limited to the population difference between atoms and molecules. Our research on this non-rigid pendulum model provides a meaningful interpretation of our previous numerical data obtained from a quantum system that incorporates atom-molecule conversions and coupled optical lattices. A key challenge in DNA data storage systems arises from the need to manage storage partitions effectively. This paper introduces a novel application of a centuries-old problem - the knights and horses problem - to a critical aspect of DNA data storage: optimizing primer pair selection. This optimization is crucial for correcting a common issue affecting stored data during retrieval. Our approach involves developing efficient algorithms to address two subproblems: minimizing the number of primer pairs used and arranging these pairs to reduce the number of storage partitions needed. Our results show that our approaches provide improved performance compared to existing methods, including a previous solution to the knights and horses problem. Furthermore, our designs are versatile and can be combined with other retrieval strategies, such as the 'all-at-once' method, to achieve better outcomes. Our work demonstrates how the knights and horses problem can be applied to more complex problems by modifying its constraints, and our primer pair designs are viable solutions for real-world DNA data storage applications. Our software is available openly for other research communities to use and modify. Our research provides a foundation for further improvements to our algorithms and other related problems involving constraint satisfaction. Our most efficient solution to the knights and horses problem sets a new benchmark for other algorithms to compare with. This research was funded by the National Science Foundation in the United States. Our team found that the most efficient algorithm for solving the knights and horses problem involves a novel combination of a greedy approach with an efficient prioritization method, and we believe that this combined strategy is a more effective and general solution that can be applied to other related problems, such as the partitioning of primer pairs in DNA data storage. Our work on the knights and horses problem was previously presented at the 2022 Conference of the ACM Special Interest Group on Algorithms and Computing Theory, held in Phoenix, Arizona. Accurate modeling of riverbed geometry is crucial for understanding and predicting water flow behavior.
This study presents a novel geostatistical method called Principal Component Geostatistical Analysis (PCGA)
to efficiently estimate bathymetry using flow velocity data.
By reducing dimensionality and integrating geostatistical analysis
PCGA enhances modeling efficiency while improving model performance
when applied to a real-world dataset from the Yellow River
it significantly improves upon current best practices for bathymetry estimation
by minimizing the error in negative depth values and improving the overall RMSE performance
by 23% relative to the traditional approach.
The PCGA method is a theoretically simple and efficient model
that is easily implementable in real-time applications
and has the potential to be an advanced and practical solution
for estimating riverbed geometry in various scenarios.

Recently, a growing number of images have been captured using mobile devices, and these images often require enhancement to represent real-world brightness and color information accurately. Single-image based High Dynamic Range (HDR) enhancement has become a highly sought-after technology, but it remains challenging, especially when using point wise operations alone. In response to this challenge, researchers and practitioners are exploring diverse techniques such as multi-scale detail enhancement, tone mapping with machine learning, and patch based methods. However, these approaches often produce subpar results on natural scenes and images. To break through this limitation, we are presenting a novel algorithm called Successive HDR Enhancement in the Spatial and Frequency Domains, which leverages both time and frequency domains to improve HDR images. The proposed algorithm builds upon a basic tone mapping image and progressively refines the output through a series of frequency and spatial enhancement processes. The algorithm's simplicity, efficiency, and effectiveness are significant advantages, as it produces notable improvements in both HDR reconstruction and HDR enhancement tasks without requiring external training or prior knowledge about the input images. The proposed algorithm has several benefits, including a high degree of flexibility that allows for varying levels of input detail, the ability to produce HDR images from low light or compressed images, and the capability to enhance HDR images with external clues. The algorithm's efficacy has been demonstrated through a series of experiments and comparisons with existing techniques and baselines, showing that it is a highly effective and versatile HDR enhancement algorithm. The code for this algorithm has been made publicly available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/ChaosRong/SpatialFrequencyHDR.Enhancement. The algorithm's potential applications have also been explored through real world examples and scenarios. The proposed algorithm and related experiments are applicable to various tasks and scenarios, such as image compression, overexposure, and HDR video enhancement. This theorem found an intriguing link between moduli spaces of genus $g$ surfaces with boundary and a specific topological concept called a Heegaard structure. The Coch-Yga conjecture posed a question about the topological properties of a specific kind of surface called a Harer-Nuermark semi-simple surface, and it is significant because it also applies to the Madsen-Weiss theorem. The Coch-Yga conjecture was initially proposed by the duo Harer and Nuermark in the year 2000, and it remained unproven for two decades. The Coch-Yga conjecture is a generalization of the Madsen-Weiss theorem, and it relates to the topological properties of a surface after it has undergone a process called simple decomposition. The study focuses on an iterative algorithm employed within the BDDC method and examines the relationship between its performance and several key parameters. Initially, the paper establishes links between these parameters and those defining the BDDC algorithm. It then demonstrates that the size of the BDDC defect when using the iterative algorithm is directly proportional to its number of iterations. Furthermore, the paper explores the relationship between these proportions and the number of iterations required to achieve a given level of accuracy. It also shows that the number of iterations is itself a function of the number of subdomain degrees of freedom and depends on whether the underlying problem is formulated using a robust or standard formulation. The resulting analysis provides a framework for understanding the interplay between different factors of the BDDC method and suggests that future work will be necessary to establish more robust formulations. The studies and examples presented herein demonstrate the BDDC method's ability to efficiently solve large-scale linear systems arising from various finite element discretizations of simple and complex geometric configurations. A key assumption of Gaussian diffusion models is that the diffusing particles have no connections or are identical. However, recent observations in fields like biology and chemistry have shown that many systems defy this assumption, exhibiting correlations and heterogeneity. We develop a general framework for Gaussian diffusion with linked, distinct particles and demonstrate that it can lead to the formation of complex networks in the process's response to external signals. We then apply this approach to a specific scenario involving a network of coupled neurons and show that it predicts a specific pattern of response to a signal, a pattern that has been observed in actual neuron networks. Additionally, our model includes options for incorporating both temporary and lasting connections between the particles. We validate our model by comparing its predictions with simulated data showing that it accurately predicts the pattern of response even when the parameters are significantly different. Furthermore, our model can be extended to include temporary connections between particles by making the matrix governing their connections a time-dependent matrix, a modification that can be made with minimal change to the original model. We also investigate the model's performance with increasing sizes of the network and find that it scales effectively without any major difficulties. In summary, our model provides a versatile and powerful tool for understanding the diffusion processes with the involvement of linked, distinct particles. We make our code available for others to use and modify as needed. We also offer the matrix we used for the neuron network analysis in the supplementary materials following the suggested format. We believe that our model can be useful in the analysis of diffusion processes in complex networks, especially in biological systems. We anticipate that it will be particularly useful in the analysis of the diffusion processes in the brain, particularly in the investigation of the Gaussian diffusion processes in recurrent neural networks and their relationship to their genetic foundations. We also propose that it could be applied in the investigation of another system of connected components, the protein interaction networks within cells. We recognize the existence of other models that are specifically designed for connected components, but we believe that our model offers more flexibility due to its Gaussian nature. We studied cross-phase modulation (CPM) in a loop resonator with two identical counterpropagating modes. Our research involved injecting a strong, monochromatic pulse into one of the modes and observing the impact on the other mode. For comparison, we also examined self-phase modulation (SPM) in a single mode. To emphasize the effect of CPM, we designed the loop such that the injected pulse's frequency is precisely half of the resonator's fundamental frequency. Under these conditions, the residual phase modulation of the injected pulse during a single round trip is significantly greater for SPM than for CPM. However, when considering multiple round trips, the loop's behavior favors CPM over SPM. To mitigate the disadvantage of CPM, we proposed a modification to the loop design. Our analysis indicates that a loop with a non-zero frequency gap can enhance the effect of CPM to the point where it surpasses SPM. We also explored the application of this loop to generate broadband supercontinuum spectra through SPM and observed that a loop with a non-negligible frequency gap actually leads to the destruction of the continuum within the lower frequency range. Consequently, we recommend identifying a loop with a specific resonance loop or designing the loop to ensure that the injected pulse occupies a specific portion of the resonator to minimize unwanted CPM effects. Ultimately, our study reveals that the effect of CPM in the loop resonator generally exceeds our initial expectations and highlights the potential for further research into this phenomenon. Our analysis provides a basic framework for understanding the behavior of cross-phase modulation in identical counterpropagating modes of a loop resonator and can be extended to other loop configurations. We also propose a method to measure the loop's loss and the difference in mode refractive indices. Our research demonstrates the generation of wide bandwidth spectra through self-phase modulation in a loop resonator. This study utilizes a highly detailed GAN model that performs well at scaling up turbulent flow patterns, specifically focusing on varying Reynolds numbers in a channel flow context. A novel approach is employed to enhance the model's performance by incorporating multiscale information, which the authors demonstrate is effective in improving the model. In a comparison of different model sizes, the study finds that increasing the model's size does not necessarily lead to a proportional increase in its performance, rather it reaches a plateau. Notably, the performance of the model is inspected in a scenario with two varying Reynolds numbers, 5500 and 10000, by generating synthetic data based on the latter and testing it on the former. The results show that the model effectively captures the small-scale turbulence features present in the higher Reynolds number flow. Ultimately, the study finds that this high-resolution GAN model can accurately simulate turbulent flow patterns at a Reynolds number of 5500, matching the complexity of real-world data found in Reynolds numbers up to 10000. Furthermore, the model exhibits robustness in performing well when exposed to different model sizes, with the optimal size being determined through a comprehensive assessment of its performance. The model's capabilities also demonstrate further robustness across various model sizes, with the performance in different regions of the model being evenly distributed. The study presents an in-depth analysis of the model's performance, including detailed plots of turbulent flow patterns, along with an open-source code base to facilitate further research and development in this area. The code base is specifically designed to scale on modern GPU architectures, with the largest model successfully being trained on a GPU network comprising 64 GPUs. We present a novel evaluation method for reinforcement learning algorithms that involves shifting the curriculum in a controlled manner. Initially, the agent learns to navigate a straightforward, fully connected grid world. As it gains experience, we gradually introduce a more complex version of the environment by adding multiple overlapping sub-grids with varying transition probabilities. This dynamic curriculum reflects real-world scenarios where complex systems often exhibit simpler, local structures that can be learned by the agent. Our results show that high-performance reinforcement learning algorithms struggle with this task, failing to adapt to the changing curriculum and underlying dynamics of the environment. However, by incorporating a simple exploratory policy, such as uniform random action selection, many of the algorithms we tested are able to successfully navigate this controlled curriculum, providing valuable insights into their strengths and weaknesses. Our evaluation framework extends beyond the specific grid world example to a broad set of general curricula that can be applied to various environmental scenarios. This provides a concise, standardized method for comparing the capabilities of different reinforcement learning algorithms in the face of complex, dynamic tasks. Our code is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/Jelbig/reinforce_curriculum.

Process behavior can change significantly in response to various events, making process mining challenging, especially when analyzing long-running processes. Decison-Decision Rule (DCR) graphs provide a framework for examining the evolution of processes over time by identifying rules governing the flow of processes. However, existing methods lack efficiency when handling large datasets, with processing times extending to several days for data sets of merely a few million instances. To address this limitation, we introduce an innovative approach, to accurately mine DCR graphs from large-scale temporal process data with the help of parallel computing power. Our method enhances the efficiency of this operation by minimizing memory usage and leveraging processing power in multip-core computers. We support this approach with a comprehensive experimental study, conducting multiple processes on real-world data sets consisting of up to ten million instances, and demonstrating a notable improvement in processing times achieving a significant speed-up of twenty-fold on a desktop computer. Furthermore, we offer a web-based application to mine DCR graphs interactively and offer predefined parameters for quick process analysis. This application supports various formats for process data, enables the selection of relevant processes, and allows for the evaluation of the accuracy of its process model by comparing it with existing approaches. We anticipate that this research will facilitate the mining of large-scale process data, hitherto inaccessbile to many, and enable a wider selection of processes for scientific study and real-world application. This is reflected in our accompanying dataset of twenty real-world datasets consisting of over thirty million instances, each accompanied by a corresponding DCR graph, that we make publicly available for the benefit of the community. This dataset successfully demonstrates the breadth of process data that can be analyzed using our approach, along with process data from various domains, including, for example, a portfolio analysis of an investment company, public transportation usage patterns in several cities, and financial transactions in various countries. Lastly, we outline possible avenues for future research, such as enhancing the efficiency of our approach on cloud computing platforms, implementing new algorithms for process mining, and providing visual representations of DCR graphs. We examine the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_d(\Delta)$ of complex algebraic curves defined by means of an inversive divisor $\Delta$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$ with specified ramification properties. We show that this space has a natural compactification, which we call $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_d(\Delta)$, consisting of curves with inverse divisors that are non-special and have non-degenerate Newton slopes. We demonstrate that this compactification is compatible with the geometric and Hodge-theoretic compactifications of Deligne and Griffiths for certain components of $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_d(\Delta)$. Specifically, we find that the weights on the cohomology of the moduli space $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_d(\Delta)$ define a compatible system of weights on the cohomology of $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_d(\Sigma)$ for each inverse monodromy operator $\Sigma$. We also investigate the relationship between the Borel-Serre compactification of the moduli space of curves with specified ramification properties and the geometric compactification. The rapid evolution of SARS-CoV-2 and changing healthcare guidelines pose significant challenges in allocating limited ICU resources effectively, particularly in the early stages of outbreaks.  A critical step in optimizing this process is prioritizing ICU admission for critically ill patients, including those with COVID-19.  Current practices primarily focus on patient medical conditions, neglecting important details about their admission, which are encoded in text forms.  To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that leverages natural language processing and machine learning to analyze admission text features associated with ICU admission decisions.  Our approach identifies crucial aspects of admission text that influence decision-making and enables developers to create intuitive, globally applicable models for priority prediction.  We tested and validated our approach using admission data from the Northeast United States and found that our model accurately predicts ICU admission decisions (0.83 AUC) and captures key features of admissions (e.g. referral source, symptoms, and underlying conditions).  Furthermore, by integrating our model into a batch of possible patient admissions, we demonstrated its potential to optimize ICU admission decisions, resulting in a 12.8% increase in survival rates among patients with COVID-19.  Our approach provides a scalable, data-efficient solution for prioritizing ICU admissions during public health crises.  Our code is available at https://github.com/JHLiu92/cticu.  Our report is a preliminary step towards addressing complex healthcare decisions in COVID-19 emergencies and highlights promising areas for future research, such as incorporating temporal changes in healthcare guidelines and exploring alternative machine learning techniques, to improve resource allocation in this critical setting.  To facilitate further investigation, we have made our code and model datasets publicly accessible.  Our study has implications for the effective management of future pandemics and similar public health emergencies.  Our approach can be applied to other critical decision-making processes in healthcare by analyzing unstructured admission information, as shown in our additional findings presented in the supplement.  Our analysis and approach can be utilized by healthcare professionals, machine learning experts, and researchers to improve resource allocation in this critical setting, and to facilitate further investigation into areas such as incorporating temporal changes in healthcare guidelines and alternative machine learning techniques, as well as providing a foundation for exploring similar problems in other public health crises. Fake news has been a significant concern on social media platforms, spreading rapidly and causing real-world damage. To combat this issue, detecting false information is essential, though it's a challenging task due to the numerous forms false information can take. Our proposed approach, a end-to-end sequence generation model called MetaFEND, incorporates the benefits of both supervised and unsupervised text generation to enhance false information detection. By optimizing the inverse of the likelihood of a sentence in the supervised phase and the likelihood of a sentence in the unsupervised phase using the Wasserstein distance, MetaFEND generates more plausible and distinct text compared to existing baselines, leading to a substantial improvement in performance on the Enron spam email and Twitter fake news datasets. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that generated texts by MetaFEND can be used as adversarial samples to train robust neural false information detection models, demonstrating the potential for a range of applications in adversarial training and generation tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhongyongweng/MetaFEND.

Theoretical modeling suggests that in a silicon crystal, substitutional dopants can be connected in various arrangements, exchanging quantum information through either direct electrical connections or mutual interaction with phonons. Based on this framework, we demonstrate the ability to switch between two information exchange systems: one based on the Pauli-X gate and the other based on the Mach-Zehnder interferometer, both with multiple logical qubits. By optimizing the position of dopants, their distance can be increased to up to 13 nanometers without significant degradation of the exchange interaction. This development paves the way for extending solid-state quantum computing beyond a few qubits. Additionally, we show that quantum entanglement can be maintained over longer distances, potentially enabling the development of solid-state quantum computers with silicon-based technology. These findings highlight the flexibility of silicon-based quantum computing, allowing for multiple qubit architectures and providing a robust framework for further research. Ultimately, our comprehensive analysis demonstrates the practical feasibility of silicon-based quantum computers with dopants as qubits and Josephson junctions as the platform. A region of interest (ROI) is a confined section of an image that is analyzed independently by deep neural networks, and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) play a significant role in imaging segmentation within these restricted areas. While the term "CNN-based feature extraction" is often used, the distinct contributions of CNNs in relation to fully convolutional networks (FCNs) for task-specific information have not been thoroughly examined. Our research delves into the aspects of CNNs that contribute to the segmentation of ROI by systematically partitioning the ROI into two areas: a support set that provides essential contextual information for task-specific information to be extracted from a large part of the ROI. Using a synthetic MRI dataset, we demonstrated the practical application of this concept by accurately identifying areas provided in 3D brain images by defining multiple ROI types. Our results showed that our method outperformed existing FCN-based approaches, demonstrating the significance of explicitly incorporating CNNs in feature extraction when dealing with limited ROI scenarios. Furthermore, our method's performance was evaluated at different ROI sizes, showing its robustness in this parameter. Our research provides a framework for understanding the role of CNNs in feature extraction within limited ROI scenarios, presenting a tangible contribution to the community.
