To achieve this, several key operations are developed to adjust both inner and outer point distances from their initial settings, ensuring that line joins are always shared between adjacent paths. Unlike conventional techniques, the proposed algorithm ensures that the distance between inner points can differ from the distance between outer points, which enables the efficient creation of distinctive line joins, including the often challenging "L"-shaped and fan-shaped types. A basic two-fluid model is proposed to analyze the dynamics of convective flows in a temperature gradient, specifically in Rayleigh-B\'enard convection. The model assumes a smooth interface between two fluid layers of significantly different temperatures and flows, with the lower layer experiencing free convection. The model's predictions for the heat flux it carries are found to match the results obtained from direct numerical simulations, including the exact power laws with respect to the radius and time in random convection. Notably, the model successfully explains the observed scaling of heat flux in large-scale convection by indicating that the inner layer's temperature is close to the critical value, thus satisfying the conditions for quasi-steady free convection. The model also indicates that the flow's randomness arises primarily from the inner layer, whereas the outer layer flows are nearly steady. The two-fluid model demonstrates the similarity between convection within a fluid at the critical point and fluid-fluid interfacial dynamics. The importance of the inner layer's flow stability in determining the heat flux's scaling with respect to the radius is underlined by the model, as is the necessity to consider the flow within the outer layer in order to accurately predict the heat flux in random convection. Video subtitles present a straightforward and effective way to convey visual information, and our investigation suggests that they can significantly enhance viewport prediction accuracy, especially in the initial seconds of a video. Our theory is that video subtitles provide a more precise visual hint compared to video frames, and we aim to verify this assumption through user-centric viewport prediction and interactive video playback tests with 24 participants. Our results reveal that subtitle-based predictions already excel at the beginning of a video and continue to perform better as time progresses. Furthermore, we observe that video subtitles lead to a 23.1% reduction in relative error when predicting viewports for the early stages of a video and a 13.6% increase in precision when combining this approach with traditional frame-based predictions. Our research also reveals that participants interacting with video subtitles exhibit a 23.8% greater sense of presence and that subtitle-based predictions result in a 20.8% lower subjective delay perception compared to frame-based predictions. Our findings encourage future exploration of video subtitles in immersive video applications and highlight the benefits of integrating viewport predictions with video playback in real-time. Our research material is accompanied by an openly accessible code and dataset. Our work also presents an initial step towards understanding video subtitles within the context of immersive video presence and provides a viable solution for the predictive display of video content. Our approach can be applied to a wide range of immersive video applications featuring moving images and text, and it is suitable for various platforms, including VR, AR, and 360-degree video technologies. Our new proposed ensemble-based matrix-valued orthogonal polynomial framework enables the approximation of thermal states and time-evolved systems using a bond dimension that scales with the square root of its requirement in conventional methods, maintaining a linear dependence on system size. This breakthrough in dimension estimation is made possible by adapting a probabilistic approach and utilizing a distinct type of monic monodular operator, which we have successfully applied to a broad range of models including fermionic and bosonic systems. The efficiency of this revised approach is demonstrated by applying it to a 1D fermionic XXZ model and a 2D bosonic XY chain, and we have also incorporated intrinsic time-averaging to enhance the accuracy of its results. This novel PEPO framework offers a significant improvement in the efficiency of matrix product state methods, and our implementation is an essential component of the algebrago library. This development is a crucial step towards implementing large-scale, far-from-equilibrium quantum dynamics using matrix product state methods. The underlying PEPO framework and associated algorithms have been thoroughly tested against existing exact solutions and contrasted with alternative approximation methods. The resulting tools and techniques presented here are designed to be broadly applicable and are already showing promise in achieving large scale approximations with bond dimensions of up to 10^5. The theory of decoupling for linear systems with small perturbations relies on two analytical techniques: Taylor series expansion and the study of canonical surfaces. We combine these approaches to systematically analyze the decoupling property near high-grade singularities of polynomial systems. This research involves two key components. Firstly, we conduct a Taylor series analysis of the systems' equating identities to reveal their structural characteristics and accurate error estimates. Secondly, we develop an explicit criterion to determine the decoupling property by exploring the canonical surfaces resulting from the systems' defects. Our findings build upon the theories developed by Bernal and Huneau and make the underlying assumptions more flexible. Our study also introduces the concept of "developed surfaces" – a novel geometric framework that provides a precise understanding of the systems' decoupling behavior, especially in relation to the Mounier-Sperber Theorem. Moreover, we provide a unified framework for classifying the decoupling properties of developable surfaces, thereby extending the classification proposed by Mounier and Sperber. Finally, we examine the connections between the systems' decoupling behavior and the geometry of their corresponding curves of surfaces, in addition to analyzing the numerical computation of developing surfaces. Our approach involves a significant expansion of the systems' analytic theories, as well as the development of an algorithm to compute the systems' curves and surfaces using a combination of symbolic and numerical methods. Our research on the Taylor series analysis, combined with the study of canonical surfaces, provides a comprehensive framework for the analytic study of polynomial systems with multiple variables and large coefficients, offering a meaningful contribution to the underlying mathematics. Our integrated approach, which leverages both symbolic and numerical methods, facilitates a deeper understanding of the systems' analytic structures and their corresponding curves and surfaces, thereby providing a useful framework for the study of various related problems, including the regula falsi method, the Newton-Girard identities, and the properties of resulting surfaces. We have investigated the interference between surface plasmons and a Rayleigh anomaly at the interface between a metal and a magnetophotonic crystal, investigating the effects of this interference on the reflectance and ketomagneto-optical activity in the surface plasmon band. The interference between these two surface waves results in a pattern of minima in the reflectance spectrum at points corresponding to the high-symmetry points of the crystal lattice, and exhibits a significant effect on the ketomagneto-optical activity in the surface plasmon band, particularly in certain orientation configurations. Additionally, the ketomagneto-optical activity is found to be most pronounced in crystals with high crystallographic symmetry, and the interference can induce a non-reciprocal transmission through a linear chain of nanospheres, demonstrating a unique property of magnetophotonic crystals that can provide robust ketomagneto-optical activity. We have also analyzed the possibility of implementing these structures using nanocylinder arrays, and found that the ketomagneto-optical activity is more sensitive to the radius of the cylinders than their period. Moreover, the sensitivity of the activity to the incident light frequency varies greatly across the surface plasmon band, and the structure exhibits a strong sensitivity to the thickness of the metal layer, making it suitable for thin-film applications. Nonetheless, the ketomagneto-optical activity in these crystals can persist over a wide frequency range, and the surface plasmon band displays a strong anomaly on the reflectance spectrum edge, presenting a promising feature for magnetic photonic crystals. We have also numerically simulated the propagation of a surface plasmon coupled to a Rayleigh anomaly along a metal-air interface, and the resulting propagation distance varies significantly with the crystal orientation, demonstrating the potential of these crystals for ketomagneto-optical activity in surface plasmon propagation. Knowledge distillation (KD) is a technique for accelerating neural networks by replacing them with more compact models. However, standard KD requires access to the original network's output, making it incompatible with black-box settings where only input/output data is available. We introduce decision-based black-box knowledge distillation (DB3), a novel approach that replaces output-based KD with a comparison of the model's classifications against the label, differentiating it from traditional KD methods. We successfully apply DB3 to unsupervised learning scenarios and demonstrate its effectiveness in reducing the size of classification models by 1.5 times and improving performance on the Cifar-10 dataset using MNIST as a teacher. Additionally, DBB3 facilitates transparent learning, enabling the extraction of both correct and incorrect classifications. Our approach is feasible on a vast array of classification tasks, showcasing the versatility of DB3. Our code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/DB3.

Given a solvable group G and a multiplicity-free module M, we establish the compatibility of the composition factor lattice of submodules of M with its underlying structure, demonstrating that the composition factor lattice can be completely reconstructed from the composition factor information of certain submodules spanning a specific basis of M. This basis is determined by the action of conjugation by G on the set of irreducible constituents of M. As an example, we apply this approach to construct the composition factor lattice of modules arising from a specific induction process related to Artynkewicz's theorem. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this construction yields the same composition factor lattice when compared to a alternative construction obtained through the use of Brauer trees. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the composition factor lattice of these modules can be equivalently described as having a particular structure, namely being isomorphic to the lattice of subgroups of a certain group, which is demonstrated to be a nilpotent group possessing a specific group order architecture. This research was initially presented at the group theory section of the 2011 Australian Mathematical Sciences Meeting. It has since been expanded to address additional concerns related to the composition factor lattice of modules, particularly those involving nilpotent groups and reductive groups. It also builds upon the results obtained by Tenner in the case of symmetric groups. It is further observed that the composition factor lattice of these modules exhibits a certain normality property, which can be categorized as a more general property known as lattice isomorphism, when compared to the lattice of subgroups of a particular group, also known as the parabolic subgroup of a Borel subgroup within the group. We propose Co-Imitation Learning, a novel framework for skill discovery in uncertain environments. Based on the concept that simultaneous imitation of multiple possible courses of action can generate diverse behaviors, our approach encourages the acquisition of robust skills by network. Unlike conventional methods that require expert demonstrations, our model leverages Co-Imitation Learning to utilize positive reward feedback in the environment. We demonstrate the efficacy of Co-Imitation Learning by applying it to open-loop state-prediction and control tasks. Furthermore, we introduce a sample-based method to facilitate efficient exploration and provide theoretical proof of robust skill convergence. Experimental data showcase the Co-Imitation Learning framework's ability to effectively handle uncertain environments with limited demonstration knowledge. The code for our model is publicly available on GitHub at this link: https://github.com/ghulamai/Co-Imitation Learning. 

This work has been previously published at the following location: The 35th Convention of the Pattern Recognition Society (ICPR 2020). It is also relevant to the following question: How does the proposed Co-Imitation Learning framework generate diverse behaviors and enhance skill robustness through the imitation of multiple possible courses of action? 

The proposed Co-Imitation Learning framework pre-trains the network by encouraging the imitation of multiple possible courses of action, which can lead to the generation of diverse behaviors and improved skill robustness. Although diverse behavior generation is a challenging task that requires significant data, our approach succeeds with just a single trajectory of expert demonstrations due to the inherent uncertainty in dynamic systems. In addition to generating diverse behaviors, the robust skills learned through Co-Imitation Learning demonstrate superior performance in challenging and unfamiliar scenarios. The performance benefits of Co-Imitation Learning are evident in tasks such as navigating through a previously explored environment and identifying anomalies in time series patterns. 

Experimentally, the proposed approach is put through a state-prediction task in a dynamic system with both successful and failed states, and through a control task in a dynamic system with external influences, in addition to the proposed Co-Imitation Learning framework's performance in detecting anomalies in time series patterns. In this research, we investigate how the polarized decoding cutoff rate influences the performance of a sequential decoder when list decoding fails, assuming a fixed code length and an error probability of $0.01$. We analyze the average number of errors encountered by the sequential decoder as it adapts to varying bias values, and we observe that its behavior follows a normal distribution. Notably, we discover that the most likely bias value results in the highest number of errors, which we term the "most hazardous bias". The polarized cutoff rate is found to serve as a benchmark, and we establish that the most hazardous bias equals the polarized cutoff rate when the code length is extremely large. Furthermore, we derive a simplified formula to approximate the most hazardous bias, which we demonstrate offers comparable performance to the more complex original metric for various code sizes. Ultimately, our research provides a practical and evaluating tool for the performance of a sequential decoder in real-world applications. The findings presented in this research paper are part of a larger study on polar codes, list decoding, and sequential decoding, and the results offered can be applied to the practical use of sequential decoder failure in various scenarios. The most hazardous bias metric can serve as a standardized evaluation criterion for various list decoding protocols and cryptographic applications requiring low error probabilities. The research conducted in this study has been publicly available since 2023. Using reinforcement learning, a better understanding of the underlying principles of translation has been achieved, but improving the learning efficiency and optimizing the action space remains an important task. Two main reinforcement learning methods exist: policy optimization and value function-based approaches, but current research largely focuses on the latter, leaving the former underexploited. This paper investigates the effect of optimizing the action space to accelerate policy learning and finds that both policy and value function optimization are beneficial for improving the efficiency of learning from raw feedback, but value function optimization has a more significant impact when the feedback is coarse. Additionally, a novel policy optimization method called the Policy Hindsight Experience Table (PHET) was developed to facilitate efficient learning from raw feedback without the need for hypothesis storage. Experimental evaluations show that PHET achieves better performance than the baseline agent learning from the same amount of feedback but with a larger action space, and its performance is comparable to that of value function-based methods learning from the same amount of precise feedback. This efficiency of PHET is further validated on a real-world translation task called the repeated translation scenario. This scenario requires the model to continuously translate new input texts without the need for hypothesis storage, using the PHET algorithm as pretraining. Evaluations show that PHET provides better translation quality and greater stability than baseline agents learning from the same amount of new data each time. This paper provides a detailed understanding of policy optimization, presents a novel approach called PHET, and showcases its applicability to real-world translation tasks. Moreover, the underlying principles and algorithms of PHET are generalizable to other action space optimization tasks involving continuous exploration and large action spaces. This is particularly true for PHET's underlying hypothesis that many optimization objectives are beneficial when applying hindsight experience, leading to a new research area called Hindsight Optimization. This is demonstrated by applying Hindsight Optimization to improve the efficiency of learning from reinforcement learning feedback with the PHET algorithm, and a similar approach called Hindsight Optimization of Expected Cumulative Rewards (HOECR) was developed to facilitate efficient learning from coarse feedback without the need for hypothesis storage, showing that HOECR leads to better performance than baseline value function-based methods learning from the same amount of coarse feedback. This means that value function-based methods learning from the same amount of coarse feedback can be considered a special case of action space optimization involving hindsight experience. Consequently, this paper is relevant to areas such as machine translation, summary generation, and text generation from high-level sketches. Quantum information flow between an open system and its surroundings can move in both directions, as demonstrated using a single-photon cut-and-join process with a quantum dot system. When a single-photon is entangled with two energy levels of the system, both retrieval of the original entanglement and regeneration of new entanglement with a two-photon state are possible. This phenomenon is influenced by the system's initial state and can be steered numerically, offering a potential application in quantum information processing. Furthermore, both classical and quantum information embedded in the system's energy levels and the joiner's two-photon state can be successfully recovered. This process has the potential to enhance both quantum memory and quantum simulation by utilizing the same platform. As the system's parameters change, its performance can be assessed through quantum figure-of-merit and optimal parameter tuning is available. This process also presents an intriguing example of quantum reciprocity, demonstrated by the mutual information's symmetry between the system and its surrounding. As the system's energy levels evolve, both minimal and maximal information flow states exist, which can be identified and used for developing strategies to enhance the system's performance. This leads to an understanding of the underlying dynamics, with both time-dependent and parameter-dependent dynamics revealed through the study of both the system's energy levels and the surrounding's photon entanglement. This knowledge can be utilized to maintain optimal performance in the system through quantum feedback control. This research paper provides new operator formulations for both semi-recursive and fully recursive hypersurfaces within the Euclidean space of a higher dimension, making it an invaluable contribution to the biharmonic hypersurface theory. By redefining the Farkas-Leibniz operator and the second order Beltrami operator, we uncover key properties that these operators possess. Furthermore, we establish that a hypersurface is considered minimal if and only if it satisfies a specific harmonic equation, and in our investigation, we also uncover both classical and modified Cohn-Nelsen conjectures that these operators can satisfy. By exploring the relationship between biharmonic and minimal surfaces, we discover that these surfaces share a common characteristic: they both adhere to a specific Laplacian equation. Our study also uncovers multiple cases where a hypersurface can be classified as both minimal and harmonic within the Euclidean space of a higher dimension, and we achieve this by using these operators to our advantage. Our most notable discovery involves an intricate relationship that the Laplacian operator shares with both the Beltrami and Farkas-Leibniz operators, and from this relationship, we can derive the classic Euler-Lagrange equations. By doing so, we can ensure the equality of the mean curvature with the Dirichlet mean of the hypersurface. This research paper offers several significant advancements to the biharmonic hypersurface theory, and it also offers several useful theorems that can be found within the Euclidean space of a higher dimension. By utilizing these theorems, we can explore and analyze both the minimal surface problem and the Chern-Osserman theorem. Our study also provides multiple case studies that can be applied to both the Riemannian and pseudo-Riemannian manifolds. Our most notable achievement involves developing an operator-based approach to the biharmonic hypersurface theory in the Euclidean space of a higher dimension, and this approach allows us to redefine both the Farkas-Leibniz and Beltrami operators. We discover multiple relationships between these operators and the Laplacian operator. We also discover that these operators can satisfy both the classical and modified Cohn-Nelsen conjectures. We can apply these theorems to explore and analyze both the Chern-Osserman theorem and the minimal surface problem. Our study also provides an operator-based approach to the biharmonic hypersurface theory in the Euclidean space of a higher dimension, and this approach enables us to redefine both the Farkas-Leibniz and Beltrami operators

This study examines the concurrency control mechanisms of three widely used MongoDB deployments: WIREDTIGER, REPLICASET, and SHARDEDCLUSTER. Our analysis reveals that these deployments adhere to specific versions of snapshot isolation, including strict snapshot isolation, semi-strong snapshot isolation, and weak snapshot isolation. Our findings are supported by code reviews of MongoDB's source files and are validated through test suite executions on MongoDB clusters. Our research contributes to the understanding of MongoDB's concurrency control behavior and highlights potential limitations when using MongoDB, particularly in transaction-based applications. Furthermore, our analysis of MongoDB's source code provides valuable insights into its concurrency control implementation. Our approach and findings are relevant to the broader context of NoSQL database security and accessibility. Our code and research artifacts are publicly available on GitHub. This work is an expanded version of the paper presented at the 2020 ACM Richard J. Berry Databases Conference. Our research has been funded by the National Science Foundation under grants number CNS-1513106, CNS-17033169, and ECCS-1805461, as well as the National Research Council of Canada. Our team also gratefully acknowledges the generosity of MongoDB Inc. in providing us with deployment information and clarifications. Our research has been conducted in accordance with the ethical guidelines outlined by the National Science Foundation's Committee on Human Subjects. Our code and research artifacts are actively maintained and are planned for continued update in the foreseeable future. Our future work will focus on evaluating the performance and security implications of MongoDB's concurrency control mechanisms and expanding our analysis to other NoSQL database deployments. Our analysis has already been applied to NoSQL database deployments used in two previous research projects. Our framework is applicable to other deployed systems with publicly available source code and can be used to explore additional aspects of their behavior. Our research has also been used in the teaching of various database and systems-related courses, including graduate-level concurrency control courses, undergraduate-level database courses, and advanced undergraduate-level operating system courses. Our code and research artifacts can be used as real-world examples in the teaching of ethics courses, particularly in the context of research ethics. Our team is open to collaborative opportunities with other researchers and educators. Our code and research artifacts are available at https://github.com/DBSystemGroup/MongoSI. Our previous related research can be found at https://dbsystemgroup.org/. Our team's website is maintained in accordance with ethical guidelines to ensure transparency and openness. Our research is actively maintained to reflect any future developments and is expected to benefit the database systems community for an extended period.

We demonstrate that the $e$-positive properties of chromatic symmetric functions can be characterized via certain types of Dyck paths, effectively showing that they form a subfamily of the $e$-positive polynomials resulting from the enumeration of Dyck paths by branch weights. This finding is a direct consequence of a more general framework involving the application of branch weights to the bivariate moments of random matrices from the classical groups, specifically including the representation of these moments as structured sums of monic polynomials. Furthermore, we reveal that the chromatic symmetric functions align with the $e$-positive class defined by the weights $(x^2+1)/(x+1)$, which is equivalent to the weights underlying the enumeration of Dyck paths with $2n$ branches. This equivalence emerges after transforming the moment parameters from the representation of the classical groups. We also introduce the concept of $qe$-positivity, which encompasses both $e$-positivity and $h$-positivity, and prove that the chromatic symmetric functions exhibit $qe$-positivity. By extending the application of branch weights to the moment matrices of pairs of classical groups, we establish that the resulting $qe$-positive polynomials include, but are not limited to, the extension of chromatic symmetric functions to graded instances. This extension maintains the property of being $qe$-positive, whereas the original property of being weakly $h$-positive breaks under grading. Additionally, we identify the relationship between the Hilbert series of graded instances and the enumeration of Dyck paths with weighted branches, which can be further modified to accommodate branch multipliers. This enumerated version of the Hilbert series itself remains $qe$-positive and connects to the weights on the classical groups via the symmetric function theory. This connection enables us to enumerate standard tableaux by size, which can be compared to the enumeration obtained through the Cauchy operator. Both enumerations yield the same series, which is inherently $qe$-positive. We also derive a more general formula for the enumeration of Dyck paths with weighted branches, which is a direct extension of the formula for the branch weights corresponding to the classical groups. This extended formula represents the weighted enumeration as a structured sum of structured products of monic polynomials. We explore this general formula within the specific context of the weights $(x^2+1)/(x+1)$, which is equivalent to the weights underlying the enumeration of Dyck paths with $2n$ branches.

We investigated the dynamic hysteresis loop of a two-dimensional Ising model, consisting of triangular units that each contain three coupled Ising spins. Our study used a temperature of one point one five, at which the model exhibits a degenerate ground state with the characteristic 12-fold symmetry of the triangular lattice. To simplify the study, we focused on a small 6-spin sublattice that maintains the same symmetry and degenerate ground states as the full triangular Ising model. Our simulations of this sublattice showed that the hysteresis loop curve can be precisely predicted and has a precise rational shape that is characterized by a specific ratio of its major and minor loop areas. Notably, this ratio is independent of temperature and is equal to three and one quarter. Our predictions were verified through extensive numerical simulations of the hysteresis loop dynamics. Moreover, our results demonstrated that the hysteresis loop area and the temperature difference between ascending and descending processes in the sublattice are proportional to each other, with a specific proportionality constant that is equal to two and three quarters. Our study also found that the sublattice exhibits a first-order phase transition that can be identified through the analysis of the hysteresis loop curve. Additionally, we demonstrated that the proportions of the hysteresis loop curve remain unchanged when the external field is varied, whereas the area of the loop curve changes in a way that is proportional to its proportionality constant and is thus proportional to the temperature difference between ascending and descending processes. Finally, our study showed that the sublattice exhibits the characteristic characteristics of spin glass behavior, including the presence of Edwards-Anderson order parameter, the failure of the extremum condition to describe the hysteresis loop curve, and the success of the full distribution of the hysteresis loop curve in explaining the behavior of the hysteresis loop. Our results also demonstrated that the sublattice can be accurately simulated using a single-sample Monte Carlo method that is based on a single random initial configuration of the Ising spins. Our study provided a clear understanding of the complex dynamics of the hysteresis loop in the two-dimensional Ising model consisting of triangular units, offering predictive power that can be validated through numerical simulations. Solar wind protons are highly energetic, and their distribution diminishes as distance from the sun increases. To comprehend the underlying dynamics, a mathematical model is developed with the solar wind modelled as a thin, empty shell absorbing energy from the sun. The model assumes the energy it needs to escape, varies significantly across different heliocentric distances. As a point of reference, the model is compared to the energy distribution of protons at 1 AU, where the majority possess less than 1.36 kiloelectronvolts of energy, and the smallest 10% have more than 0.73 kiloelectronvolts of energy. It is further applied to guess the heliocentric distances at which solar wind energy becomes sufficient for heavier particles like helium and electrically neutral photons. The model suggests that the distribution of energy becomes more evenly spread as distance from the sun increases, and it is predicted that the heliocentric distance required for heavier particles like helium and electrically neutral photons is between 0.03 and 0.1 AU, or 4,500 to 15,700 kilometers. It is also determined that the average energy needed for the disintegration of heavier particles like helium and neutral photons is between 0.5 to 1.5 MeV, or 279,000 to 847,000 kelvin. The model indicates that the most likely heliocentric distance for the disintegration of heavier particles like helium and neutral photons is around 0.06 AU, or 9,300 kilometers. The energy required for the disintegration of heavier particles like helium and neutral photons is thought to be similar to the energy necessary to overcome gravity in the Sun's corona, the region outside the solar core where nuclear fusion occurs, and it is proposed that the distribution of energy could help explain the variability of solar wind. The model is generally consistent with the idea that the energy of solar wind protons increases with distance from the sun, and it is predicted that the most energetic protons will be found at the greatest heliocentric distances, beyond a few AU. The model also suggests that the most energetic particles are more likely to cause solar flare events, and it is proposed as a possible explanation for the limited range of heliocentric distances from which solar wind is released, as it could be the result of a limited supply of high-energy particles available to be released. The model is a mathematical assumption and the actual distribution of energy necessary to overcome solar gravitation at small heliocentric distances may differ from the proposed distribution

Recently introduced multilingual emotion recognition models have shown significant performance, but these models typically require substantial amounts of labeled data in the target language to achieve high accuracy. This challenge is particularly significant for many minority languages where high-quality training data is hard to obtain. To overcome this limitation, a novel cross-language emotion recognition framework has been developed, utilizing relevant resources from a high-resource language to improve modeling of emotion categories, and also leveraging translated text to enhance the efficacy of the model. The proposed approach incorporates a multi-brained network architecture to facilitate efficient learning and recognize emotions in an unbiased manner. To evaluate the proposed approach, the framework has been applied to recognizing emotions in Spanish and Italian, however the methods presented here have broader applications for modeling cross-language relationships. Notable improvements have been observed in recognizing emotions in these languages with only lightweight training, as evidenced by the results showing the proposed approach can achieve superior performance compared to conventional transfer learning methods. Furthermore, the proposed framework has been found to provide intuitive brain-degree visualizations that reflect cultural and linguistic differences. The code for the novel framework has been made publicly available on GitHub, and the research has been presented at the 2023 IEEE Spoken Language Technology Workshop. This finding is made possible by a change in variable that transforms the problem into one with a singular initial condition, leading to the formation of a shock wave with growing intensity over time. This model, inspired by the Hubble flow around a central black hole, was initially solved using the self-similar method by (Bisnetain et al., 2022), however, those authors failed to identify the singular nature of the shock wave. In contrast, we demonstrate the distinct characteristics of this shock wave by showing that it corresponds to a region outside the smooth region predicted by the self-similar solution. For example, the beam-beam interaction's impact on the q-k clustering of dark matter particles or the distribution of extra dimensions might be significant enough to be detected by precisely measuring the beam-beam closed orbit differences. To explore this idea, we first review the methods used to measure beam-beam interactions and then examine the sensitivity of various accelerators to beyond the standard model particles. We develop a distributed optimization algorithm for non-malicious agents that can be applied to solving convex risks minimization problems under network interference. While the algorithm maintains high communication effectiveness in the presence of malicious agents, it ensures that the optimal solution is approximately achieved in a bounded period of time. To accomplish this, the algorithm incorporates recent information about the optimal solution and employs a novel dual updating strategy that leverages the distinction between persistent and transient components of the dual process. These innovations enable the algorithm to operate in two phases: an initial phase where the algorithm adapts to the current dual process, and a subsequent phase where it accelerates towards the optimal solution. To obtain scalable performance, the algorithm's parameters are chosen optimally in a data-driven manner, taking into account the underlying network topology and the distribution of the optimal solution. This is accomplished using a secondary dual learning process that provides a way to estimate the algorithm's parameters and the optimal solution based on a limited number of samples. The scalability and performance of the algorithm are evaluated through numerical experiments conducted on various network and solution landscapes. Moreover, the merit of incorporating recent information about the optimal solution is demonstrated by comparing it to alternative approaches, including those that utilize traditional learning curves. Finally, the algorithm's applicability is illustrated through a real-world application example involving a solar power management system. The code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/YueYu2017/DISTRO. We investigate the efficiency of sequence transformers like BART in a linearization task where the correct order of words is crucial. To test the BART's performance in this context, we use the partial tree linearization task, a more straightforward version of the fully formed tree linearization task. In this task, the input is a sentence with some word orders already established, and the goal is to determine the optimal order for all words. We compared BART to other highly effective generative models, including T5 and T0, on this task and found that it performs significantly worse than these models, despite being a more challenging version of the task. To improve BART's performance, we developed a method that fine-tunes the model to rewrite sentences with altered word orders and found that this approach significantly enhanced the model's performance. Nonetheless, BART continued to underperform in comparison to T5 and T0 even with this optimization. To further gauge the model's capabilities, we conducted an additional experiment that involved changing the word order of a subset of words in a sentence and attempting to identify the original order; surprisingly, BART exhibited a marked decline in performance in this task. We also explored various applications of the model in rewriting sentences with altered word orders and found that it struggled with these tasks despite being relatively successful in predicting the actual word orders from linearized trees. Our research reveals that sequence transformers like BART are not as effective in the word ordering linearization task, especially in tasks that require the modification of existing word orders, and also highlights the potential limitations of these models in processing syntactic structure through self-supervised learning. We establish an explicit connection between Lusztig's quantum group $U_q(g)$ and the twisted version $U_{q^2}(g)$, and in the process, we construct an appropriate basis $\bar{\eta}$ for $U_q(g)$ using the Fock basis. This basis meets certain criteria, including being compatible with the action of the braid group via $\sigma$ and the Dynkin automorphism $\theta$, and it enables us to define a scalar product on $U_q(g)$. Additionally, we demonstrate that the duals $U^*_{q^2}(g)$ and $U_{q^2}(g)^*$ are equivalent to $U_{q^2}(\theta(g))$ and $U_{q^2}(\theta(g))^{op}$, respectively. Moreover, we derive explicit formulas for the matrix elements of representation operators in the basis $\bar{\eta}$. Given a representation $\rho$ of $U_q(g)$, we define a corresponding twisted representation $\rho^{(2)}$ of $U_{q^2}(g)$, and we prove that the matrix elements of $\rho$ can be expressed in terms of those of $\rho^{(2)}$ using $q$-exponential functions. We introduce a novel concept of erasure correction codes that can be represented using tensor networks. These codes must follow a specific structure, where only one type of tensor is used, and we've established that these networks effectively achieve the maximum entropy rate when correcting random erasure distortions. As a result, we can conclude that any single-tensor network that can correct for erasures necessarily operates at capacity when the tensor network is subjected to uniform erasure noise. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these codes can be constructed using approximate quantum entanglement clipping, leading to an access scheme that can be utilized for correcting uniform lossy compression. Additionally, we examine the scenario where the tensor network is allowed to operate at less than maximum entropy rate, and in doing so, we obtain an expression for its achievable rate. Utilizing this expression as an example, we show that it is possible to develop an erasure correction code from an arbitrary single-tensor network that is capable of achieving the maximum entropy rate with corrected distortions. Additionally, we explore the case where the tensor network is allowed to operate at less than maximum entropy rate and derive the applicable rate region. Moreover, we examine construction methods for these codes using qubit-clipping, approximate quantum entanglement clipping, and coherent state-clipping, leading to corresponding access schemes. Lastly, we establish an upper bound for the average qubit-cloning cost required to recover the original qubit based on its clipped version. This recovery qubit-cloning cost is found to be directly related to the conditional von Neumann entropy of the clipped qubit conditional to its classical label. Moreover, we find that it satisfies an important inequality that arises from considering a scenario of uniform lossy compression, and in doing so, we obtain this inequality's relevant expression. Finally, we demonstrate that this inequality's value can be interpreted as the average qubit-cloning cost required to recover the original qubit from its compressed form. Deepfolding network's success in modeling 3D objects from point clouds relies on a precise alignment of local features. To prevent distortions due to unsymmetric coordinate transformations, we propose the Point Cloud Pyramid (PCP) framework, which leverages a multi-scale, self-aligned structure to facilitate feature inference across different scales. PCP frames facilitate the explicit alignment of local features, thereby imposing an inconsistency penalty to counter twisting transformations and ensure that the assigned labels are consistent across the network. We achieve this consistency by introducing a twisting loss function that measures the deviation of coordinate transformations from the symmetric group, effectively ensuring the generalization against unsymmetric coordinate transformations. We apply the PCP framework to various 3D object recognition tasks and achieve the best results on SHREC datasets for both medial axis trees and 3D models, demonstrating its robustness against unsymmetric coordinate transformations. In addition, PCP outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on ModelNet40 and the Medial Axis Dataset. We also introduce a novel evaluation method, the twisting accuracy of a model is determined by the proportion of coordinate transformations that result in an accurate prediction, demonstrating PCP's generalization against twisting transformations. We hope this evaluation method can be widely used in point cloud recognition tasks. We open-source the PCP framework at https://github.com/zwang84/PCP_framework. Our analysis takes the core idea that reduced network models can be used to assess stability in complex networks, and applies this concept to multilayer networks by focusing on a specific approach - the adiabatic perturbation method. We simplify the Adiabatic Perturbation Approach by minimizing the impact of the perturbation's progression speed, which allows us to analyze the stability of all states in multilayer networks by examining a single condition. We then establish a direct relationship between this stability condition and the time it takes for a state to change, enabling us to classify all possible state dynamics in multilayer networks, including single-layer networks as a special case. We demonstrate the applicability and usefulness of this simplified approach by applying it to specific multilayer network scenarios, including a target-tracking system and a financial network example. We also compare our simplified approach to the original Adiabatic Perturbation Approach by examining its limits and selecting the most stable states shared by both methods. We argue that the adiabatic condition can be too stringent in some situations and propose an additional criterion based on the time it takes for a state to change, which provides a more dynamic perspective on network stability. Testing environments are vital for ensuring software quality, but the manual process of providing input and comparing output can be time-consuming and pricey, even for automated testing. To accelerate and automate testing, this research presents TestStepper, a testing framework that employs an automated algorithm to identify and fix errors in code by replicating the manual process of close scrutiny of input and output. Following an in-depth examination of common pitfalls that lead to program errors, the researchers developed an automated procedure to determine the cause of an error and provide corresponding fixes. To validate the effectiveness and efficiency of TestStepper, the researchers created a vast set of testing scenarios consisting of fifteen distinct use cases across three programs with known issues, and the results showed that TestStepper accurately detected the source of the errors and offered suitable solutions in almost all cases. In contrast to Strsteper, a similar algorithm used in Stepper that requires significant manual input, TestStepper necessitates substantially less code changes and generates more precise fix predictions. Moreover, the researchers discovered that TestStepper is highly efficient, requiring significantly less time to resolve each error than Stepper. Moreover, the testing framework includes various features such as input and output examination, close scrutiny of intermediate program values, and repair strategies that address different types of errors, including syntax errors, logical errors, and partial output errors. To facilitate widespread adoption of TestStepper, the researchers open-source the framework and make it available for public use. We investigate the long-term behavior of right-angled Artin groups within infinitely branching trees. These groups display a mixture of properties associated with both surface groups and fully irreducible Coxeter groups. A key concept in this context is a separating subgraph, which we use to classify and study specific aspects of these groups. Along with examining their action on an infinite tree, we also explore actions on infinite graphs characterized by having no edges leading to fixed points, and demonstrate that these actions result in a free minimal action. Furthermore, we establish that these groups are strongly faithful against polynomial in their generating set size, a distinction we observe among analogous groups associated with root systems. Additionally, we provide an examination of their cut-point geometry and prove that these groups have a property we call "strong connectivity". Lastly, we outline possible connections to the study of Coxeter groups and surface groups within infinitely branching trees. The underlying theory and examples also serve as a comprehensive survey of related topics. For policy learning using efficient value function estimates, selecting the optimal sample size for testing can be critical. This study examines how test sample size affects the policies learned using efficient value function estimates, specifically focusing on a case where the underlying policy is optimal and the learner has access to additional data to evaluate policies. Initially, a small test sample size may yield policies close to the optimal policy due to the efficient value function estimate's tendency to converge rapidly to the optimal value function. However, as the test sample size increases, the learned policy may diverge from the optimal policy, taking the following path: it starts near the optimal policy, then oscillates due to the multiple optimal policies issue, and finally converges to the optimal policy again. This research demonstrates that under certain conditions, if the test sample size is sufficiently large, the learned policy will ultimately converge to the optimal policy with the highest value, rather than one of the optimal policies with lower values. Furthermore, we establish that the threshold for the sufficient large test sample size is directly proportional to the square of the dimension of the state-action space. This study also provides a test sample size, which is larger but more conservative than the sufficient large threshold, to serve as a practical guideline for policy learning tasks. This test sample size is found to be minimal for achieving the maximum value among the optimal policies in a specific example. The study uses a linear MDP with multiple optimal policies to illustrate the impact of test sample size on policy learning using efficient value function estimates, offering insights that can be applied to non-linear MDP cases. The research concludes by highlighting the limitations of the current study and suggesting potential future work, such as exploring policy learning using efficient value function estimates in non-linear MDP scenarios with multiple optimal policies. The algorithmic framework examined in this study can be used as a baseline for comparing the performance of other policy learning algorithms in dynamic systems with multiple optimal policies. Our research analyzed the transverse momentum distributions of charged hadrons, pions, kaons, and protons from ALICE collisions at the LHC, specifically looking at their connections to elliptic flow. To facilitate this investigation, adjustments were made to the data to eliminate effects of particle selection and elliptic flow, allowing for direct comparison among the various particle types. These comparisons held true for both low and high transverse momenta levels, and resulted in the observed momentum distributions exhibiting little difference, conforming to Kalitzke's hypothesis. Furthermore, modified power-law distributions provided the best fit for the data, using $p_{\rm T}$ normalizations that matched observed production ratios, and incorporating slight deviations for kaons. Over and above this, the research also examined the same distributions within limited transverse momentum ranges, finding them to be relatively smooth, with no noticeable patterns related to collision centrality. The validity of these findings was further confirmed by alternative methods of data analysis. The discovered consistency with Kalitzke's hypothesis holds significant importance, given its implication that charged hadron momentum distributions are inherently unaffected by collision density, making them more uniform across different collision environments. The absence of variance in the distributions also suggests that the main driving force behind hadron production is rather hadron conformation than hadron collision frequency. The comprehensive nature of this research is further highlighted by the fact that results were obtained without relying on collision model assumptions. Ongoing puzzles in hadron physics, particularly hadron formation mechanisms, remain area for future research. The discovered patterns also need to be applied to hadron production in lower energy collisions. A new multiple-time-step integration algorithm (MTSA) has been developed to enhance the computational speed of particle-laden flow simulations by utilizing a hybrid combination of numerical integration methods for both fluid and particle movements. Unlike conventional time-stepping strategies, this hybrid approach permits variable time steps for particles relative to the fluid, specifically allowing larger time steps for particles while maintaining accuracy in particle interactions with the fluid. This change prevents particle time steps from being limited by fluid time steps, thus fully leveraging the potential of different time step optimization techniques for both particles and fluid. We have tested this hybrid algorithm by integrating it with the Immersed Interface Method (IIM) and evaluated its performance under different time step ratios. Our results show that this hybrid approach achieves significant computational speedups of up to ten times for a given problem, demonstrating the substantial benefits of variable time stepping in particle-laden flow simulations. Furthermore, this new algorithm has been found to be accurate, stable, and robust, and it is particularly effective in modeling flows with suspended particles for which large time steps are necessary, such as sediment transport under waves. We believe that this hybrid algorithm presents a valuable solution for the efficient simulation of various flows featuring particles with different time scales, including but not limited to sediment transport under waves. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ghaeman/MTSA. Our study suggests that variable time stepping can be a powerful tool for enhancing the efficiency of particle-laden flow simulations, and it is anticipated to contribute to the development of future highly efficient and highly resolved simulation techniques. To enhance the efficiency of robotic hopping on soft ground, robots must accurately follow desired trajectories. Unfortunately, the physical interactions between a robot and a deformable surface complicate the system's dynamics, making it difficult to track intended paths. This study introduces a new control method, known as the ``matching potential approach,'' that simplifies the representation of feedback control for robotic hopping on a soft surface. This approach succeeds in tracking desired trajectories for a hypothetical idealized robot in mid-air and can be applied to improve the performance of robotic hopping on a soft ground by adjusting the foot's landing location. As a result, the robot is able to track its desired trajectory with reduced energy expenditure. A novel method for computing meson charge radii in perturbation theory has been developed, where the use of the heavy light meson field transformation matrix, generated by varying the charge, enables the determination of charge radii through a straightforward differential calculation of the mass operator. This approach has been successfully tested in the heavy light meson model with a Gaussian form factor and has been used to compute the charge radii of mesons made of heavy quarks (b, c, d, s, t) and different light quarks (u, d, s) using the leading order perturbation theory and the value of the fine structure constant from quantum electrodynamics. The calculated charge radii agree with previously calculated values and provide a basis for further extensions to next-to-leading order. The paper also presents predictions for meson charge radii with quark masses obtained from the $m_{\tau}$ decay and the $[\bar{u}\bar{d}]\bar{s}$ meson mass scale. The calculated charge radii are given with an estimated precision of $10\%$. The method introduced here is a generalizable strategy for computing distinguishable properties in perturbation theory. The code used to calculate the charge radii is now publicly available and can be utilized to calculate other observable quantities. The code is developed using C++ and FeynPlus, with the use of the quantum chromodynamics framework based on the Feynman diagram technique. The charge radii of mesons made of heavy quarks can be distinguished by their energy levels when in a strong magnetic field, as predicted in the paper. The relationship between the charge radius and energy level spacing is calculated and the code is capable of providing this information. The code can be utilized in studies of heavy meson physics in a strong magnetic field. The analysis of complex information networks, particularly those comprising textual data, has given rise to multiple probabilistic models, including the Hierarchical Document Topic Model. This model assigns a topic hierarchy to textual networks, providing a compact representation that facilitates various tasks, and offers several advantages over traditional statistical methods for network analysis. However, due to its computational intensity, the model has primarily been applied to small-scale networks. In response to these limitations, we have developed a novel Variational Hierarchical Document Topic Model, which provides an efficient approximation by dividing large networks into sub-networks, and facilitates the estimation of model parameters using convex conjugate functions. This result allows us to leverage existing efficient algorithms for topic models. We have further developed a batch inference method to enhance the model's performance by integrating the results from sub-networks. We have tested and validated our model across multiple datasets to demonstrate its superior performance and practical applicability to large-scale textual networks. This includes a real-life application to a healthcare dataset containing 33,324 documents. Our code is available at https://github.com/VITA-USTC/VHDTM. Quantum annealing's effectiveness relies on its ability to navigate the complex landscape of energy gaps between the initial and final states. The annealing schedule's design plays a crucial role in overcoming this challenge. To optimize protocols, it is essential to investigate the annealing gap's dynamics and its dependence on the quantum flux's rate. In this research, a generic quantum annealing model was utilized to examine the annealing gap's behavior in both homogeneous and disordered conditions. Our findings reveal that the gap width varies non-linearly with the quantum flux's rate, exhibiting distinct behaviors in homogeneous and disordered environments. Its width reaches a minimum before increasing in both cases. Our approach also enables the evaluation of the optimal schedule, leading to a gap width of nearly zero. This condition is found to correspond to a threshold of non-vanishing quantum overlap in the average, providing a key metric for assessing optimized protocols. Our results demonstrate that the average quantum overlap can serve as a crucial indicator for evaluating and optimizing quantum annealing protocols. To demonstrate the applicability of this finding, we generate an optimized schedule for the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model, successfully reducing the required annealing time by a factor of eight in both homogeneous and disordered conditions. Our research insights can be utilized in experimental implementation, having been tested with real-time quantum annealing hardware on up to 54 qubits. Furthermore, our approach is versatile and can be adapted to other quantum processing units (QPUs), enabling the evaluation and optimization of annealing protocols on existing hardware, leading to better resource utilization and more successful executions. Our research findings are relevant to the development of future quantum annealers, informing the design of better machines that can successfully execute various problems, including those defined by classical neural networks. One of the key advantages of using quantum systems as instruments for measuring physical parameters is their enhanced precision, resulting from the principles of uncertainty as expressed in the quantum covariance matrix. The compass state, with its precise spatial symmetry, exhibits considerable variance, making it an effective quantity for damping ratio measurement. Nonetheless, variations in the state's number, arising from both initial conditions and continuous number flow, compromise its precision by introducing an error. This study delves into the implications of this number variance on the compass state's ability to measure damping ratios in both closed and open systems. In the case of a closed system, the ensemble average of the number has a negligible impact on the precision, whereas an linear relationship exists between this average and the desired precision in an open system. Additionally, this study compares the compass state with another efficient instrument, the Yurtsever state, finding that the latter exhibits a 23.08% greater variance in number that could compromise its metrological performance. Nonetheless, both states benefit from minimal variations in the average number. This study ultimately highlights the importance of controlling the compass state's number variance to maximize its practical application in measurement damping ratios. Furthermore, suitable preparation conditions are proposed to minimize the ensemble average of the compass state's number, ensuring its optimal performance in measurement of damping ratios in both closed and open systems. This approach is anticipated to enhance the scalability and efficiency of quantum metrology systems. This research could serve as a foundation for exploring the dynamics of other quantum systems with extensive symmetry, with respect to their scalability in measurement of physical parameters. A theoretical examination of the cooling efficiency in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks is conducted through the study of dust particle interactions, specifically with regard to grain scales equivalent to several kilometers. The study evaluates the impact of low-density dust particles on the behavior of cool gas in the outer regions of these disks. Using a comprehensive model that takes into account the effects of turbulence, a study of dust particle interactions reveals that the cooling efficiency of the gas is significantly hindered by the presence of dense dust particles, especially in areas far from the central star. In these distant areas, the friction generated by the movement of particles relative to each other and their dissolution into the surrounding gas causes a marked decrease in cooling efficiency, a phenomenon exacerbated by the presence of large dust particles and, to a lesser extent, pebbles. This development could result in a greater understanding of the characteristics of far-reaching protoplanetary disks, particularly those lacking massive dust storms that would disrupt the behavior of dense dust particles, and may also influence the formation of massive planets within these disks. Furthermore, this effect might aid in explaining the limited extent of some protoplanetary disks despite the presence of newly formed stellar masses. The presence of dense dust particles in the midplanes of these disks could also lead to the formation of pressure gradients that drive the movement of pebbles and particles towards the central star, a phenomenon that may be observable in future high-resolution, high-sensitivity millimeter-wave observations. The presence of dense dust particles could potentially influence the formation of massive planets and their eventual migration to their current positions, and may also impact the availability of solid material for planet formation in these disks, with implications for the formation of Earth-like planets. The study's findings suggest that the behavior of dust particles in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks is a complex phenomenon that is significantly affected by their own density, a factor that must be considered in the interpretation of future observations. The examination also highlights the importance of accurately simulating the effects of particle interactions on the behavior of cool gas in these disks, and could aid in the development of more reliable models for predicting the outcomes of planet formation in these environments. The study's results are set to be tested through observations of disks surrounding T Tauri and young solar analogs using the VLA and ALMA telescopes, with the aim of verifying the predicted effects of dust particle interactions on the behavior of cool gas in these disks. We establish key theorems for solitons characterized by scaling, exponential growth, potential growth, and shrinking volume, and these results can be viewed as extensions to some previous results established by Chen and Li. Additionally, we provide some specific examples to demonstrate the applicability and the precision of these theorems. Furthermore, we discover that all potential-growing solitons are categorized into a specific type of exponential-growing solitons, and this discovery can be viewed as a refinement of some previous classifying results obtained by Wei and Xu. Moreover, we achieve some specific estimates related to the harmonic function and the potential function, which can be viewed as an extension to some results obtained by Li and Wang when considering a harmonic function and a potential function on a compact manifold with a specific scaling property and volume-growing property. Recent research on neural networks has identified vulnerabilities to embedded "backdoors," which misinterpret specific input patterns. However, implementing dynamic backdoor attacks on neural networks has proven difficult, especially in classification tasks with multiple categories. The typical solution involves creating a large disparity between the labels for certain inputs and others, which can lead to flawed conclusions when compared to static backdoor attacks. In this research, we successfully implemented dynamic backdoor attacks on neural networks in various classification projects, demonstrating that the phenomenon of embedded vulnerabilities is often misinterpreted and inaccurately attributed to "cognitive noise." We discovered that the mechanism of dynamic backdoor attacks is inherently linked to the method of class labeling, which can be exploited to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanics of neural networks and their classification projects. We also developed two novel approaches to creating dynamic backdoor attacks and investigated the effectiveness of several countermeasure strategies. Our research provides a fresh perspective on the phenomenon of embedded vulnerabilities and offers a more precise definition of dynamic backdoor attacks. We have made our code available publicly for further research purposes. We are certain that our discoveries will serve as a foundation for future studies on neural network security and countermeasures. Our research findings have been published in a paper that we recently presented at the 39th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML). We plan to present additional research associated with this project at the 30th Audiovisual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS) and the 2024 Audiovisual Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR). We are excited to collaborate with interested researchers and organizations on this project, as evidenced by our current research partnership with Dr. Tinglin Li from the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China. We are open to exploring research opportunities and possible collaboration ideas with universities and technology companies worldwide. We are particularly interested in collaborating with companies that specialize in artificial intelligence security, as we believe that our research can significantly contribute to the development of secure neural networks. We are confident that our discovery of the mechanism underlying dynamic backdoor attacks will enable the creation of more effective countermeasures and secure neural networks, which can be applied to various classification projects, including those related to medical diagnosis, facial recognition, and object classification. We are excited about the possibility of applying our research to real-world problems and contributing to the advancement of artificial intelligence security in general. We are also exploring opportunities to develop practical solutions based on our research, which can be utilized by industry leaders and companies in the artificial intelligence sector. We are committed to making our code publicly available

A random walk approach is presented as a scalable solution to reduce communication expenses, where a team of agents navigate a collaborative information exchange network, learning a target function by combining their individual data sets. The model's information structure ensures that each agent only needs to send a random walk distance worth of data to the next agent, significantly reducing overall communication costs. It is shown that this random walk model converges to the desired function with rates comparable to those of centralized learning, despite significant communication savings. This conclusion is supported by an explicit algorithm and corresponding convergence rate estimates, revealing that the random walk method facilitates efficient communication by reducing the number of messages required for convergence. This advantage holds even in comparison to other distributed learning methods that utilize central controllers, such as federated learning and distributed gradient descent. For prison-based mental health programs, there is particularly little evidence available.  A study was conducted to examine the results of a 12-session cognitive-behavioral therapy program for reducing violent and general criminal behavior among inmates with mental health issues.  The study compared outcomes for a group of prisoners who participated in the program to a group who did not.  Both groups were followed for three years after their release from prison.  The data showed that prisoners who received the therapy had lower rates of violent and general crimes than those who did not, with a particular reduction in violent crimes among African Americans.  The study also found that the therapy had a positive effect on reducing crimes for prisoners with schizophrenia, but not for those with bipolar disorder or major depressive disorder.  The results of the study suggest that the therapy can be an valuable tool in reducing crimes and improving public safety.  The study also highlights the need for more effective methods of referring prisoners to the therapy program and for more research on prison-based mental health programs.  The study's limitations are discussed along with its advantages, and it is concluded that random controlled trials are necessary to confirm the findings.  The study's results are significant because they demonstrate the positive impact of a relatively short-term program on long-term outcomes for a high-risk population.  The results also have implications for the development of future prison-based mental health programs and suggest that cognitive-behavioral therapy can be an effective approach to reducing crimes among inmates with mental health issues.  The most effective programs will depend on factors such as crime type and prisoner ethnicity, and it is suggested that mental health programs are not one-size-fits-all.  The study's findings also highlight the need for prison-based mental health programs to be part of a broader approach to addressing the needs of prisoners with mental health issues, including their physical health needs and their needs for employment, education, and housing on release from prison.  The most cost-effective way to reduce crimes among prisoners with mental health issues is by providing them with effective treatment while they are still in prison.  The study shows that the therapy program pays for itself and generates significant cost savings for the community. A common challenge faced in semi-supervised medical image segmentation arises from labeled data being scarce yet labeled images being noisy. To address this issue, a novel, fully convolutional, and loosely connected network is proposed to tackle regularized image segmentation. In this framework, a handful of manually labeled images are used to train a base model, which is then applied to a vast amount of labeled and unlabeled data to produce a probability distribution between different classes, achieving a balance between consistency regularization and confidence regularization. Current evaluations typically rely on annotated final grades, yet this approach overlooks vital information, such as the content of course work, which has implicit labeling. Inspired by implicit labeling techniques, we propose a novel approach, deep knowledge tracing assessment, that utilizes unsupervised learning to leverage course content and assign numerical values to implicit labels. We further develop a novel unsupervised knowledge tracing assessment model and test it on multiple datasets to demonstrate its effectiveness. Our approach provides a meaningful, data-efficient solution to evaluating deep learning knowledge tracing, even with limited annotations. With the veriT system now part of the standard tools for checking theorem validity, and many theorem provers generating the veriT format for checking validity, this paper updates the documentation on this format which now supports not just validity checking but also checking consistency of first-order theories. Moreover, the veriT format is now the standard input format for the Mathieu veriT tool, which won the award for best system at the 2011 and 2013 International Joint Conferences on Mathematical and Symbolic Dynamics. This updated documentation is intended for developers of the veriT system and other tools that generate the veriT format. The proof and implementation guidelines described in this paper are aimed specifically at developers of the veriT system and other tools that generate the veriT format, which is now the standard input format for the Mathieu veriT tool, and thus may also be of interest to a broader audience of developers of other satisfiability solvers that generate proofs. In the context of resource allocation among players with conflicting interests, where each player's value for a specific item follows a uniform distribution, we investigate two prominent schemes: the Round-Robin mechanism and the cut-and-choose algorithm. The Round-Robin mechanism allocates items to players in a cyclic order, whereas the cut-and-choose algorithm assigns an item to a player selected randomly within a specific range. Both schemes are relatively unfair, as they prioritize one player over others for each item allocation. Our analysis compares these schemes to each other and other fair allocation methods, such as the proportional mechanism, which prioritizes no player over others. Our main findings include: (1) both the Round-Robin and the cut-and-choose algorithm schemes are at least twice as unfair as the proportional mechanism, which is relatively fair, (2) the Round-Robin mechanism is significantly fairer than the cut-and-choose algorithm scheme, (3) the former is at least five times as unfair as the latter, (4) both schemes fail to meet the 1/n fair guarantee even for two players, (5) the former meets the 1/3 fair guarantee for n=4 or more players, and (6) the latter falls short of the 2/3 fair guarantee for n=3 or more players. Offline learning for offline multiple agent systems involves using historical data without self-modifying the environment. A significant challenge in this context is agents sharing similar learning paths, which slows down learning for new agents. The Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) framework addresses this issue by separating public and private data, and using the former to build a general learning trajectory. This general trajectory can be used to accelerate offline learning for new agents sharing similar trajectories with historical agents. Our approach enhances learning efficiency for multiple agent systems by 23% to 50% in offline settings. Furthermore, the SIT framework enables efficient online learning by reducing the initial data phase by 30% to 60%. To achieve this, we developed a method to measure the distance between learning trajectories and applied it to two different datasets with impressive results. Our approach and the SIT framework have utility beyond offline learning, including reinforcement learning in online, dynamic environments. This is especially pertinent in scenarios requiring fast adaptation to new situations. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghyi/SIT-FRL. Moreover, the SIT-FRL model has been used in subsequent work that has an associated paper available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.02599. Both codes and the associated paper can be found at https://yichengli.github.io/projects/SIT-FRL/. Our approach and associated data are applicable to various industries, including but not limited to online shopping, smart energy management, and self-driving technology. Our work has been mentioned in relevant sections of the accompanying paper available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.02599. We investigate the connection between single-particle entanglement, nonlocal effects, and quantum steering in three-qubit Heisenberg XY and XXZ chains, using the concurrence metric. Our analysis indicates that the average single-particle entanglement serves as a key factor in the nonlocal correlation and quantum steering observed in these molecular systems. Furthermore, a significant relationship between the average single-particle entanglement and molecular shape parameter $d$ exhibits linearity for both Heisenberg XY and XXZ chains. These findings provide insight into the origin of nonlocal effects and quantum steering in these qubit arrays, offering the potential for reliable evaluation of these features without directly numerating the entanglement among individual qubits. Our results also demonstrate that the distinction between entangled and separable qubit arrangements can be determined by the linear correlation between the average single-particle entanglement and $d$. This discovery is demonstrated through numerical simulations of both theoretical models and experimental data, with potential applications in superconducting qubits. Despite the focus on three-qubit chains in this analysis, our research also reveals all-qubit chain dynamics are responsible for nonlocal effects and quantum steering, with the relevant physics scalably extrapolating to larger qubit arrays.
